**Daggerfall Online now opens on a launcher**: the patch notes on the left, your options on the right, and Play at the bottom. Nothing starts until you press Play.

**New title: Penitent**, in gold fading into sky blue, with a glyph of a blue sword inside a gold diamond. It's Diggleborf's: press it on the account card to wear it.
valenvalarys is now a Disciple.
Everyone online is disconnected once when this update goes live, and reconnects.

**An out-of-date game can no longer go online.** A copy of the game from before online characters arrived could still join, play and trade, but only as an offline character, and nothing it did online could ever come into the realm. It now says "this game is out of date - update it to play online" and stays offline until you update.
The macOS app and the portable Windows app do not update themselves: download the newest build from the website to play online.

If you played a character online on an older version of the game after the realm opened, and Bring online now refuses it, ask the developers on the Discord. They can let that one character in, once, through customs like any other (its loans called in and its gold capped).

**Bring online keeps every house, ship and piece of furniture.** Customs used to leave houses and ships behind (with the furniture you bought for them) when everything you owned came to more than your level's allowance. Now they always come with the character.
The realm's bank **won't buy back** a house or ship that came through customs, and furniture that came with it gives no gold back when you take it out. You keep them to live in and use.

If a character you brought online shows **Never saved**, its first save didn't land. Its tile now says **Undo bringing in**. It gives back everything that came with it: your online home, its furniture, your guild place, and the character's one trip through customs. Or press **Bring online** on it again to finish.
Deleting one no longer takes its home and furniture with it.

The Overworld's controls are one compact block in the bottom-right corner, so the rest of the screen stays free. From top to bottom: where you are, your journey, the Path switch and Map, the filters, and Return.
It is always shown while you are in the Overworld. Standing still, the journey section says "Not travelling". Travelling, it shows the destination, time left, the time controls, Camp and Exit.
The trip line under your location also shows "Travelling at ×N" while you travel with the movement keys.
The block has no compass of its own. The HUD's compass at the top of the screen already shows the heading.
The movement hints moved into a tooltip on the block's top line.
On touch screens the block sits at the top right, clear of the touch buttons.
Starting a journey while standing in the Overworld no longer flashes the old travel bar at the top of the screen for a moment before it moves into the block.

While the Overworld is up, the notices on the right side stack upward from just above the block instead of being centred over it. On touch screens, where the block sits top-right, they start just below it.
A marker at the right edge under a notice fades while the notice is showing.
The **Path** switch is remembered between sessions.
**Roads** (default) prefers road travel. Clicking near a town travels to the town.
**Free** walks across country and still goes around mountains and across water the same way. Clicks near a town go to the exact spot. If there is no free route, it takes the roads and says so.
In either mode, once you are next to a town, or while holding Shift or Alt, every click goes to the exact spot.
A **Show** section with Towns, Distant, Dungeons, Enemies and Travellers. Each switch shows how many markers it holds, and the settings are remembered.
Enemies covers roaming bands, camps and raiders.
Always shown regardless of filters: your destination, anything chasing you, and your party.

Markers held at the top or bottom edge now sit right at the edge. They only step inward where a HUD piece is actually in the way: the compass at the top, the hotbar and bars at the bottom. Before, the tallest piece pushed every marker along that edge inward across the full width.
A marker that would appear behind the hotbar or compass is held at its edge instead of being hidden under it.

A marker in view whose location falls on the compass or the hotbar is drawn faint there, so the compass letters and the slots stay readable. It is still clickable and returns to full strength once the camera moves it clear.
Markers on the side edges keep clear of the block, and of the quick-slot area if shown.

Under Enhanced Plus, the Overworld's place plates, labels and distances use the Plus pixel face with its hard one-pixel shadow, matching the block, the hotbar and the player names. The classic Enhanced look is unchanged.
Near a roaming band (inside about 420 m) its lead monster's animated sprite fades in over the land, sized like your own sprite. It is fully visible inside about 240 m. Hiding Enemies hides these too.

Fast travel still slows as enemies get close, but it starts much later. The game used to guarantee 5 real seconds before you reach an enemy's sight range; it now guarantees 2 (`THREAT_WARN_S` in `systems/travelThreat.js`, one number to tune).
A rider at ×40 now starts slowing about 1.3 km before a band's sight range instead of about 3.2 km. On foot at ×40 it's about 280 m instead of 700 m.

"You see a dungeon ... metres to the ..." (said once when you enter the map pixel holding a generated dungeon) now stays up for 5 seconds at any travel speed.
Double-click a band or camp marker in the Overworld to be asked: "Attack the Zombie band (2)?", "Attack the Orc camp (4)?", "Attack the Lich?"
The question appears in the Overworld itself, over the map; the view stays up. Its Yes / No buttons are the block's own (the same as Roads / Free).
Enter or Y answers Yes, Escape or N answers No. Clicking the map dismisses it.

**Yes:** you travel straight toward them at full travel speed. That enemy no longer slows you down (a band's chase included; for a camp, every member). Any other enemy along the way still does. Meeting them starts the encounter as usual.
A single click on an enemy marker still walks to that spot, as before. Clicking anywhere else, or a town, cancels the attack.

In **Free** mode a journey no longer bends at pixel middles on the way (it used to go diagonally, then straight, and read as being pulled toward the road or a place first). The route is pulled taut: it goes straight to the spot wherever the way is clear, and only bends where water or mountains force it to.

**Add your own Daggerfall Unity texture mods.** Settings → Mods → *Replacement packs* has a new **Add texture mods** button. Pick one or more `.dfmod` files (DREAM 90s and mods like it); they are stored in this browser, listed with their title and version, and each has its own **Remove**.
world textures, flats, NPCs, commoners and monsters, with the mod's xml billboard sizes;
item icons and paperdoll pieces by dye and material, with helmet masks, placed by the mod's xml `<rect>`;
the paperdoll's backdrop, body and head;
talk-window portraits.
The bundle reader learned **BC7** (the format DREAM's paperdoll uses). A mod's bundle is read once when you add it; after that the game opens it only when one of its pictures is needed.
Not supported yet: mod scripts (DREAM's time-of-day backgrounds and dungeon-exit script), normal/height/emission maps, and terrain texture arrays.

**Every pack can come off.** *Remove music pack*, *Remove sound pack*, *Remove texture pack* and *Remove all texture mods* sit beside their Attach buttons once something is attached, each behind a confirm. Removing textures takes full effect the next time an area loads.

**Big HD packs (DREAM's full-resolution set).** A `.dfmod` is no longer read into memory whole: it is read piece by piece from where it is stored, so a multi-gigabyte bundle opens in moments. The game never waits on a mod on its way in - a mod that still needs reading is read in the background - and no area waits more than 20 seconds for one. **Texture detail** (256 / 512 / 1024 / full, default 256) sets the largest size a mod picture is loaded at; HD packs above 512 can run out of memory. If a mod ever stops the game from starting, open the game with `?nomods` at the end of the address and remove it from the packs card.

Handheld-weapon frames from a texture mod now reach the first-person weapon.

**Out-of-memory fixes, round two.** Every attached mod used to get its own background worker, and each area sent all its picture requests at once - with ten-plus HD bundles that was ten-plus decoders running full-size pictures side by side. Now all mods share two workers, each decoding one picture at a time; a request nobody is waiting for any more (older than 15 seconds) is dropped instead of decoded. Mod pictures also have a memory budget (up to 1536 MB, less on smaller machines): past it, the rest of the session draws the classic art for new mod pictures instead of running out of memory.

**PERF-2D warning while talking to an NPC.** The talk window could leave a UI 2D run open across a tick, so a background pass (rain, sky, grass) that drew while the window was up landed inside it and logged the renderer's `PERF-2D` warning. The talk window now closes its own run at the end of every draw.
Weapon frames from any `.dfmod` (Weapon Widget, Diverse Weapons, texture mods) were drawn upside down - "held overhead". The bundle reader already answers pictures top-first; the extra flip is gone.

Diverse Weapons HD (Handhelds I/II, Inventory) is accepted: its crunched textures now decode, it is read as a texture mod, and its frames replace the built-in Diverse Weapons sprites. Weapon frames keep at least 512 px.

DREAM's ground: the terrain tile sets a texture mod ships (`302-TexArray` and the like) replace the classic ground tiles - only while such a mod is attached, and only as a whole set. Reload once after updating: the ground keeps the set it was first built with for the session, and older mod indexes are re-read in the background.

**HD paperdoll.** With a texture mod attached the paperdoll is drawn at 4x (440x736 instead of 110x184), so DREAM's paperdoll art keeps its detail instead of being squeezed to Daggerfall's size and blown back up. Classic layers are scaled up pixel for pixel exactly as before; clicks, item placement and the other players' dolls are unchanged. Without a texture mod the doll is drawn exactly as before.

**Improved Interior Lighting (ShortBeard 1.0.5).** Attach its `.dfmod` like the texture mods. While Enhanced Lighting is OFF it takes over the lighting indoors, as its scripts do: every room light warm orange with its intensity and range 10, flickering; a light on each fireplace; in dungeons the original lights replaced by one on every torch and brazier billboard; the torch in the mod's colour. With Enhanced Lighting ON nothing changes. Not carried over: the mod's shadows (the classic lighting has none), and the fireplace spotlight is a point light.

**Water tiles with DREAM's ground.** Town water, docks and puddles showed as brown mud under a blue sheen: the port finds a puddle's shape by the water tile's colours, which works for Daggerfall's palette art but not for DREAM's truecolour tiles. The shapes now come from the classic tiles and are laid over DREAM's.

**Test switch: the mod's shadows.** Add `?iil=shadows` to the address with Enhanced Lighting ON and the mod attached: the mod's lights then run on the Enhanced Lighting lane, which gives them shadows - soft light shadows and NPC / enemy billboard shadows. Without the switch the rule above holds (the mod only replaces classic lighting).

**Water at night (Gothway Garden).** The water was lit by a torch or a lamp as if it were ground: the water tile's blue ripples times a warm flame read as a field of brown mud with blue at its edges. Water now takes a quarter of that light diffusely and shows each light as a moving highlight on the waves instead. Same with or without DREAM.

**Modded lighting switch.** Features > Sight has a new row, *Modded lighting (Improved Interior Lighting)*: Off / On (default) / With shadows. It only does anything with the mod's `.dfmod` attached, and it takes effect at once. With shadows gives the mod its own shadows - lamps, people and monsters cast soft shadows indoors and in dungeons - in Daggerfall's classic look, with Enhanced lighting OFF: the port's shadow maps under the classic shading (no tonemap, no bloom, no highlights). Outdoors stays classic. With Enhanced lighting on, Enhanced lighting is in charge as before.

**Attach lighting mod.** Settings > Mods > Replacement packs has its own *Lighting mod* section: an **Attach lighting mod** button (it accepts only Improved Interior Lighting - the original or BlazeBlue32's fixed 1.1.1 - and says so if you pick something else), the attached mod with its Remove, and a pointer to Features > Sight > Modded lighting. It is no longer listed among the texture mods.

Crossing the water works with Iliac Puddle No More on (the default): your boat goes into the sea and sails. It never left the shore - the journey stopped with "Your boat has run aground.", or walked on without it.

Boats sail on the open sea. With Iliac Puddle No More on (the default), every boat put in the sea - a deed's beside its port, a rowboat from its parts - was taken for run aground: it would not row, and raising its sail said "Unable to raise sail. Boat is obstructed." Boats you have already placed sail from where they are.
Spawned dungeons (normal and Elite) no longer appear on beaches or out in the sea. Before, a dungeon could stand on a square of sand jutting into the water off a coast.
A spawned dungeon now only appears where its ground is dry land, above the beach line. Coastal land well above the water still gets dungeons.
The Overworld no longer marks a far spawned dungeon at the water's edge that was never really there.
Every player still sees the same dungeons in the same places. Pixels that used to hold a shoreline spawn are now empty land (or sea) for everyone.

**Your armour at a glance.** Each body part's armour shows on its panel of the worn map, the same numbers the classic paper doll shows. At the figure's head, one **Armour** figure: the armour a blow meets on average, with each part weighed by how often blows land there. Hover it for the weights.

**Compare before you wear.** Hover over or click a piece in your pack and its card says what it would replace. It then shows the piece's damage against the weapon it replaces, the overall figure, and each body part it changes, now → after, with the difference in green (better) or red (worse). What the card says is what wearing it does.
An unidentified piece keeps its enchantments to itself until it is identified.

**The map has a key.** At the lower left of The Bay are the classic map's four filters: Dungeons, Temples, Homes and Towns. Click one to hide or show those places. The classic map uses the same switches, and your save keeps them. Beside each is the mark of every kind of place it covers.

**Places wear their classic colours**, inked into the parchment: dungeons orange, graveyards red, and the rest as the classic map dots them. Keeps and ruins share the dungeon's orange, so they are never mistaken for a graveyard.
Zoomed all the way out, the map still shows cities only, and the key greys out the rest.

**First-person journeys can follow the roads.** Travel Options' tile in the Features menu has a new switch, **First Person Travel Follows Roads** (off to start). With it and First Person Travel both on, a journey you pick on the travel map takes the Overworld's route, onto the road and round the mountains, walked in first person.
A place the roads cannot reach is refused, with the reason, instead of being walked to in a straight line.

The **Stores page** (on the Enhanced pause menu) has a **Forge** section. Stand inside a **Weaponsmith's** or an **Armorer's** (50 gold a smelt) or your own home with a **Forge** station, and smelt from your Stores:
two of a raw metal or ore make one **ingot** (Iron, Silver, Moonstone, Dwarven, Mithril, Adamantium, Ebony, Orichalcum);
one Copper and one Tin make **Brass**;
one Iron Ingot and one **Charcoal** make **Steel** (Charcoal comes with Logging, later).
Up to 100 at a time. Smelting trains **Smithing**.
In a home, a placed piece can be made a **Forge** for 50,000 gold, like the other crafting stations - offered only online, while the professions are open to you, on the Enhanced interface.

Withdrawn metals and gems are Daggerfall's own items. The new ores, the ingots and the stone are new items drawn with Daggerfall's own pictures; the ores and ingots are coloured by their metal the way Daggerfall colours an Ebony blade.
**Prospector** (rank 50): surface veins within 200 m show on the compass, and gems come a little more often.
**Deep Delver** (rank 50): dungeon veins give half as much again.
**Stonebreaker** (rank 100): quarrying always gives Cut Stone.
**Motherlode Sense** (rank 100) is shown but cannot be chosen yet - it comes with the Motherlodes.
Court writs now ask for metal and stone as well as herbs.
Escape now ends a gathering act in a dungeon too.
A harvest's message could appear twice when the server was slow; it now appears once.
Selling Marks at a slow bank can no longer pay you twice.
If a sale's reply is lost, your Marks are no longer lost when you sign out. The sale waits for your account and pays when it completes.
One character's pending sale no longer blocks selling for your other characters.
When a guild disbands, or its last member leaves, any Marks in its treasury go to the guildmaster. Before, leaving could destroy them.
Closing an Oblivion Gate can no longer record the gate without paying its Marks.
The bank's "counting" box gives up after 15 seconds instead of trapping you.
"Sold today" updates as you sell.
"Ask to join" and letter answers now open your letters. Before, the board closed and nothing opened.
Brand-new or muted accounts can no longer hide notes by reporting them.
A note hidden by reports stays visible to its author, who can take it down.
A recruitment note stops recruiting if its author leaves the guild or can no longer invite.
A note you are writing survives closing the board.
Double-clicking Report or Take down no longer sends it twice.
You can't take a bounty your party has already cleared today, and a clear only pays party members who took it first.
Giving up a bounty and taking it again keeps your kills. It no longer summons a fresh pack.
A party now gets one pack per hunt, whoever arrives first, and shares its kill count.
Shared bounties pay rewards at your own level.
A quickload inside a dungeon no longer doubles a bounty pack.
A reward notice is never lost behind another window or a death.
You lose exactly what the death screen shows. A resurrection by a party member costs nothing.
Several tool uses in a row now wait their full time (they were capped at about a minute).
Bonus finds and rewards held behind a wait survive a reload.
Escape leaves a search again, and Enter works on buttons in the new windows.
**Online only.** Marks open in stages. Developers get them first, then everyone. When your account has them, you'll see a **Marks** line on your account card.
**Marks** are the online world's own currency, kept by the account service. Nothing on your computer can make them, so they're worth the same for everyone.
**Earn them by closing Oblivion Gates.** Each gate counted on your record strikes **50 Marks** to your account, up to two gates a day. Your chat says how many you got.

**Sell them at any Bank of the Empire.** Open the Bank and use **Sell Marks**. The Bank pays **8 gold a Mark**, up to 300 Marks a day. The gold goes into your account at that bank, so it never weighs you down. You can't buy Marks with gold.

Online, a town's **rumour boards** (every board that is not a Bounty Board) now open the **Notice Board**: a corkboard of pinned notes in the Enhanced Plus style.

It shows, in order: the town's own news (the same words the classic board gives), a line pointing to the town's Bounty Board if it has one, **the server's notices** under a red seal (while an Oblivion Gate stands, and announcements from the developers), then **players' notes**, newest first.
A board belongs to its **town**: every rumour board in a town shows the same notes.
When a town's board has notes or server notices you have not read yet, **"N new"** floats over it as you approach.
Registered players can **pin a note**: a subject and up to 800 characters, standing for **1, 3 or 7 days**. You can have **3 notes up** at a time, across every board.

**Ask to join the party** or **Ask to join the guild**: the reader gets a letter to you, already addressed and begun, and you invite them as usual.
**Challenge to a duel**: if you are standing near the reader outdoors, it challenges you on the spot; otherwise it becomes a letter.
Only a Guildmaster or an Officer (a rank that can invite) can pin a guild recruitment note, and the note names the guild.
You can take your own note down at any time.
Any registered player can **report** a note. You stop seeing it immediately; after three different reports it is hidden from everyone until a moderator looks at it.
Moderators can remove any note from the board or with **/note remove <id>**. A muted player cannot pin notes, and their notes leave every board while the mute lasts.
**Work for a living in the wilderness.** Buy a tool at a General Store or Pawn Shop, then "use" it from your inventory out in the wild:
a **Wood-Axe** to chop Wood Bundles;
a **Pick-Axe** to mine gems and metals;
a **Sickle** to cut plants for alchemy;
a **Fishing-Net** to catch fish - stand in the water, or cast from a boat or pier at sea;
a **Basket** to gather apples, oranges, mushrooms and eggs;
a **Spade** to rob graves in a cemetery - and maybe disturb the dead.

Tools also turn up as loot: now and then in a General Store's stock or a house's cupboard, in dungeon treasure (most often in prisons and mines), and on the bodies of warrior-type foes, orcs and giants.
Most foraging takes an hour or two of game time and tires you. It only works by day (the Spade works at night too), away from towns, with no enemies near and while you're not fully loaded.

Your attributes, the climate and the season decide what you find. Luck can turn up something extra.
Each tool lasts 50 uses.
Eat the fish, fruit, mushrooms and eggs for a little fatigue, health or magicka. With Climates & Calories on, your fish and fruit are C&C's own, to cook and eat as usual.

Commoners and nobles may ask you to fetch firewood. Bundles in your wagon count too.
The console command `Foraging_Tools` gives you one of each tool (not online).
Foraging is on by default. You can turn it off on the Features screen.

Online, nobody can move the shared clock, so a foraging job's game time becomes a short wait instead: 8 seconds for each game hour, so 12 seconds for an hour and a half of chopping. The wait starts once you close your inventory. Any bonus find is shown when the wait ends. An enemy coming near ends the wait early, and the rest of it is forgiven. Logging out mid-wait keeps what was left for next time.

Roleplay & Realism: Items' worn-condition loot now applies to every dungeon's treasure, not just some. Covens, laboratories, harpy nests, giant strongholds and dragon's dens were missed before.

**Selling never costs you gold.** Enchantments and affixes can lift Mercantile past 100, and past it a shop's offer kept falling, until selling took gold from your purse. Online, shops now count any Mercantile or Personality past 100 as 100: a sale pays what it pays at 100, and never less.
**Nothing is free past 100 either.** Far past 100, a shop sold its goods for a gold apiece, and rooms, cures and spells paid you to take them. Online they now cost what they cost a character at 100.

**Travel Options' fare scaling counts your Mercantile.** With the mod's inn or ship fare scaling set above 1, every scaled fare was priced as if you had no Mercantile at all. A good haggler now pays less, as the mod intends, and enchantments that raise Mercantile count too.
**Each character has its own Renown again.** Every character keeps its own level, and the level beside a name is that character's.
**Nobody loses a level.** Each character starts from its own Renown, plus everything your account earned while Renown was shared.
**A character made while Renown was shared** starts with what the account earned in that time.
**Renown still comes at three quarters** of the old rate, and the hourly limit is still shared by all your characters.
**A town defended pays the character that fought for it**, at that character's own level.
**A guild is founded on the founding character's own Renown.** It needs Renown 10.
**A Court writ's Renown goes to the character who delivers it.**
**The account card shows a row for each character's Renown.** The level beside your name is the character you played last.

Fixes and improvements.

**The Steel Brigandine has its own look.** With Roleplay & Realism: Items on, a Brigandine Jerkin made of steel is now drawn as a red, riveted, knee-length brigandine with a belt and front clasps, instead of Morrowind's plain steel cuirass. It is the second model made for this port alone, after the Dwarven Thunderlock.
It moves with your body as you move, and the skirt bends with your legs.
On the ground and in your pack's icons, the jerkin still shows the steel cuirass.

**The town's guards and townspeople are safe from your blade during a raid.** A stray swing or your horse could still hit a guard or a townsperson in the streets. That counted as Assault or Murder, turned the whole squad fighting beside you against you, and cost you your reputation. While a raid is on, your swings and your horse now pass everyone in the streets by, just as they already passed the raid's defenders. Outside a raid, nothing has changed.

**A hated name is charged, even in beast form.** Where a region hates you or has banished you, the watch comes for you now and then on a charge of Criminal Conspiracy. In beast form the watch still came, but with no charge you could answer. They hunted you and never stood down. As in Daggerfall, the charge now stands, so the watch can halt you and the matter can be settled.
**"Cast When Strikes" weapons work on the Warden.** A weapon's strike spell on the Gate's Warden did nothing in the real game. It now reaches him.

**Fast travel slows for enemies 40% later.** The journey still slows as enemies get close, but it starts slowing 40% nearer. You get 1.2 real seconds of warning before an enemy's sight range instead of 2. No enemy sees you any sooner or later than before.

Online, a weapon's strike spell does its damage to a monster another player spawned, but its other effects (paralysis, sleep, soul trap and the like) do not reach it yet. Strike enchantments also do not fire in duels.

**The quest you're on, on your HUD.** A small card at the top right shows one quest: its title, the start of its newest journal entry, where it points ("Llugwych in Wayrest province", or "(you are here)" when you're already there), and how long you have left on a deadline your journal gave you, which turns gold under a day. A main quest's card says "Main Quest".
**It follows along.** By default the card shows the quest your journal last changed. When there's no quest to show, it isn't there.

**Or choose one.** Press **Track** beside a quest in the journal (the Quests tab of the pause menu, or the chronicle) to keep that quest on the card. Press it again to stop. The quest your HUD follows says "On the HUD" beside its button. Your choice is saved with your character, and let go when the quest is over.
**The journal opens where you are.** The Quests tab now opens on the quest the card is showing.
**Online,** the party list moves down to make room for the card.
**It stays out of the way.** The card steps aside for the Overworld's panel, a journey's junction and, on a phone, the chat, and moves down when a larger HUD scale grows the compass.
Turn it off under Features, Interface, "Quest tracker". The Classic interface is unchanged.

**Your journal now says where a quest points.** Under each active quest, in the Quests tab and in the chronicle (the L key), a line names the place its latest journal entry sends you, in the same words Daggerfall uses: "Llugwych in Wayrest province". It only names what the entry itself says, or what is already on your map: a quest that says "a house in Daggerfall" still leaves the house for you to find, and a town the entry names but your map lacks is named without its province unless the entry names that too.

**Show on map.** Beside that line, a button closes the journal and opens the travel map on the place, as Daggerfall's own logbook always could with a click. It appears outdoors, where the map can open. If the map still can't open (an enemy near, say), it tells you why, as it always has.
**"Not on your map yet."** If the place is named but not yet on your map, the journal tells you to ask around for directions. Townsfolk can mark it for you.
**The chronicle shows how long you have left.** A quest with a deadline now shows "Time remains" on its card, counting down live and turning gold under a day.
Older journal entries that named a different place keep their own Show on map in the Quests tab.

**Your quests on the map.** Open the map and every active quest's destination is marked with a gold diamond above the place. The quest you're following is filled in dark; the others are outlined, and the legend shows both. Point at one to see the quest, where it is, and how long you have left; several quests at one place are listed together, the one you're following first. Press a diamond to pick its place, and the place's card names its quests.
**And on the compass.** When you're outdoors, a gold diamond on the compass shows which way to go for the quest you're following.
**Only what you already know.** A place is only marked once it's on your map, the same rule Daggerfall's own logbook uses before it offers to show you a place. Nothing is revealed early.
**Not on your map yet?** The quest card on your HUD says so and tells you to ask around. Townsfolk can give you directions and mark it for you.
Turn it off under Features, Interface, "Quest marks". The Classic interface, and Daggerfall's own map windows if you prefer them, are unchanged.

**Your journal tells you when it changes.** A notice slides in at the right edge when a quest begins, when its journal gains a new entry, when a deadline your journal gave you has less than a day left, and when it is completed or ends. Each one gives what happened and the quest's title, and a new entry or a deadline adds one line: the start of the entry, or the time left. A main quest's notice says "Main Quest".

**One notice per quest.** If a quest changes twice in quick succession, you get one notice, not a stack of them - and it keeps the news that matters most: an ending over an entry, a deadline over an entry while it is still under a day.
**Only real news.** An entry written again with the same words, or a clock the quest never told you about, is not news.
**Read aloud.** A screen reader announces each notice once, whole.

**It waits for you.** A notice's time only runs while the HUD is showing. News that arrives as you open a window is still there when you close it, and a deadline's notice then says the time left as it stands. Loading a game clears the notices of the game you left.

**It waits for you.** A notice's time only runs while the HUD is showing. News that arrives as you open a window is still there when you close it, and a deadline's notice then says the time left as it stands. Loading a game clears the notices of the game you left.
**Your choice.** Turn it off under Features, Interface, "Quest news". With it off, the journal changes silently, as it does in Daggerfall.

**The journal showed an old entry as a quest's current one.** When a quest rewrote an earlier journal entry (a deadline moved, a plan changed), the Quests tab and the chronicle kept showing the entry that came before it as the quest's latest. They now show the entry you were given last. The Classic logbook is unchanged.

**Standing still no longer tires you.** Fatigue used to drain at the walking rate even while you stood still, as it does in Daggerfall. That emptied a full bar in about an hour of standing around, with no status effect to explain it. Standing still on the ground now costs no fatigue.

**A little less work every frame.** The game was re-checking its launch settings dozens of times a frame, 84 times in a busy town. It now checks them once. On our test machine that saved over half a millisecond of every frame in a town. Nothing you see changes.

**The slowdowns reported after the Sea Update** were measured against the older versions. The long stutter after loading into the outdoors was fixed on 27 September, and the slowdown walking through dungeons was fixed by 28 September. In every place we tested, the game now does less work each frame than it did before the Sea Update.

**Marks are now called Drakes**, everywhere you see them: your account card, the Bank ("Sell Drakes", "8 gold a Drake"), the Market and Work tabs, writs, the professions' prices and your guild's **Drake treasury**.

**"Cast When Strikes" weapons work on monsters another player spawned.** Before, only a strike spell's damage reached a monster someone else in your party or cell had spawned. Paralysis, sleep, drains, pacify and soul trap landed on your own copy of the monster and were gone a moment later. The whole spell now reaches the real monster, which still gets its saving throw as usual. A Hand of Sleep blade puts a shared foe to sleep, and the strike's damage counts as your blow.

**Your soul trap fills your own gem.** A soul trap from your weapon on another player's monster is yours. When the monster falls, whoever lands the killing blow, its soul goes into an empty soul gem in your pack, not the other player's.
Strike enchantments still do not fire in duels.
When your strike puts a soul trap on another player's monster, you do not see "Trap active." You find out when it dies.

**You can accept a palace guard's terms of entry on a phone.** The row of touch buttons (with **abc** for the keyboard and **⏎** for Return) now shows for every window inside castles, dungeons and buildings, not only in the street. Tap **abc**, type your answer, then **⏎**.

**A boat deed works in every port town.** It looks for a port all around you now (it used to look mostly west and north), and every harbour the map shows counts. If there is no port near, it tells you the nearest one and which way it lies.

**Boats lost before the sea update's fixes are given back.** A Large Boat or Rowboat stuck under the ground or on the seabed (you could hear it, but never find it) is packed into its parts in your inventory the next time you come near it. Use the parts to place it again on the water. A crewed ship is left where it is: use its deed at a port to call it.

**Temple libraries open at the rank the temple promises.** A temple's bookshelves refused every member at every rank. They now let you read from the library rank your deity grants (Curate, rank 4, for Stendarr).

**Curing another disease no longer cures a werewolf's or vampire's bite.** A cure (a temple's, a spell's or a potion's) takes your ordinary diseases first. If the bite's infection is all that is left, a cure still ends it - so you can still be rid of it before it takes hold.

**Travelling online counts the days you travel.** A journey sped up with Travel Options or on the Overworld now passes its days for your character online, as it does offline - so a guild's wait between ranks, your hunger and everything else that runs on your own time move with the miles.
**Spawned dungeons that have gone are off the map.** An Elite (or any spawned) dungeon whose time had run out kept its marker, and its walk, whenever you came near it again. It no longer does.

**A dungeon bounty's pack stands where you can reach it.** The lair is now one of the dungeon's own quest spots - where Daggerfall puts every quest's target - instead of any monster's place, which could be a sealed room or under water.

**"World: Sign in to play online" no longer repeats for ever on a slow connection.** The game waits longer for the sign-in to answer before it joins. If it still fails, the game's console now says why.
**Fixed a crash when the game was minimised or put in the background while a world was loading** ("Cannot access 'be' before initialization").
**The Bank of the Empire has forgiven every loan.** The next time you load an online character, any loan it owes is cleared, and the game tells you how much was forgiven.
**You keep the gold you borrowed.**
If you had **defaulted** on a loan, that's forgiven too. The Empire will lend to you again, and your deposits are no longer taken to pay the old debt.
Reputation lost from a past default isn't returned; it recovers over time as usual.
This is a one-time amnesty. Loans taken from now on have to be repaid as normal.

**No more lag near World of Daggerfall mountains.** Standing or walking near one of World of Daggerfall's mountains could slow the game to a crawl, and every monster nearby made it worse. Its giant rocks are hundreds of metres across, and the game checked your footing against far too many of them at once. It now checks only the rock faces within reach of you.

**Routes go around World of Daggerfall mountains.** A route picked on the Overworld map knew only Daggerfall's own mountain country, so it could send you straight into a World of Daggerfall mountain. It now goes around them, as it already went around the Mountain regions. Roads through a pass are still used, and if you're already standing among the rocks the route walks you out.

**Routes follow the road around towns.** A road on the map meets in the middle of a town's square, so a route through a town used to aim you across the town itself, into the walls. The road actually runs around the town, and now so do you: in on the side you arrive from, around the edge, and out the side the road leaves by. Travel Options walks around a town the same way when you follow a road by hand.
Loose rock fields are not treated as mountains, because you can walk through them. You steer around their boulders as before.
Routes still pick their way over hilly and wooded country, and avoid only true mountain regions and steep drops.

**The watch no longer hunts a bad name out of thin air.** Before, a low standing with the law brought guards after you every couple of minutes in town, even with nobody around. Now a guard has to actually see you. If you are known to the watch (a poor standing in that region, or banished from it), a guard who spots you stops you: **pay a fine** on the spot, **come quietly** to court, or **refuse** and be chased. After a stop the watch leaves you be for a while, and after you answer for it (a fine, a sentence, an acquittal) you get a day's grace.
**The watch waits for a fight to end.** A guard no longer stops you in the middle of a fight or a duel.
**Invisibility hides you from the watch,** just as it hides your crimes from witnesses.
**Surrendering always works** - unless you killed one of the watch during that chase.
**A crime is charged once.** Running from one group of guards and meeting another no longer charges you for the same crime twice.
**Dying online ends the chase.** You wake up no longer wanted, but anything already charged against your name stays in full. Only serving a sentence gives any of it back.

**Serving your sentence pays your debt.** Paying a fine or serving time now gives back what the arrest cost your standing. Assault, murder and treason still leave half of it as a lasting mark. Winning your case in court clears it all.

**Only murder and treason can get you banished,** and it no longer lasts forever: it lifts after 30 days, or you can buy a **pardon** at a temple in that region (the watch does not enter temples).

**Temples take penance.** Speak to a temple's donation priest in the region: for a price that rises each time, the temple restores five points of your standing with that region's law.
**Paying the temple ends the conversation.** After a pardon or a penance, the priest no longer goes straight on to the donation box, where one more key press gave away another 1,000 gold.
**Bounty contracts help.** Finishing one improves your standing with that region's law.
**The Standing page shows the law of every region that knows your name** - how it sees you, and what it will cost you (a stop's fine, or a pardon's price and the days left on a banishment).
**Every change is announced.** When a crime, a sentence, a penance, a contract or a raid's defence changes your standing, a line says so.

**Guilds put you on probation before they expel you.** Falling below zero standing gets you a warning and time to mend it; you are only expelled if you are still on probation and have fallen well below zero at your next review.

When a skill reaches 100 and its group still has a free slot, the game asks whether you want to master it. It tells you how many skills of that group you can master and how many are left. **This decision cannot be undone.** If you say no, you can still master it later from your skill screen. Miscellaneous skills always stop at 100. Mastered skills are marked in gold on every skill screen.

**Where to find it:** on the Enhanced Plus Stats page, a **Master Skills** button sits next to Ascend (highlighted with a count when a skill is ready). Its page lists your primary, major and minor skills in three groups, each showing its free slots. Every skill shows its value and bar and, on the right, either a gold **Mastered** tag, a **Master** button (asks before it commits), or why not yet ("12 to 100", "No slot left"). On the Skills list, a mastered skill gets a gold name and a gold bar under it for its climb from 100 to 200. On the classic sheet, the primary, major and minor pages show "Mastered 1/2 (M)"; click it or press M to choose.

**Online** Master Skills is always on; the first mastery question also explains how it works. **Offline** you choose: the first time you master a primary skill you're asked whether to activate Master Skills, and you can switch it on or off at any time in your skill screen (not inside a dungeon). Switching off never deletes anything: skills above 100 show as 100 until you switch it back on.

Below 100, skills rise exactly as before. Past 100, a skill only learns from enemies that are tough **for that skill**; weak enemies and repeating the skill give little or nothing. The tougher the enemy, the better the gain.

Dungeons now answer a strong character. This starts as your three best combat or magic skills climb past 75, is fully felt at 100, and keeps growing as they climb toward 200. It needs Master Skills (always on online).

Party up with players well below your level (3 levels or more) and you automatically become their mentor:
Your level, skills, attributes, health and gear are brought down to about your group's level while you play together.
Enemies, loot and your spells match the group's level, so the fight stays fair and your friends' contributions matter.
Weak enemies still teach your skills above 100 nothing, so there's no farming or power-levelling.
Your real progress is never touched. It returns the moment you leave the group.
Type **/mentor** to see whether you're mentoring right now.

A board's hunt at a graveyard stands in the open air outside it, never in the crypt; graveyard notices get their own stories and show "graveyard" on the board.

BOUNTY-FARM-CLEAR: foes could stand inside the farmhouse (or barn) and could not be reached. The farm pool now records every building's footprint; `_standCampEncounter` takes an optional `spotOk` and the farm pack's anchor and every member are refused inside (or within 1.5 m of) any farm building. The farmyard ring widened 18 -> 24 m to leave room.

BOUNTY-FARM-GROUND: farms no longer stand on mountainsides. A spot whose ground rises more than 8 m across the block is refused; with no flat spot the farm fails and the pack stands as an ordinary hunt.

BOUNTY-OVERWORLD: every bounty you hold now shows on the Overworld at its hunt's pixel: a BLACK ring (the maps' own circle) with a pale rim so it reads on dark ground, labelled "Bounty: <foes>" (and the place, for a dungeon/graveyard hunt) and its distance. Off screen it is held at the edge with an arrow pointing the way, like the journey's end. It is never hidden by the Show filters, and it goes when the bounty is paid, dropped or lapses.

BOUNTY-SNAP: clicking a bounty's ring (or its edge arrow) on the Overworld walks you to the hunt: a dungeon's or graveyard's entrance, a farm bounty's yard about 20 m short of the farmhouse, otherwise the middle of the hunt's pixel.

The click area is small on purpose: 10 px around the ring or arrow, never the label. A click just beside it is an ordinary ground click, so walking near a hunt never snaps by accident (BOUNTY_SNAP_PX in ui/travelViewHud.js).

BOUNTY-GROUND: a board no longer sends an open-ground (or farm) hunt to a mountain pixel - the same mountains the Overworld refuses to walk into. Dungeon and graveyard hunts are unchanged (they go to the place's door). File: src/scenes/world.js (the board's siteOk).

**A beast can't surrender.** When the city watch stops you while you're transformed into a werewolf or wereboar, you're no longer asked to surrender. You get two choices instead: **F - frighten** or **N - fight on**.
**Frighten:** you roar at the watch. If it works, the guards run from you and leave, and your crime is forgotten. If it doesn't, they stand their ground and the guard's blow lands.
**Frighten:** you roar at the watch. If it works, the guards run from you and leave, and your crime is forgotten. If it doesn't, they stand their ground and the guard's blow lands.

**Your chances** depend on your level against the level of the guard who stopped you: an even match is 50%, and each level of difference moves it by 5%, never below 10% or above 90%. The city watch is always a few levels above you, so expect roughly 20% to 35%.
A frightened guard runs from you for a few seconds and then leaves; no body is left behind. Guards already on their way are called off too. Guards who came to defend the town from monsters stay.

A blow that would kill you no longer forces you to surrender while you're transformed. It lands.
If you turn into the beast while the surrender question is on screen, you can't surrender any more: answering fights on.
If you turn back into your human form while the frighten question is on screen, you can't roar any more: answering fights on.
Hitting a guard who is running from you is an ordinary hit. It doesn't turn calmed creatures nearby against you.
The watch never stops a beast on sight. If you change while a guard is stopping you, "come quietly" does nothing: a beast can't be taken to court.
Not yet tried with other players watching. They should see the frightened guards run off and disappear.

**It sits on your torso.** It used to be drawn too low on the Morrowind body, and because it takes the chest's place, your character's chest and shoulders were missing above it. It is now fitted to your own body's chest when it is put on, its collar at the base of your neck, whatever your race or sex.

**A house you brought online through customs can no longer be sold for nothing.** Selling it paid 0 gold and took the house and its furniture. The bank of the Empire does not buy back a house that came in through customs (as with a bought deed), so the door now says so and keeps it yours. A house you bought online still sells as before.
**Pressing Sell twice no longer says "The account service had a problem."** The second press waits for the first sale's answer.
**You no longer respawn high in the air after dying in a dungeon.** You wake at the dungeon's own door, on the ground, instead of falling (and dying again) over a nearby town.
**A save taken while falling keeps the fall.** Loading it lands the fall's damage as it would have, instead of letting you land safely.

**Fixed the endless "Chop and Gather Wood..." lock.** Chopping wood twice quickly could hang the game when the wait ended, and every login after hung again. Characters already stuck recover at their next login once the wait finishes.
**Creating an online character now starts the game.** It used to drop you back to the main menu after saving (the character was saved, and loaded fine from the Online door).

**Bringing a character online says when it was played on another of your accounts.** If the realm knows the character from a different account (another browser, a guest account, the desktop app), it tells you to sign in with that account instead of saying it has no record.
**Taking more gold from a guild treasury than you can carry pays it as a letter of credit.** A large withdrawal used to leave you too heavy to walk.

**With Protect Bystanders on, your blows pass townspeople and the town's walking guards by during a fight.** A swing at an enemy just out of reach no longer lands on the townsperson behind it (no murder, no assault, no lost reputation). With no enemy near, attacking a townsperson is still a crime, as before.

**The inventory works on phones.** The item list now has room on a phone, upright or on its side: the character picture is hidden until you tap **Body** in the pack's header (your choice is remembered), the worn panels stay a tap away, and the tabs scroll in one row. Tablets and narrow windows keep the picture, smaller.

**Raise and lower a cloak's or robe's hood from its card.** In the pack, a worn cloak or robe now has **Raise hood** / **Lower hood** (it used to say Use and step through drawings), shows whether the hood is up, says "You raise your hood." or "You lower your hood.", and your figure updates at once. A **Hood** chip marks the panel while it is up. (Vampires: a raised hood is what lets you out by day.)
**A tavern drink quenches your thirst fully**, whatever you order. Ale, wine and spirits still make you drunk.
**Inns and taverns refill your waterskins.** Every tavern menu has "Fill your waterskins", at the price of its cheapest soft drink.
**Each region's tavern serves its own menu.** The menus were off by one climate (Sentinel's deserts were served the bay's dishes).
**Being indoors helps.** Inside a building the temperature is never worse than the street outside - a desert inn at night is as cool as the night.
**Light clothes in the heat.** In hot weather your clothes count for half their warmth, so dressing lightly in the desert helps.
**You are told when you recover.** Coming out of Scorching or Freezing says "You are cooling down." or "You are warming up.", and drying out says "You have dried off."

**Doors no longer slow every check down.** Every door, lever and moving platform in a dungeon is checked separately from the walls, and until now every one of those checks looked at every door in the dungeon, however far away. A player's performance recording showed this costing more than the walls themselves. Checks now only look at the doors near them. Enemies walking into walls and floors cost less too. On our test dungeon with 30 enemies chasing you, their movement went from about 17 ms a frame to about 2.5 ms. Enemies and you move exactly as before.

**The window title no longer says "loading the saved game" while you play.** The title showed each loading step and never changed back once the game had loaded. It now reads "Daggerfall Online" once you're in.

**Updating no longer leaves Daggerfall Online missing.** The app used to install as more than 18,000 separate files. An update removed every one of them, then put the new ones back one at a time, with no window on screen. While it ran, the game's folder was empty and its shortcut went nowhere. If you clicked the shortcut then, Windows offered to delete it. If you restarted the PC then, the app was gone. The game's files are now packed into a single archive, so the app installs as fewer than a hundred files. An update now swaps a handful of files instead of thousands.

**The next update is the last slow one.** The version you have now removes its old files the old way, one at a time. After that, updates are quick. If Daggerfall Online seems to have vanished during that update, the update is still running: give it time to finish before reinstalling.
The portable Windows build no longer unpacks those 18,000 files every time you launch it.
**Repairs cost a third less.** Every smith and guild now charges two thirds of the old repair price, online and offline.
**Instant repair is on by default.** Smiths hand your gear back straight away instead of keeping it for days. You can still turn it off in the settings.

**New: Field Repair Kits.** Find them in dungeon treasure piles and on enemies that carry loot. A Field Repair Kit mends any weapon or armour, whatever its metal, by 15% of its condition (the most worn piece first), then it's used up. Smith-made Repair Kits still mend 25% of their own metal.

**You can always see what you gathered.** Some harvests used to show more messages than fit on screen, such as a gem, Resin, a body's part and meat, a new rank, or the specialisation reminder at rank 50 or 100. When that happened, the line saying what went to your Stores was the first one pushed off, so it looked as if you got nothing. Everything you gathered is now listed on one line, for example "+1 Bear Hide, a Big Tooth and 2 Raw Meat to your Stores", and that line stays on screen when other messages arrive.
**Your first harvest each session says where your goods went.** Gathered goods go to your **Stores**, not your pack. You can find them on the Enhanced pause menu, on the Stores page.

**Every harvest that is waiting to be counted says so.** Before, only the first slow harvest in a session showed a message. If you are signed out, it now tells you that the harvest is kept for ten minutes and counted once you sign in. If a harvest is never counted, the message says so plainly.

**A gathering that stops early tells you.** If you let go, walk away, open a window or leave the dungeon before the end, you now see "The gathering stopped before its end - nothing was taken." Before, only the meter disappeared. Pressing Escape still ends it quietly.

**XP and materials were always counted.** Only the on-screen messages went missing. Your ranks and Stores already hold everything you gathered.

A body **your own blow felled** can now be skinned where it lies, on the street or in a dungeon, until the day turns at midnight UTC. Bodies someone else killed, bodies inside buildings, and yesterday's bodies are searched as before.

Ten foes give a hide: the **Rat** (Rat Pelt), **Giant Bat** (Bat Leather), **Grizzly Bear** (Bear Hide), **Sabretooth Tiger** (Tiger Pelt), **Spider** (Spider Silk), **Giant Scorpion** (Scorpion Chitin), **Slaughterfish** (Slaughterfish Scales), **Harpy** (Harpy Feathers), **Dreugh** (Dreugh Shell) and **Dragonling** (Dragonling Scale). Bigger game needs more Hunting: the bat and the bear 10, the tiger and the spider 25, the scorpion and the slaughterfish 40, the harpy and the dreugh 55, the dragonling 70.

You need a **Skinning Knife** in your pack. With one, look at a body and the prompt says what **E** will do. Press the **act choice key** (the **Up arrow** by default; the prompt names it) to switch to **searching the body** instead: its loot is exactly what it always was. If you're standing right over the body, the prompt asks you to step back.

**Hold E** with your crosshair on the first point of the dotted line across the body, and draw it along the line to the last point (mouse, right stick or a finger). Bigger game has more points: 5 to 9.
Follow the line closely, taking between 0.6 and 6 seconds from your first move along it, and it's a **clean pelt**: a one-in-two chance of a second hide.
Stray far from it and the pelt is **torn**.
Let go of E before the last point and the trace starts again. Press Escape to stop. Nothing is lost either way.
**Gentle acts**: just hold E for a little over a second.

A skinned body gives its **hide** to your Stores. One body in four also gives Daggerfall's own ingredient: a **Big Tooth** (bear, tiger), **Spider's Venom**, a **Giant Scorpion Stinger** or **Dragon's Scales**. A torn pelt loses it.
The rat, bat, bear, tiger, spider and scorpion also give a **Raw Meat**, and the slaughterfish a **Raw Fish**, to your Stores. The harpy, the dreugh and the dragonling give none.
Hunting XP depends on the foe's tier, half as much again for a clean pelt. The XP message says if the pelt was clean or torn, or if a true line was drawn too quickly or too slowly to be clean.

You can skin at any hour. You can't skin in a settlement, out at sea, with enemies nearby (in a dungeon too), or when fully encumbered. In a settlement or at sea, **E** opens the body's loot. Each body can be skinned once.

Your **account** can take **30 hides a day** across all its characters, and only **3** of them from the harpy, the dreugh and the dragonling. A clean pelt's second hide counts, and the day's last skinning gives what's left. The Professions page shows how many you've taken today.
General Stores and Pawn Shops sell the **Skinning Knife** (100 gold, 0.5 kg, 50 uses) when you're playing online. You hold it like a dagger while you skin.
It can also be made at the anvil from 1 Iron Ingot and 1 Pine Plank.
Each skinning wears it by 1. When it breaks, you're told "Your Skinning Knife broke."
**Tracker** (50): outdoors, living foes you could skin within 100 m are marked on your compass.
**Tanner** (50): hides cure one to one instead of two to one.
**Butcher** (100): two Raw Meat a body instead of one, and the meat you withdraw spoils half as fast.
**Trophy Hunter** (100) is listed but can't be chosen yet.

A **Loom** section is on the Stores page, beside the Anvil and the Workbench. Use it inside a **Clothing Store** (50 gold a craft, cure or weave), or in your own home with a **Loom** station (DECOR, 50,000 gold).
**Curing**: two hides make a leather. The rat, bat, bear and tiger make **Cured Leather**. The scorpion, slaughterfish, dreugh and dragonling make **Hardened Leather**.
**Weaving**: three Spider Silk make a **Silk Bolt**. Harpy Feathers go into arrows (below).
Curing and weaving give no XP; the skinning already did.
At a Clothing Store, a recipe short of Linen or Wool offers **Buy from the Weavers** (Linen Bolt 2 Drakes, Wool Bolt 3 Drakes a bolt). If you don't hold enough Drakes, it says so.

**Leather armour**: cuirass, greaves, helm, pauldrons, gauntlets and boots at Daggerfall's Leather. Use **Cured Leather** from Outfitting 10 or **Hardened Leather** from 55. A cuirass takes 6, greaves 4, the rest 2. Hardened Leather makes a better piece.

**Clothing**: every one of Daggerfall's 76 garments, men's and women's, in **Linen**, **Wool** or **Silk**. Small garments take one bolt, middle ones two, large ones three, and boots a bolt and a Cured Leather. Your own character's clothing is listed first.

**Dye**: choose one of Daggerfall's **ten clothing colours** before you sew, or leave it undyed. Every garment takes a dye. The colour is sewn in: the piece keeps it wherever it goes, including on the market.
**Rugs** (3 Wool Bolts), **tapestries** (4 Wool Bolts), **Large Skins** (2 pelts) and **Small Skins** (1 pelt), from a rat, bat, bear or tiger. These go among your things, to set down in your home.
A **Fishing-Net** (2 Linen Bolts), Foraging's own.

A craft gives 20 Outfitting XP a tier of its cloth or leather, and 500 more the first time you make that recipe - except a piece made only of **Linen and Wool Bolts**. The Weavers sell those without end, so it gives the craft's XP but no first-time bonus. Boots, with their Cured Leather, and everything in Silk or leather still give it.

**The stitch**: the needle keeps a beat. Press **Space**, **Enter** or **Stitch** in time with it, eight times. All eight on the beat is a clean craft: one quality step up. A tap on **Stitch** counts the moment your finger goes down, and a key held down counts once. **Escape** sets the needle down (nothing is spent). **Quick craft** and **Gentle acts** work as they do at the anvil.
Specialisations: a **Tailor** (50) sews clothing a quality step better and a **Leatherworker** (50) leather armour. **Couturier** and **Saddler** (100) are listed but can't be chosen yet.
The workbench has a second arrow recipe: 1 Pine Plank, 1 Iron Ingot and 1 **Harpy Feathers** make twenty arrows, the same as the Twigs recipe.

**Every Stores material can be withdrawn to your pack now**, including Cured Leather, the Bear Hide, and Linen and Wool. The hides and leathers withdraw as their own items. The ingredients come out as Daggerfall's own, Raw Meat as Climates & Calories' Raw Meat, and Raw Fish as Climates & Calories' Raw Fish (Foraging's Fish if Climates & Calories is off).
The market trades the new hides, leathers, and Linen, Wool and Silk Bolts. **Leather Armour**, **Clothing** and **Furnishings** can be listed and commissioned.
The Professions page's Smithing unlocks were missing Silver, Elven and Dwarven, and Mithril. They're back.

The anvil's **Strike** counts on your finger's press too, and a held key strikes once. Only one station's work runs at a time: with a forge and a loom at home, one Space no longer strikes and stitches at once.
The Stores page keeps the field you're typing in, and the search keeps your cursor where you left it, when the page updates.
In a dungeon, the Pick-Axe won't work with enemies nearby either.
A harvest's second find (a Logging tree's Resin) now shows in the Stores straight away, not after the next refresh.

**Pressing E at a vein, tree or herb you can't work yet now tells you why.** Before, E did nothing at all when your rank was too low, you had no tool, or you had reached the day's limit. Now, if nothing else is there to use, you get a message such as "Mine Silver: needs Mining 25 - your Mining is 0". A door, chest or enemy right beside the node still gets your E press first, as before.

**Every dungeon vein needs Mining 25 or more.** A dungeon nobody has confirmed yet holds only Silver, which needs Mining 25. Raise Mining at the ore veins in the wilderness rock fields first. They can be mined by day.

**Using the Pick-Axe from your inventory or hotbar is Foraging's mining, not a vein's.** It only works in the wilderness, so in a dungeon it says "You cannot mine in here!". To mine a vein, carry a Pick-Axe, look at the vein and press **E**.

Ships no longer treat you as an enemy while you're off every ship. Ashore, on a quay or swimming, a pirate out on the water no longer stops you resting or travelling, no longer triggers "Sail ho!", and no longer halts a journey along the coast. Once you're aboard a ship again, at the helm or on a deck, the sea's dangers apply as before.

Ships no longer treat you as an enemy while you're off every ship. Ashore, on a quay or swimming, a pirate out on the water no longer stops you resting or travelling, no longer triggers "Sail ho!", and no longer halts a journey along the coast. Once you're aboard a ship again, at the helm or on a deck, the sea's dangers apply as before.

Not every pirate attacks on sight. Some are bold and take on anything, but most are wary: they only come for a ship they outgun, or one that's already crippled or badly holed, and they run from a ship that outguns them. A small boat is still fair game for them. A well-armed ship is often left alone.

Ships fight each other on their own. You'll see pirates running down merchantmen and navy ships hunting pirates without you taking part. When a ship strikes her colours to another, the winner comes alongside, boards her and sets her on fire. You can intervene: a ship tied up to her prize is a sitting target, and she lets go of the prize to fight back once she's hit.

When a ship strikes her colours to another, the winner comes alongside, boards her and sets her on fire. You can intervene: a ship tied up to her prize is a sitting target, and she lets go of the prize to fight back once she's hit.
The navy hears cannon fire and sails toward it, so a fight near a crown's ship often brings help.

Ships chase properly. A pirate chasing a fleeing ship now runs her down from astern with her bow guns firing, then comes alongside for the broadside. Before, she kept turning to fire and lost the chase.
News of fights between other ships reaches you only when they're close enough to see.

**The arrow keys are the helm.** Up makes more sail and down takes it in. With square sails you handle yourself, that steps through all sails, then fore-and-aft only, then none. Left and right steer, like A and D. At the helm the arrows no longer turn your view. End still raises and stows the sails, and every key can be rebound under Controls > Come Sail Away.

**The arrow keys are the helm.** Up makes more sail and down takes it in. With square sails you handle yourself, that steps through all sails, then fore-and-aft only, then none. Left and right steer, like A and D. At the helm the arrows no longer turn your view. End still raises and stows the sails, and every key can be rebound under Controls > Come Sail Away.
The helm panel shows your controls at a glance (sails and steering, with your current keys), and its sails button uses the arrows.
In irons: if your sails are up and your bow points into the wind with no speed, the helm tells you how to get out: strike sail and row round.

**Footsteps on a deck sound like wood.** Walking a boat's or a ship's deck no longer splashes as if you were wading the open sea (Immersive Footsteps read the water under the hull). Iron boots still ring and chain still chinks.

**No hunting at sea.** Tracks, birds and green hollows are for dry land: at a helm, on any deck or in the water the hunt never rolls, and a bounty's trail and a wilderness band leave you alone there too.
**Hold fire.** With the guns laid, press Activate (E, left click, the pad's A, or a tap) to put them down unfired. They stay loaded, and the readout says so while you aim.
**Ships handle.** Your ship picks up speed in about 7 seconds instead of 25, and slows to boarding speed in about 8 seconds when you stow the sails instead of 25.
**Ships handle.** Your ship picks up speed in about 7 seconds instead of 25, and slows to boarding speed in about 8 seconds when you stow the sails instead of 25.

**Steering that answers.** The rudder works even at a standstill with the sails up, and bites hardest at half sail, so easing off sail tightens the turn: a Small Ship turns on a circle of about 50 m at half sail and 125 m at full.

**Steering that answers.** The rudder works even at a standstill with the sails up, and bites hardest at half sail, so easing off sail tightens the turn: a Small Ship turns on a circle of about 50 m at half sail and 125 m at full.
**The Carrack sails.** It could neither move nor turn; it now makes way and steers like the other big hulls.
**Classic handling** is one switch away: Features > Naval Combat > Ship handling.
**The AI ships handle the same way**, turning and gathering speed at your own ship's pace.
**A ship with no crew left surrenders.** Kill every hand aboard and her colours come down (her fires keep burning), so empty ships no longer keep firing.

**Nobody walks the rail any more.** Boarders and your own hands stay on the deck: they no longer climb the bulwarks, stand on the rail or walk off into the sea. Musters spread across the open deck, never outside the rail, in the hold or in a closed cabin.
**Boarders ride the ship.** Enemies and crew on a moving or rolling deck move with it instead of sliding off the stern.
**Your crew wear green.** Every crewman fighting beside you has a green health bar over his head, fading with distance and hidden behind the land and under menus.

**No friendly fire.** Your swings, arrows, spells and their blasts, a thrown torch and a mount's charge pass your crew by, even a crewman standing alone in reach. Your crew's own arrows and blasts pass you by too.
**One crew each.** A ship's boarders fight as one crew, so a pirate captain no longer turns on her own men with infighting on.
**Online:** your crew stand as allies for everyone in your room, with green bars, and nobody's weapons hurt them.

**The crew are people now.** The painted figures on the decks are gone near you: each crew member is a real animated character (warriors, rogues, archers, barbarians, a bard) walking the deck, turning, stopping at the rail. Far ships keep their painted crew, which you couldn't tell apart at that range anyway.

**The crew are people now.** The painted figures on the decks are gone near you: each crew member is a real animated character (warriors, rogues, archers, barbarians, a bard) walking the deck, turning, stopping at the rail. Far ships keep their painted crew, which you couldn't tell apart at that range anyway.

**They talk.** Two crewmen wander over to each other and chat, a line each over their heads. Others mutter about the weather, the captain, the next port. Pirates, merchants and navy sailors each have their own things to say.
**They sing.** Every so often the crew strikes up a sea shanty. The bard (if there is one) sings the verse, and everyone joins in on the chorus.
**They go to quarters.** When a ship's guns are out, her crew hurry about and shout battle orders. When grapples are thrown, both crews line the rail facing each other.

**Boarding is seamless.** You land on the enemy deck right across from where you were standing, not in the middle of her. Her crew fight where they stood, and your hands are your own crew, going over the rail with you. Boarders on your deck come over the rail from their ship, and your crew stand to where they are.
**Your crew's hands come home.** After a fight, your crew are back aboard your ship.

**Pirates fight smarter.** A pirate chasing a fleeing ship actually runs her down and brings her bow guns to bear, instead of falling back and giving up. Ships find their way round a spit or an island to reach a prize or a boat lying behind it, so hiding behind land is no longer a safe harbour, and they give up a prize they truly cannot reach.

**Galleys fight at the right range.** Their great guns can't aim down at a low boat close in, so a galley now keeps her distance from small hulls instead of sitting helpless beside them.

**Fair fights.** Who wins a duel between two ships now depends on how fast each can make the other surrender, by wrecking her hull or by killing her crew. The ship the numbers favour now wins most duels. Wary pirates judge their prey the same way, so a well-armed boat is left alone more often.

**Merchants don't take prizes.** A merchantman that beats off a pirate sails on.

**Loose ends.** Two ships that surrender to each other no longer sit there forever. A galley's ram forces a ship to surrender rather than sinking her outright. A ship being chased stays in the fight. A navy no longer chases gunfire that happened somewhere else.

**Mending waits for the fight to end.** Your crew only repair the boat while no enemy is near the boat itself, even if you've gone over the side.
**Changing Ship handling mid-voyage is safe.** The setting now applies the next time you take the helm (a Carrack could freeze in place before).
**"In irons" works with waves on**, and its advice fits the handling you use: with Responsive handling, just put the helm over.
**The Carrack can cross the sea on the Overworld.**
**During an Overworld sea crossing**, the helm panel and the sail keys stay out of the journey's way.
**E holds fire**, as the readout says. It no longer throws grapples while your guns are laid.
**Online, boarding is shared.** Everyone in your room sees the fight on deck, with your crew as allies (green bars), and can join in.
**No stacking.** Boarders, your crew and you each get your own spot on deck, even on small boats.
**Beaten boarders' ship surrenders properly**, her fires out, ready for you to board in turn.
**Your fallen crew stay fallen.** Each hand lost in a boarding costs your ship that much crew.
**Warm Ashes' raids**: the raid's own allies are your crew, so your deckhands step aside instead of wandering among the raiders. The raiders come over your rail first.
**Captured prizes stay captured.** A prize's surrendered crew no longer reappear hanging over the water after a load.
**Every deck is reachable.** Forecastles, poops and stairs are part of the deck now, so nobody (you included) can hide on a raised deck out of a boarder's reach. Small boats have room to fight on.
**The dead stay aboard.** Bodies ride the ship and go down with her instead of hanging where they fell.
**Standing on a quay next to a ship no longer counts as being aboard** (the hunt and bounties work there again). Riding another player's boat does count.
**No hitch at first sight** of a Coasting Trader or a Pirate Sloop: every boat's deck is ready when the world loads.
A quay over shallow water sounds like wood, and a galley's helm is solid.
**They stand to before the grapples fly.** When a boarding is coming, both crews head for the rail on the side the other ship will be, in order along the rail.
**They keep out of each other's way.** No two crewmen stand in the same spot, and they let each other pass.
**Your crew grow back on deck** when you hire or press new hands, and a boat with no crew left shows nobody.
**They read the room.** Talk stops when the guns come out, a ship that has struck her colours goes quiet, the next shanty waits its turn, and a ship going down keeps her crew to the end.
**Everyone sees the same crew** on a player's boat, and a disguised owner's crew wears his disguise.
**Every player's crew of two or more has a bard** to lead the song.
**They pause with the game** under a menu, and stand down when the naval arc is switched off.
**No pickpocketing your own crew** (or a town's defenders). A failed attempt on anyone else makes them fair game, as it should.
**A Vampiric Effect at range spares your crew** and doesn't wake up surrendered prisoners.
**A crewman's area spell spares you and his mates.**
**The watch won't stop you mid-sea-fight.**

**Spatter lands the way the blow threw it.** Spray used to be spaced evenly around the body and stretched straight outward, so every kill left the same starburst. Now blood lands in one to three uneven clumps. A swing throws most of it the way you swung, and some drops fly off anywhere. Most drops are small, a few are large, and now and then one flies much further than the rest.

**Streaks come from how a drop hit, not how far it went.** A drop that falls steeply lands round. Only the fast, flat, far-flung ones smear into long streaks, pointing the way they travelled. This is what removed the wheel of spokes around a body.

**Droplets fly from the wound and land where their stain appears.** Each drop arcs through the air under gravity and leaves its mark on the exact spot it lands, on the floor, the wall or the ceiling. The pool under the body still appears as soon as the hit lands.
Drops that hit the ceiling still drip back down afterwards.
**Stain art is twice as detailed** (128 pixels per stain, up from 64), and every shape is generated from noise, so edges are ragged at every scale.
**Pools** are several blobs run together, with fingers where the blood ran and small splashes to one side.
**Spatter** has a core with tendrils thrown out in one or two directions, beads at their ends, and a fine mist on the side they flew.
**Streaks** are teardrops that curve as they thin, leave a line of droplets past the tail, and splash back behind the head.
The larger stain sheet is built in the background while you play, so the first hit of a session doesn't stutter.

No spam protection, because running a lot is the normal way to use the skill. Instead, **only real movement counts past 100**. Holding the run key while standing still or running against a wall won't count, so nobody can train it AFK.
**Running:** only the ground you actually cover counts. Sliding along a wall counts for the part you really moved.
**Swimming:** swimming through the water counts, and so does diving. Treading water in place doesn't.
**Climbing:** only climbing up or down the wall counts. Pressing into a wall you can't climb, or into a ledge above you, doesn't.
**Jumping:** a jump that carries you somewhere counts. Jumping in place doesn't.
Being carried doesn't count, for example standing on someone's boat.
