Hire a trader for your home: place a figure from the decorator's new **Vendors** category and make it the **Hired trader** station (25,000 gold, online). Put pieces from your pack up for sale at it; they stay up for 30 days.
Visitors buy from your trader inside your house. The **Vendors** tab on any Notice Board lists the region's traders whose houses you can enter, searchable by item, owner or town.
**Set waypoint** on a trader's house: a gold coin marks its town on both world maps, the house is named on the town map, and the compass points the way.
The new **Vendor** page (pause menu, under Professions) shows your traders, what is for sale, what has sold, and your takings to collect.
The rest bar now heals health, stamina and magicka as it fills. If the rest is interrupted, you keep what it healed.
Rain and snow now fall in front of grass and banners instead of behind them.
Rain keeps falling while you travel on the Overworld map.
Your wagon stays attached to the horse. It no longer stretches out and snaps back when you speed up, stop, turn or cross a slope, whether you ride it or it follows you.
On the Overworld your cart's wagon is drawn at your rider's size, attached behind the horse. Other players' wagons stay attached to their riders too.
The wagon, your storage and the Materials Bag now have a search box and a category menu (All, Materials and the nine pack pages).
Shift-click an item in your pack to put the whole stack into your wagon, storage or Materials Bag in one click, with no split popup. In the classic skin this works for the wagon and storage.

The text hunting minigame (Climates & Calories) no longer runs. You won't get "You spot a set of animal tracks..." prompts in the wilderness any more, and no Yes/No search box, result page, or "You are not the hunter, but the hunted!" beast follows them.
Long journeys are no longer interrupted by hunting prompts.
Hunting the profession (skinning a body you killed with the Skinning Knife) is untouched.
**Overworld** and **Quick dial** can be bound in the Controller bindings window, and put on any d-pad tap or hold.

**Arranging the hotbar on a controller**: in any window, press **LT** to raise the hotbar. Press **A** on a slot to pick it up, then **A** on another slot to move or swap it. **Y** clears a slot. Press LT again when you are done.

**Add to hotbar asks which slot.** With a controller in hand, the item card's and the spellbook's "Add to hotbar" picks the entry up and raises the bar. Press A on a slot, or hold **LB/RB** and press that slot's own button (X too). All 16 crossbar slots can be reached.
Picking up the mouse while something is in hand drops it and lowers the bar.
Arrows and pellets you shoot in a bout are **handed back** by the healers. Conjured arrows are not, and arrows you drop or sell during a bout are not either.
The Curse of Daggerfall's ghosts no longer come for you at the arena's gate, in its stands, on the floor or in the undercroft. They wait outside the grounds, and resting there is not interrupted.
In two-against-one bouts, an enemy's area spell no longer hits its own partner. A Grand Melee's HUD now says **"each alone"**, because every fighter there is on their own side.
**The undercroft has enemies again** in its deep cellars, past the fighters' hall. The hall itself stays peaceful, and resting there is still never interrupted.
**Node distance filter**: a "Nodes" button picks how far away gathering groups still show: any distance, 0.5, 1 or 2 km.
**Carriage towns**: towns with a carriage driver at the gate show a **wheel** on both maps, and the Overworld edges their plate in brass.
**Name colours**: friends' names are blue and guild-mates' names are violet. Your party stays green.
**Player filters on both maps**: Friends, Guild, Others, and a minimum Renown. On the travel map they sit in the key.

**Town seats**: hovering a town that can be captured shows who holds it and this week's battle (mouse only; on touch, the travel map's info box says it). The map's info box also names the holder now; before, it always said "unheld".
On horseback in the Overworld, your sprite **faces the way you are riding** again.

**Encounters on the road** (World settings, on by default): while you travel, an enemy far below your level (a rat for a level 3+, an imp for a level 6+, an orc for a level 15+) no longer stops you. Other encounters sometimes come as a small patrol. Resting is not travelling.

`/event sunbaby` now cycles: the laughing sun baby turns evil — a red, horned, grinning sun over a burning sky — and rains fireballs on Daggerfall, then calms down, then becomes Todd Howard over sixteen times the flowers. It just works.
Everyone online sees the same phase at the same time. The fireballs are harmless.
The sun now snaps between its faces in a second instead of slowly melting.
Todd Howard's phase now shows Todd Howard himself.

Every shop now sells the **Portal Stone** for **5 Welkynd Shards** (the shards you get by salvaging Magic, Rare and Legendary gear). Find it on the shopkeeper's menu, under "Portal Stone (5 shards)", or press **P** on the classic interface. Shops never run out.
Use a stone from your pack or hotbar while outdoors and pick any place on the map. A portal opens two metres in front of you and stays open for **30 seconds**.
Anyone who walks into it travels there instantly, including other players nearby when you are online. Bring your friends.
One stone opens one portal. Stones are bound to you: they can't be sold, traded or dropped.

A portal won't open, and won't take you, while enemies are nearby, during a duel, in a siege, or while you are travelling a route. It needs open ground with room in front of you, and won't open in water or aboard a boat.
Every existing character receives **10 Portal Stones**, once, the next time it is loaded. They join any stones you already carry.
Welkynd Shards you are wearing as a crystal are no longer spent by the Reforge or a shop.
A new online world event. Every four hours a great sea serpent rises on one of the Iliac Bay's packet lanes, out in open sea.
Bells ring in the harbours fifteen minutes before it rises. The chat names the port it lies off and the local time it rises, the map rings its waters, and inside the ring your compass points the way.

Sail out and fight it from your deck with your ship's guns. Every ship that joins makes it tougher by the same measure as her own guns, so a fleet of any size fights it for about the same length of time. It is a fight to meet up for: one ship alone cannot bring it down, and a fleet of three or more can.
**The Hunt:** it lashes with its tail, rams down a lane, bursts up under its mark and spits venom that pools on the decks.

**The Coil (from two-thirds health):** it wraps a ship and crushes her if left alone. Focus fire on the coils to break them - every blow on a coil hurts the serpent too - and it lies stunned: every blow lands half again as hard, and its head takes double.

**The Maelstrom (from one-third health):** a whirlpool drags ships toward its grinding eye while the serpent rears and roars. Its waters are marked on the sea as it forms, and every ship can sail out of it.
Its boss bar names each attack as it winds up, warns **MOVE** when one is aimed at your ship - all the way down a ram's lane - and counts down a coil's health.
Bracing your guns halves its blows on your hull and canvas, as it does a cannonball's. Your guns lead it as it swims.
If your ship is wrecked, the serpent stops going at her, and she stops making it tougher.
Fifteen minutes after it rises, a storm closes its waters and no new ship can join. Ten minutes after that it dives and is gone.

Every ship whose guns did their share (a tenth of what she brought to the fight) earns a hoard: gold, a Rare-or-better piece and a Magic-or-better piece. A hand who stood the fight out aboard a ship, close to the serpent, earns gold and a Magic-or-better piece.
Each serpent slain is worth six quests of Renown (half for standing it out), and your account card and your inspect card count the serpents you've slain.
If you were away from its waters when it fell, your share comes to you the next time you're online.
Guests receive the hoard; only registered accounts keep the count and the Renown.

The Timers window (the hourglass on the pause menu) now counts down the sea serpent. You can see when Sethrakul rises, how long until the storm closes its waters, and when it dives. Once the bells ring, the row names the port it lies off.
The next serpent's rising is shown once the current one is under way.
The hourglass button no longer has the word "Timers" beside it; it is the hourglass alone.

The Discord channel that announces the Oblivion Gates now announces the sea serpent too. The harbour bells are posted 15 minutes before it rises, with where it was sighted, when it rises and when the storm closes its waters. The post pings the same opt-in role as the gate posts, and each time is shown in your own clock.
When Sethrakul is slain, the channel names the port and the top fighters.
A kill is only posted for the site most players' games agree on. A faked fight never reaches Discord.

The Market tab can see your Materials Bag and pack again. Since the bag arrived, everything you gathered went there, and the market only looked in your Stores, so it showed nothing to sell. Listing materials and filling buy orders now count what you carry and move it into your Stores first.

Buy orders now show on every Notice Board, not just in their own region. You can fill an order from anywhere; if it's in another region, the courier fee comes out of your pay, and the board shows what you'll receive.
The List form now says the truth: your listing stands on every board in the Bay, and buyers outside your region pay a courier.

A gold purchase that's refused (because the listing sold or its price moved) now gives your gold back exactly as it was paid. It used to come back as coins in your purse, even if a letter of credit or your bank account had paid; a large letter could come back as more coin than you can carry.
The same fix applies to founding a guild, guild deposits, renting a room, buying a home and paying for decor.
Buying the 20th unit of a 1-silver listing no longer fails and retries forever.
Filling single units of a 1-silver order no longer gives a wrong reason, and the last unit can always be filled.
Pressing Buy again after a lost connection no longer buys twice.
The market tab no longer goes blank while another action finishes.
Crafted pieces with the same name now show their quality and wear in the List form, and every piece you carry is offered, even past 64.
A closed market says why instead of the tab vanishing. A failed load keeps its filters and the Weavers' and Apothecaries' counters.
Messages after an action no longer follow you to other views, and an open dropdown no longer snaps shut.
Your home trader's stock has its own limit of 60 and no longer uses up your 30 board listings.
The Materials view always includes your own region's listings.
SirMcMobdon's own aura, granted with the Shadow Fang title and glyph. Wear it from the account card's aura picker.
A hooded cape of living shadow with crimson accents: a red lining, a stitched mantle, wolf's-teeth embroidery down its opening, and a hem that frays into trailing smoke.
The wearer's wolf glyph is on its back and its clasp. Emblems of the glyph rise off the back and fade away.
It casts a pool of shadow at the wearer's feet and kindles in from the hem when first worn.
In third person the cape hangs from your body's own shoulders, head and knees as they animate. Crouching presses it down, and a striding knee pushes the cloth out.
It trails behind a run or a strafe, swings past and settles when you stop, lags behind a turn, and lifts as you fall.
It folds away while you ride. Other players see your cape hang and swing on your body the same way.
Transforming into a werewolf tears the cloak apart along its seams, with embers along the tears. Its shreds float around the beast.
It forms again when you turn back.
The account card said "Wearing shadowcloak." (an aura's internal key). It now shows the aura's name, for every aura.

**SquidKamer's Low Poly Trees** is in the game: the trees, bushes and stumps of the wilderness and of every town's gardens stand as real 3D models instead of flat pictures - 253 of them, across every climate and its winter.
Each wild tree has its own size and turn, so no two stretches of wood look alike. Trees in towns and gardens keep their size.

**The view reaches as far as it always did.** Up close you see the 3D tree; further out, a picture made from that same 3D tree stands in its place, and the two fade into each other as you walk. The distant woods draw exactly the trees they drew before, one picture a tree.
The near trees are drawn only where you are looking, and the mod's pictures are kept only while trees near you use them.

**Works with Seasons of the Iliac Bay.** A tree takes autumn, spring and snow exactly when its flat would - in the climates the mod changes - and keeps its own colours in the ones it leaves alone. Without the mod, winter brings the trees' own snow-capped winter models.
On by default: **Mods -> Low Poly Trees**. Turning it off brings back the classic trees the next time the world loads.
Felling a tree for Logging still works as before, and a tree still gives the same cover in a fight.
The trees' leaves and bark are painted from your own Daggerfall files when the world loads, so nothing extra is downloaded beyond the mod's shapes (about 3 MB).
The developers' own aura. Wear it from the account card's aura picker.
Wings of flowing golden light grow from the wearer's back. Each wing has long plumes and short inner feathers, with waves of light running out along them.
The wings breathe slowly and beat once every eight seconds. Sparks streak out past their tips, and a soft glow with turning rays shines behind the shoulders.
They cast a pool of gold at the wearer's feet and a gold light on the world around them.
They sit on the wearer's back on both Morrowind bodies and Eye of the Beholder sprites, and they lean, turn and trail with the body.
An aura you put on or take off now shows to everyone around you within a second or two. Before, they saw it only after you changed area.
Up to 32 auras are drawn at once (was 16).
A player who drops out of sight for a moment no longer has their aura start over from nothing.
The cloak and the wings now sit at the sprite's real shoulders. Before, they floated well above the head whenever a weapon, staff or spell was out.
They face the way your sprite faces. Walking backward, the cloak no longer covers your sprite's face.
The cloak is no longer drawn around your camera in first person.
While you swim, the cloak folds away and the wings close.
Players in beast form now carry the wings at the beast's own shoulders.
The Golden Radiance no longer vanishes when you look down on its wearer from high above.
The Seraph Wings' light stays gold in dungeons.
In first person, looking down no longer washes your view in gold from the wings' backlight.
After swimming, the Seraph Wings open again when you ride or crouch. Before, they stayed closed and unlit, and the Holo Shadow Cloak stayed folded.
The tip of every wing strand no longer shows a faint twist.
On Eye of the Beholder skins the wings now sit farther back and no longer clip through the body when seen from the side or at an angle.
Before your first step, the wings now hang behind you instead of over your sprite's face.
The wings are slimmer, shorter and much softer: fewer, thinner strands of pale gold, a smaller and fainter glow behind the shoulders, and a dimmer light on the ground and the world around you.
Arena fighters now telegraph their heavy blows at each other, not just at you - step out of the marked ground.
Losing a ladder bout resets that tier's run; every tier's champion is an elite.
No potions or cheese spells (Invisibility, Chameleon, Shadow, Levitate, Calm, Charm, Teleport) in ladder bouts, and a height ceiling over the sand. Bouts between players keep their kit.
Winning a ladder bout you have won before pays no purse, points or Renown.
The online ladder needs a registered account, and each ticket is good for one bout.
Online, the champions run, look elite, and a time-out needs real damage on the judges' card; a tie is a draw.
Fixes: a run that could get stuck for good, champions fleeing as revenants, a worn ring losing its effect after a bout, collapsing mid-bout resting an hour, Recall off the sand.
A quest's foe that is not yet hostile now shows "Quest: <title>" under its name on the enhanced plaque.

**Graveyard crypts are no longer sold as homes.** The crypts in graveyards (Wayrest's, the Wickcroft Tombs' and 65 others) were for sale online, but they have no inside: entering one only said "This house has nothing of value." They are no longer offered. If you already bought one, you can still sell it back at its door.

**The Possessed Child can be finished in Tigonus.** In some houses Beautiful Cities builds a cellar and then lays a floor over its stairs. A quest person or item that was placed in such a cellar now stands upstairs, next to the covered stairs (128 buildings).

**Houses and the stone gazebo no longer float.** Beautiful Villages builds on hills, for example around Ipsham's temple and at the roadside taverns' gazebo. Those hills are now drawn at their real size and shape, so what stands on them is back on the ground.
**Dying clears paralysis.** After you respawn online, any paralysis from a ghost or spider is gone, and so are a wraith's silence and any fatigue or magicka drain. Diseases still carry over.
**"Open Water" only appears over water.** The fishing net no longer offers a cast while you are looking at the beach, and a net you are still winding up can't be thrown onto the sand.

**Dungeon beds count as beds.** Online, you can now rest at a bed in a dungeon, the same way you rest at a campfire. The bed must be on your floor. Palace beds don't count, and resting at a bed doesn't use up a Bedroll lying next to it.

Loads now have a face. Starting or continuing a game, going online, a dungeon's door, a fast travel, a guild teleport, Recall, a respawn and a save loaded in play all show a loading screen: where you are headed, what the game is doing, and a running bar.
The screen stands on one of your own screenshots, with where and when you took it - or, with none, on the main menu's night sky and a tip.
It never covers something you need to see: character creation, the pause menu, a level-up and the dream videos all come first, and the screen comes back only if the world is still loading.
Choose **Your screenshots**, **Night sky** or **Off** on the new **Loading screens** tile under Features (Interface). The Classic UI is unchanged.
The screenshot key (F8 by default) now also keeps every shot in a gallery in your browser - up to 120, and nothing is ever uploaded.

A new **Screenshots** page: on the main menu (bottom right, beside About) and on the pause menu's System tab. Open a shot large, choose which ones appear on loading screens, save one to your files, delete one, or add pictures from your computer.
A switch on that page decides whether the key still downloads a PNG as well (on, as before).

An enemy winding up a telegraphed attack no longer drops it at the first scratch. Hits landed during the wind-up fill a **poise** meter (shown under its health bar on the Enhanced HUD); heavy weapons, hits to its back and hits to its weakness fill it faster. Fill it and the wind-up **shatters**: the enemy is **staggered** for about a second, helpless and taking 25% more damage.
**Iron** attacks (red and hatched - a giant's slam, an elite's heaviest, a revenant's signature) cannot be interrupted. Get out of the way.

**Missing costs the enemy.** An attack that hits nobody leaves its enemy **open** for about a second, taking 30% more - and your first hit staggers it. Step out of the attack in its last moment for a **perfect dodge** and a longer opening.

**Missing costs the enemy.** An attack that hits nobody leaves its enemy **open** for about a second, taking 30% more - and your first hit staggers it. Step out of the attack in its last moment for a **perfect dodge** and a longer opening.
You can read it coming: the body **glints** as the wind-up begins and again just before it lands, with a sound for each, and the mark on the ground is easier to see.
Wind-ups vary in length, lunges **track** you for their first half, skilled blade-fighters sometimes **feint** (a feint never glints - the glint is the honest tell), and brutes **chain** two blows.

New attacks: the **ring** (safe at its feet), the **charge** from range, the **leap** onto where you stand, and an archer's **aimed shot** you can step off. Landings now do something: a lunge pushes you back, a sweep makes you bleed, a slam rattles you, and an iron slam knocks you down.
Champions and revenants telegraph at any level; elites and revenants more often, and with their kind's whole set of attacks.
Online, everyone sees an enemy's wind-up, and enemies wind up at other players too - each player dodging on their own screen.

A revenant **learns from how you beat it** and comes back adapted - mail against your blades, warded against your fire, arrow-wise against your bow, patient against your dodging. At most three adaptations, never immunity.

Every revenant has a **hidden weakness** - an element, a metal, a weapon or the daylight. Strike it to reveal it: it takes 50% more and staggers twice as easily. Its own flinches, and the townsfolk, hint at it.

From rank 3 its **will must be broken** before it will kneel: strike its weakness, stagger it, or perfectly dodge its attack. If you don't, it escapes at the killing blow - stronger, and adapted again.
**The last stand:** from rank 3, the first killing blow brings it roaring back instead (at 30%, 35% or 40% of its health by rank) - faster, harder, ember-lit, with a burst around it. Once a stand.
From rank 2 it has a **signature attack** named for it ("Grushnak's Skullsplitter"), iron from rank 3, and a **band** of one to three of its kin, who scatter when it falls.

**The hunt:** each revenant has a **lair**, a named dungeon near where it was made. Ask around ("Any news?") and townsfolk may tell you where - and sometimes its weakness. Once heard of, the lair is marked on your maps and in your journal; walk in and you will find it resting there.
**It takes something:** online, a revenant that kills you takes one of your unlocked items. Kill it or spare it to get it back.
**It festers:** left alone past its due day it grows stronger, and three times over it ranks up on its own.
New ways to make one: a special enemy that **knocks out your companion**, or one **you run from**, becomes a revenant too.

**Sworn companions have loyalty:** kept well they are devoted (and warn you of an attack from behind); neglected, they desert; and a disloyal Unhinged, Craven or Brutal one may turn on you once your health falls under a quarter.

The **Revenants page** (Holdings tab) and the revenant's card show everything you know - its habits, weakness, will, signature, band, lair, what it took and how long it has festered - and it speaks every new moment in its own voice.

Townsfolk are no longer strangers who appear and vanish. Every town's people are residents with a name, a face, a home and a trade - the baker, the smith, the innkeeper, the priests, the watch - and they keep them for good.

Each has a day: they get up (early birds and night owls), go to work, run errands at the shops, meet friends in the square, spend the evening at the tavern or the temple, and go home to bed. The watch walks its beat in shifts.
Online, everyone sees the same people in the same places at the same time.
They stop and talk among themselves, and greet you as you pass - by name, once they count you a friend.

Doors open: step into a tavern in the evening, a shop or a temple, or a house, and the people whose day has them there are inside - talking at the tables, and now and then getting up to cross the room. Nobody walks into your own home.

Merchants, pilgrims, couriers, pedlars and adventurers travel between towns by day and camp by night. Merchants hire sellswords and travel in caravans; anyone armed puts on their gear before they leave town.

Travellers meet the land's monsters. Come upon a party under attack and you can fight beside them - save them and they will remember it; arrive too late and the fallen stay dead, and a newcomer takes their place in time. The towns talk about what happened on their roads.
In port towns, sailors crew the ships that call there, and travellers sail across the Bay - now and then one is lost at sea.
On the Overworld, parties on the road are marked, and a party in trouble shows in red.
Adventurers dive the dungeons near their towns. Meet a company down there and they fight at your side.
Some never come up. Their remains lie where they fell for three days, with what they carried and a keepsake - bring it home to their family, and the town will talk of it.
What you do changes how each person feels about you: a kind word, help in a fight, a life saved - or a blow, a theft, a crime they saw.
A friend greets you by name and comes to your aid on the road. An enemy will not speak to you, and an armed one will draw on you beyond the town walls.
Striking down a resident is permanent: their household turns against you, and every witness counts the crime.
The chronicle (L) has a new **People** page: your friends, your enemies, the people who know you, and the dead.
The Travel Options speed dials are gone: a journey runs at x100 on a road or track, and x60 off it.
Wilderness enemies only come for a fast traveller who fails a Stealth check. An enemy that has noticed you wears a "!" and slows the journey; one that has not leaves you be.
Online, the ship's time dial is gone - time at sea keeps the world's pace.
**Living world** is on by default, on its tile under Features (World); a change takes effect when a town next loads. Off - or on the Classic UI - towns keep Daggerfall's own wandering townsfolk.
Tuned for big cities: the living world's work in the largest city was cut from up to 120 ms a frame to a few milliseconds, and arriving in a town no longer hitches.

**Vanilla Enhanced now ships with the game, and it is the default look.** It is carademono's remaster of Daggerfall's own textures: the ground, the trees and rocks, the city walls and the dungeons. There is nothing to download.
Prefer Daggerfall's own textures? Pick **Classic** on the Texture Overhaul card. Your choice is remembered, and Classic switches your texture mods off without removing them.

While Vanilla Enhanced is worn, the card offers its two add-ons as switches: **Masked Roads** (by carademono and Kokey) and **Snowless Swamps and Jungles**. The card remembers your add-ons when you switch back to Classic.
The new textures are decoded in the background, so loading them doesn't stutter the game.
Texture mods now load in Daggerfall Unity's order. A mod loads after the mods it is built on. Where two mods carry the same texture, the one loaded later is drawn.
Each texture mod can be switched off and on without removing it, on the Replacement packs card at the foot of Features. The built-in mods are listed there too.

Switching texture mods mid-game now applies to everything drawn after the switch. Before, a switch could leave a mix of classic and new textures until the page was reloaded. What is already on screen keeps its look until its area loads again.
The Texture Overhaul card on the main menu now sees the texture mods you attached. Before, it could show "Classic" while your mods were on.
A texture mod that can't be read is now listed on the Replacement packs card with the reason and a Remove button.
With a loose texture pack attached, the card explains why Classic can't be picked, and how to remove the pack.
If you attach your own copy of Vanilla Enhanced (for example a newer version from Nexus Mods), it is used instead of the built-in one.
Ground textures now appear on the terrain, as in Daggerfall Unity, when they come from a loose texture pack or from a mod that ships the ground tile by tile.

Two new icons in the main menu's top-left corner: **Patreon** and **Ko-fi**. Each opens its page in your browser (from the desktop app, your system browser). Hover one and it lights up; it is reachable with the keyboard and a controller too.
The main menu no longer gets cut off on short windows, such as a 720p screen in a browser. The logo always shows in full, and the menu scrolls down to its last button.
On narrow and mid-size windows, the logo now sits below the corner icons and your profile picture instead of underneath them.
The website now offers **Ko-fi** beside Patreon in its top-right corner (https://ko-fi.com/daggerfallonline).
**Fire**: a fireball bloom. Embers are thrown out and fall, land and smoulder. Flame licks up, and a scorch glow and a shock ring spread on the floor.
**Frost**: a splash crown of droplets that rain down and ripple where they land, ice glints winking on the floor, and cold mist.
**Shock**: jagged lightning arcs strike from the impact into the floor, flickering and re-striking, while fast sparks skitter away.
**Poison**: green globs are lobbed out and splat into small bubbling pools, under a sickly vapour.
**Magic**: motes spiral out over rune rings.

**Heal**: a still, soft green glow on the floor with thin lines of light rising out of it. There is no shockwave and no ring. It shows on yourself, a party mate, your companion, a touch, or an area heal.

Every element's burst takes its colour from that element's own spell art in your game files, so the light matches the missile you just watched fly. Heals keep their green. Touch spells now show a small burst where they land.

**Area at Range** and **Area around Caster** now show exactly what they catch. A person is caught out to about 4.45 m, and the world boss out to about 5.8 m. A shockwave and racing sparks run out to that edge, and the edge glows for a moment.
The shockwave spreads across whatever the spell hit. A fireball that strikes a wall at chest height bursts as a ring on the wall, and the same goes for ceilings.
Bigger areas show more. The element breaks out across the whole area as the shockwave passes. Area heals fill the circle with rising light.
Impacts briefly light up the walls and floor around them in the element's colour.
**Fire**: a whumpf and crackle.
**Poison**: a squelch and bubbles.
The classic flash, the bloom and the camera kick stay. There are fewer element-art sparks now.
Fixed: sparks no longer jump away when the world recentres mid-burst, and none are left behind after a load or a teleport.
Text and buttons in the client no longer light up with a blue selection highlight when you click or drag. Text fields can still be selected.

The house decorator now offers the town mods' furnishings while those mods are on (Beautiful Villages, Beautiful Cities and Detailed Ships). That adds 297 pieces: the coloured beds, the paintings, tapestries and banners, rugs and hangings, set tables and stocked shelves, the captain's sea chest, the weapon rack, and more. Online, these mods are on for everyone.
Turning one of those mods on or off now changes what the decorator offers within a second. A mod turned on mid-game has its pieces offered and priced; a mod turned off stops offering them.
The decorator now offers what Daggerfall stands in its dungeons: thrones, cages, coffins, statues, chains, braziers, the knight's armour, weapons and wall hangings.

A yard now offers Daggerfall's street pieces (fences, wells, fountains, carts, lamp posts) and the trees and plants of its own town's climate. They are drawn in the town's climate and season, Seasons of the Iliac Bay included, and so is the placement preview of a fence or a well.
A tree or plant placed in a yard shows its own picture under "In this yard".

With Low Poly Trees on, a tree or plant placed in a yard now stands as the mod's 3D tree up close and as its picture far away, like the world's own trees. It is sized and turned the way you placed it, and the placement preview shows the same tree.
A yard tree whose picture was still loading as you travelled no longer appears far from its yard.

With Show Nudity off, the house decorator's Vendors no longer offer nude figures. A figure already placed in a house, ship, yard or guild hall now stands, moves and shows in the decorator's lists as its clothed stand-in, like the world's own people. It stays the same trader with the same stock.
The Arena crowd no longer seats nude figures while Show Nudity is off.
Flylighter now holds the **Crystal Fist** title, shown in purple, with its own glyph beside the name: three purple slashes.
Flylighter keeps the Disciple title too. Pick which title to wear from the account card.
A ring of tiny purple squares about the feet, stacked into columns that rise and fall like a music visualiser's bars.
It comes with the Crystal Fist title. Wear it from the account card's Aura row.
On an Eye of the Beholder character, the developers' wings now stay lined up with the sprite as it turns.
This holds on a key press, while the camera moves round, in the saddle, and on other players.
RookieG is now a developer.
Steep ramps in hallways now fill in on the 3D dungeon map once you have walked them, like the corridors around them.

A boat or ship whose hold is too heavy to carry packed can no longer be picked up into parts nobody could carry. "Pick up" now says "her hold is too heavy", and fast travel or a landfall leaves her moored. Lighten her hold to pack her.
Red brick teleporters you walk into now always send you on. Before, some only worked when clicked.
Sworn revenants and crew ashore now go after the enemy fighting you first, instead of standing still or wandering toward an idle enemy behind a wall.
The Haunted House (and other quests SEALED-CELLAR fixed): if you saved inside the house while the foe was in the sealed cellar, it now stands by the hatch when you load.

Regular (non-elite) enemies leave more of what they carry. Offline they keep 3 of every 4 items, up from half. Online it depends on your Renown: 5 of every 8 at Renown 1, 3 of every 4 at Renown 20, and 7 of every 8 at Renown 40.
Regular enemies drop blue, yellow and orange items more often, and online this boost also grows with your Renown. Blue is still rare, yellow is very rare, and orange is still almost impossible.
The boost steps up at Renown 10, 20, 30 and 40, the same steps sigils use. Online, every step pays more than loot did before this update.
The Renown that counts belongs to the player whose game rolls the loot. That is yours for the enemies you meet and for every treasure pile, and the host's for the enemies in a shared dungeon.

The weapons and armour an enemy was wearing can now drop as Magic, Rare or better. This covers every enemy, including champions, elites and bosses. Until now worn gear always dropped plain, so most humanoid enemies only ever left plain iron and steel.
Fixed: after you loaded a save, the worn gear of enemies already in the world dropped plain again.
When a body is full, it now keeps a potion or rest supply ahead of a plain piece of gear.
Potions of Healing drop more often: about 1 enemy in 13 carries one (it was about 1 in 33; animals never carry potions), and about 1 dungeon treasure pile in 5.
Potions of Restore Power (magicka) now drop too: about 1 enemy in 20, and 1 treasure pile in 10.

Rest supplies now drop online (they never did before) and drop more often: about 1 enemy in 14 carries an Ember Jar, Restorative Tonic, Meditation Candle, Waking Salts or Sleeping Draught. Dungeon treasure piles can hold any of those, plus Firewood. Online, General Stores and Alchemists now sell rest supplies too.
These are the offline chances, and the online chances at Renown 20. Online at Renown 1 the boost is half that size, and at Renown 40 it is half again bigger.
Fixed: other players saw your Ember Jar's fire as a plain campfire.
Gathering sometimes turns up silver now. About one harvest in ten (herbs, ore, stone, logs, hides or fish) finds 2–5 silver, up to 30 silver a day.

Bodies, treasure piles and searches can hold silver: 1–4 silver from about 1 body in 20, 1 treasure pile in 8, and 1 search in 7 that turns something up. That includes dungeon treasure, tavern and guild hall treasure, World of Daggerfall's treasure piles and Deep Waters' chests. Up to 20 silver a day.
Each body or pile gets one chance, so leaving a dungeon and coming back doesn't roll it again.
If a find can't reach your account (your connection drops, say), it is kept and sent later, even after a reload.
Found silver shows as a card under the crosshair (Enhanced Plus), or as a line in chat. The Bank's silver panel shows how much you have found today.
Silver finds need you to be online and signed in with a registered account that is at least a week old.
Every sea serpent hoard now holds a Deadlands Ember, the Oblivion Gate's currency. It spends at the Sigil Broker's insignia counter like an ember from a breach.
A ship that fought the serpent has a 1 in 4 chance to find a piece of **Sethrakul's Coilscale**, the serpent's own Aetheric set:
**Sea-Scale (2 pieces):** frost resistance and Endurance.

**Constrict (4 pieces):** each weapon hit on an enemy makes your next hits on that enemy stronger, stacking up to 5 times (bows count). Every enemy has its own stacks, and they fade 6 seconds after your last hit on it.

**Shed Skin (6 pieces):** when an enemy's hit takes you below 35% health, you heal part of your health at once. It then needs a few minutes to recover. It doesn't trigger when a death save, like Unbroken or Divine Grace, has already kept you alive.
Slaying the serpent now pays 40 silver (20 for a ship that stood by). This counts toward the same 150 silver a day as closing breaches and defending towns.
Set bonuses, sigil weapon bonuses and Legendary powers now switch off in arena bouts against other players, the same way they always did in duels.
Every character now carries a **Wallet**. New characters start with one, and existing characters receive one the next time they load.
It holds your letters of credit, Deadlands Embers and Welkynd Shards, and shows your gold and, online, your silver.

In the Enhanced inventory, letters of credit, Deadlands Embers and Welkynd Shards move off the pages and into the Wallet (on the Valuables page). Pick the Wallet to see what it holds and what your letters are worth. Everything inside works just as it does on the pages: pick a piece to open its card, drag it, Shift-click to stow it, or right-click for its menu.
In the classic inventory nothing moves. The Wallet is on the Clothing & Misc page: Use it to see what it holds.
On the hotbar, pressing the Wallet shows what it holds and fetches your silver for the next press. When it can't show your silver, it says why.
The Wallet weighs nothing and never leaves your pack. It can't be dropped, sold, traded, put in your wagon or storage, or set out as a home decoration, and revenants can't steal it.
Fixed: letters of credit now show on the Valuables page in the Enhanced inventory. They were filed under Misc.

Fixed a crash ("Cannot set properties of null (setting 'conceal')") that could happen when a city watchman died from his own attack. This could happen when the Ring of Namira turned his blow back on him, or when thorns, Spite of the Spurned or the Wrath of the Warden answered it.
A watchman no longer flickers out of sight for a moment each time he lands a blow on a monster.
The watch now keeps the town day and night. Three eight-hour shifts (from 06:00, 14:00 and 22:00) and a day off, so there are guards on the streets at night too.
Patrols walk in pairs, side by side, around their own district of the town. In larger towns a watchman stands at each gate, facing the road.
Off duty, a watchman wears his own clothes and is an ordinary townsperson. He changes at home, never in front of you. Larger towns keep a larger watch.

A watchman on duty now greets you by your standing with the law of the region: by name if you are honoured, politely if you are respected, with a curt word for a common citizen, a warning if the law has its eye on you, and a reminder that the watch knows your face if you are a known criminal.

A first minor offence in a region (picking a pocket, trying a locked door, trespassing or sleeping in the street) now draws a "Hold!" warning instead of an arrest. It still costs you standing with the law, and the next one in that region brings the arrest. Serious crimes and known criminals get no warning.

A monster that gets into town can now attack townspeople, not just you: it goes for whoever is nearest, and one blow kills a townsperson. Archers, spellcasters and human enemies still leave townspeople alone.
The watch now comes to defend townspeople a monster is attacking, just as it does when a monster attacks you.
Townspeople run from a monster that comes close, along the street rather than through walls, and keep their distance until it has gone. While frightened they don't stop for you, greet you or chat.

The watch no longer shouts "Halt!" over and over. When it comes for you, the first watchman calls out at once; after that only one of them calls, at most once every 15 seconds, and nobody calls while a window is open.
All of this is in the living world (the enhanced skin with the living world switched on). Classic play keeps Daggerfall's own watch and townspeople.
Townspeople who stop to talk now turn to face each other instead of all facing you. Someone who stops for you still turns to you.
A group waits until everyone has walked over before anyone speaks. Then they take turns, with pauses between exchanges, and you hear them only while the whole group is there, standing together.

People keep the same company for about two minutes before moving on (it used to change every 40 seconds), and each square keeps its own rhythm. The town no longer falls silent all at once and then has ten people talking in the same moment.

Much less repetition. The common trades, mornings, days, evenings and nights all have more to say, and nobody starts the same conversation twice in a row. Morning greetings are heard only in the morning, and talk of other places names real towns on the town's roads.
Indoors, people at a table start talking as soon as they sit down together. Someone who joins waits for the current exchange to end, and the group stays seated while they talk.
A stranger who said nothing as you walked past now speaks when you stop in front of them.
Paying your fine no longer counts as killing the watchman who walked away: his household no longer turns against you, and he goes back to his rounds.

A townsperson the watch turns into a guard keeps who they are, and returns to their day when the guard walks away. A watchman killed by a monster is mourned by the town instead of being counted against you.
Two crimes at the same moment no longer bring more guards than the limit, or turn the same townsperson into a guard twice.
Online, another player's watch no longer shows the same watchman twice (with the updated server).
In the biggest cities the watch now reaches its post by the start of its shift and stays to the end of it.

The large dark see-through box that hung under an enemy's health bar is gone. A foe at rest now shows only its thin wind-up track (the strip that fills amber as it winds up a blow), as it was meant to.
With the diamond quick-slot style, the status-effect icons that move beside the diamond (on a phone held sideways, or with the chat open) no longer sit on a dark box.
An empty spell quick-slot no longer leaves a gap under it that pushed the quick block up.
At sea, an empty fire-barrel battery no longer stretches the gun rose on the ship plate.

Townspeople no longer stand inside building walls or out over the harbour water. Wherever they stop to chat or wait is now open street, spread around the spot rather than bunched against a wall, and when they move between those places they go round corners instead of through them.

Townspeople no longer walk on the spot, running into whatever is in front of them, while the game works out their next route (this happened mostly in big cities). They now stand still, then set off from where they are.

Travellers on the roads no longer camp for the night, fight, or leave their fallen out in the sea where a road runs along the coast. Caught on a wet stretch at dusk, a party walks on to the first dry ground and camps there, and picks up its journey from that camp in the morning. Where no dry ground lies ahead on its road, it walks on to the town it was heading for.

Other players no longer run in place. When a player's movement stops reaching you - they tabbed out, their connection hiccupped, or the server was restarting - their character used to keep running on the spot (for up to 80 seconds if they never came back). Now they stand still until they move again. That includes players who had already gone quiet before you arrived in their area.
Distant players in a big crowd walk smoothly. A far-away player whose computer was running at a low frame rate used to stop and start every second or so; now they keep walking.

Lantern shadows cost much less to prepare. With Steady shadows on (the default), every lantern near a walker or a swaying tree redraws its shadow every frame, and each of its six shadow views used to look over everything in the town to find what to draw. Now each lantern looks once, at what can actually reach it - and a still scene does not look at all. The shadows themselves are exactly what they were.

The chat's player list no longer rebuilds and re-sorts itself every frame while the chat is open. On a busy server that was costing the frame more the more players were online. The friends list sorts faster too.
Settings are read a little faster everywhere.

Quests that wouldn't start in towns redesigned by Beautiful Villages and Beautiful Cities now start. When the mods took away a building a quest needs (a second tavern, enough houses, a weaponsmith, a pawnshop), the quest uses the nearest town that has one. This covers villages that lost a tavern, the Kynareth temples, manors, and Beautiful Cities' shops. A quest that never fit a town, even in Daggerfall's own layout, still isn't offered there.
Pothago's Dark Brotherhood contract that needs a weaponsmith now starts, using the nearest one in the next region.
A quest character whose usual building is gone from their town lives in a house of that town, not in another town.

Thieves Guild and Dark Brotherhood contracts can be handed in again after a town's layout changes. A temple priest is always found in their own god's temple, and a questor still standing where you met them stays there.
Shared party quests no longer move their quest location to another building every time the party syncs, and party members see the same house name.
An item or person placed in a quest building after it was shared now appears for every party member.
Every Beautiful Villages temple has its god's Daedra summoner again. The summoner stands apart from the priest, so clicking the priest always reaches the priest.
A speed readout. At the helm, your ship's speed through the water shows beside her name, in knots.

No more tacking. Your ship sails on every heading. Pointed straight into the wind she makes a little over half her best speed; before, she stalled or was blown backwards. She is fastest with the wind behind her, off to one side.
More speed. Ships are faster under sail. A galleon with the wind on her side is nearly two thirds faster than before.
A storm still drives her harder, up to twice what a fair breeze does. In fog she keeps nearly a third of her speed instead of lying becalmed.
Every ship answers the helm as she did before: she gathers speed, loses it and turns at her new speed as she did at her old one. At her new speed she turns on a wider circle, as a faster ship does.
Sails no longer flap uselessly or blow backwards when you point into the wind, and she can no longer get stuck "in irons".
The helm trims the sails itself, so the trim buttons and keys are gone under Responsive.
Overworld travel by sea sails straight for a port that lies upwind instead of zig-zagging. It steers well clear of islands at the new speeds, and sails through fog instead of rowing.
Heaving to beside a ship that has struck her colours stops you within boarding reach. At storm speeds it is offered as you come up on her, early enough to stop alongside.
Rowing after you strike sail no longer holds your speed: she slows as fast as she does with no oars out, then rows on.
In a storm, a galleon or Carrack no longer vanishes from other players' screens.
A short hiccup in the connection no longer puts you off a friend's ship you are riding on.

It no longer teleports. It swims every move it makes. For a Rising Maw or a coil it dashes at you under the water, and a wake on the surface shows where it is going. The Maelstrom now forms where the serpent is swimming, and always inside its waters.
It aims where you are going. A Rising Maw, a coil, a spit or a ram is aimed where your ship will be when it lands. Turn or slow when you see it coming.

It closes in on the surface. If you are too far away for it to reach in time, it surges at you above the water, where your guns can hit it, faster than you are sailing up to its own top speed. Outsail it for about 12 seconds and it gives up and picks again.
Your hits count. A broadside is judged where the serpent was when the shot landed, so a volley fired just before it moves is no longer wasted.

Two ships can win. While exactly two ships are fighting it, its attacks deal two thirds of their damage: blows, coils, the Maelstrom and venom alike, crew losses included. A rowboat or a friend riding on your deck is not a second ship. In fair weather one ship alone still cannot beat it. Three or more ships take full damage, as before.
A coil wraps round your ship the way its body lies, and no longer sweeps across your deck as it closes and lets go.
A short drop in your connection no longer throws the serpent back across the water when you reconnect. If everyone sails away and comes back later, it is where it was, not somewhere new.
Its wake no longer crowds out the splashes of your own cannon fire.
An older version of the game is told to reload, and cannot fight until it has. While it reloads, it no longer counts as a ship in the fight.
It moves smoothly on every screen, even for players whose connection lags behind, and no longer jumps when a relay restarts.
A ship that wrecks inside a coil is let go.

Fixed logins failing for everyone. The account server was overwhelmed by every game checking every town's yard decorations each minute. Yards are now only fetched for towns near you, the server keeps a short copy instead of asking its database each time, and a failed fetch waits longer each time instead of retrying every 10 seconds.

Your crew lasts twice as long. Cannon fire, fires on deck, rams and the sea serpent's blows all take half as many of your men. Against a ship of the line your hull now gives out before your crew does.
Swivel-gun boats (pirate sloops, coasting traders) still go for your crew first, but at half the old pace. Enemy crews are unchanged.

Your galleon's broadside hits like six guns. It has five gunports a side, one fewer than the old galleon, so each ball now does 20% more damage to hulls and sails. Pirates size your galleon up by it. Enemy captains' galleons are unchanged.

No gameplay changes in this update. The developers' notes and code comments that point at specific places in the game's code now name the code itself instead of a line number. Every update used to shift those numbers, and updates kept colliding over them, which slowed releases down. That no longer happens.

Hundreds of those pointers were wrong, and are fixed. While rebuilding them, every pointer was checked against the code it was first written for. The ones that had drifted onto the wrong code were moved back, so the game's design notes describe the game accurately again.
A yard decoration can now stand at most 4 m above the ground. Stacking pieces into towers is no longer possible. If you try to place or move a piece higher, the decorator says why.
Pieces already standing higher than that stay where they are. You can still move them down or remove them.

Turn placed pieces in place. In the Decorate panel's "In this room" and "In this yard" views, choose a piece and press Turn left or Turn right. Each press turns it 15 degrees where it stands, at once, for free, without picking it up. A flat picture flips to face the other way. Doors still turn with their doorway (Move).
Changing a piece's light, storage or station while it is being turned no longer undoes the other change.

Project Legacy (by Lattymoy, Ghð§† and Positronico) is now part of the game and is on by default (you can turn it off on its tile in Features). Every new character founds a house, unless you choose No lineage online: a surname, a seat in the first town you stand in, and often a brother or sister or two you can play later.
When you create a character you choose how death works for your house. Online the realm keeps your house, and the choice is an Enhanced Plus popup with a third answer:

Enduring: death isn't the end, but it costs you. Arkay takes years from your life, and the price depends on your race's lifespan. In old age you get the option to pass the mantle to an heir. When your years run out, your line carries on.
Bloodline: death is final. A Succession window opens and you pick who takes the mantle: any living member of the family, or, if the fallen was meant to have an heir, a newborn child of theirs.
No lineage (online): no house and no heirs. Death works the way it always has online. Offline the choice keeps its two answers; to play there without a house, turn Project Legacy off in Features.
Heirs are born, not copied. Their stats, skills, career and race draw on their parents', with a share of the family estate (up to 9,900 gold, paid as a letter of credit).
A character with a one-word name founds a house named for its seat: the first town you reach makes Janome's family the house "of Sentinel", brothers and sisters included, and the game tells you so.
A fallen character may leave behind an heirloom, their most valuable worn weapon or armour, renamed for the house.

Their remains lie where they fell, together with the heirloom and part of their purse. Their heir gets the death quest "The Bones of <name>": it's in the journal, followed by the Quest Guide, and circled on the map. Reach the spot and the remains open like any container: take what you want, and anything you leave stays with them for your next visit.
If you sell or drop the bones, they return to where your ancestor fell.

Lay the remains to rest at a temple or at the family seat. You get the ancestor's blessing (+3 to their best skill, at most +9 on any one skill), and the heirloom grows stronger with each generation that carries it home.

Family members you aren't playing now live in the world. If your line owns a house, they live in the family home. Choose which house that is on the Family tab's House page. With no house, they live in your family's seat town, in a house the town lends them.
They keep a daily routine like the town's other residents: asleep at home at night, out in the market and the streets by day.

A family member you've played appears in their own body: their race and the gear they wore at their last save, drawn the way other players are drawn online (the Other players card in Features decides how). Someone you've never played wears the town's own clothes.

Talk to one and they greet you as family ("Mother! You're home."). You can then Play as them, have a normal Talk, or say Goodbye. Your current character is saved first. A member you've never played starts out in the town where you met them.
Save a character inside one of your family's houses and they'll be waiting there when you switch to someone else. Save them anywhere else and they're "on their own journey" until you play them again.
In conversation, a family member shows their own face, the one picked when they were created.
A family member you kill is dead for good, and the House page records who killed them. One a monster kills in the street is dead for good too, and the town hears of it.
On by default. You can turn it off with Family In World in Project Legacy's settings.
A townsperson who counts you a friend can be courted: ask them about Courtship in conversation, once a day. How it goes depends on your Personality, your Etiquette and your tone.
When their heart is full, ask for their hand (Marriage). You're wed at the temple of their town: walk in and you're asked whether to marry there and whether they take your house's name.

Your spouse joins the house, keeping their own face and their own day. They live in your family's house in their town if your line has one there, otherwise in their own home. Every thirty days there's a one-in-four chance of a child, at most six with each spouse. Children can't be played until the mantle passes to them.
If someone you're courting dies, the courtship ends.

A child born to the house inherits part of their parent's reputation: a quarter of their standing with each region's law and with each guild, and half of how each townsperson felt about them. ("Your mother saved my son.") A grudge carries over too.
Towns talk about your house. A death, a laying to rest, a wedding and a birth are news for a week in the town where it happened and in your family's seat.
The revenant that killed your ancestor comes after their heir. The journal and the House page name it.

Characters made before this update have no house online. Online, a house is founded only when a character is made, so to play Project Legacy online, make a new character. Your existing characters play exactly as before, and their Family tab says why they have no house.
Online, your family lives in the realm: every device you play on sees the same house, its living and its dead.
Bloodline is open online. A Bloodline death online is final everywhere: no older save, on any device, can be played past it. The heir you choose is born into the realm as that member of the family.

Your house's name shows under your name online - over your head, on your Inspect card and on your character list: "☠ Ysolde II of House Hlaalu". The skull marks a Bloodline; the numeral, the second of the house to bear that name.

Two players can wed. Stand in a temple together, inspect the other player and press Propose marriage; they answer yes or no. Each of you keeps your own house, and each family records the other as a spouse. Children come to each house in its own time.
If your spouse's character dies or is deleted, word reaches you the next time you're online (within ten minutes if you are). You may wed again.
A fallen character's Stores, professions and market place fall with them: nothing of theirs can be withdrawn or used after their death.
The homes you own in the realm are your family's houses. Your family lives in them, and a character saved in one waits there, just as offline.

The pause window has a new Family tab, between Holdings and System, with three pages: the Tree (zoom, pan, play as a sibling, pass the mantle, and where each member lives), the House (model, seat, generations, the living and the fallen, and your homes) and the Hall of Ancestors (every house you have founded). Keypad `/` opens it.

Your character sheet (the pause window's Stats tab) shows your house: its model and your generation, and in an Enduring house your age against your lifespan, the years Arkay has taken, and when you become an elder.

A permadeath can't be undone by quick-loading, closing the game under the death screen, or a second tab of the same family. The death is recorded the moment it happens, and if the browser's storage refuses to save it, you're told and it's tried again.
Loading an older save of a fallen or retired family member shows the house's waiting Succession, or offers you the member who carries the line now, instead of letting you play the past.
An heir is saved the moment they're born. If that first save fails, nothing is lost: reload and they're born again, inheritance and all.
An heirloom can't be taken twice by rewinding or switching between family members, and an ancestor's remains can't be stashed in a chest to make a second set of bones.

A character copied from online to offline play starts a family of their own instead of sharing the original's (none if it chose No lineage). One copied into online play has no house there, like any character made before this update.
Holding a key can't confirm a choice by accident. The line's end and "Play as" at a family meeting both ask twice. The Family tab can be walked with Tab.

The heir no longer inherits the dead character's leftover state. Sibling kits use the sibling's own race and class. Switching characters no longer drops you at the map's corner. Plus the other fixes listed in the design record.
Online characters no longer get forced onto Oblivion leveling. A new online character levels the Daggerfall way. The Oblivion option is shown locked as "Offline characters only".
Characters already using Oblivion leveling online keep it.
An offline Oblivion character you bring online switches to Daggerfall leveling, starting from its current level. Any level-up it had already earned is kept.

Online characters on Oblivion leveling switch to Daggerfall leveling the next time you play them. You keep your level and skills, and any level-up you had already earned. A message tells you once the world loads.

On the Project Legacy question (Enduring, Bloodline, No lineage) and the leveling question, moving the mouse no longer jumps the highlight between options. The option under your pointer is the one highlighted, and clicking it selects it.

Fixed the account server falling over again, which left homes and yards without their decorations. When the server slowed down, every game asked it again within seconds, and that kept it down. Games now wait longer after each failed ask, so a busy minute passes instead of turning into an outage.
Signing into a room after a slow server answer no longer asks for a second sign-in ticket, so you reconnect sooner.
Signing in, joining a room and loading a town's house layouts now cost the account server far less work, so busy evenings are less likely to slow it down or leave decorations missing.
An online family that hasn't changed since the last checkpoint is no longer uploaded again at every checkpoint.

With the living world on, 407 of the game's 410 cities (Ripmarket among them) had nobody walking their streets at any hour. A city's walls and closed gates cut its streets off from the fields around it, and the townspeople were being laid out on the fields' side, where none of their doors are, so every one of them stayed indoors all day. The streets now fill again by day, travellers leave by the gates, and the watch keeps its posts there. Daggerfall, Wayrest and Sentinel were not affected.

In 14 cities whose palace stands in its own walled grounds (Sentinel among them), the whole city watch lived at the palace and never came out. The watch now lives where its door opens onto the streets, so it walks its patrols and keeps its posts.
People waiting at the same spot keep a little room from one another and from the groups talking there.
Two who leave a shop or a tavern at the same moment walk out in single file.
A walker steps aside, keeping right, for anyone standing or coming the other way.
In the towns measured, between a tenth and over half of the people in view at midday or in the evening were standing inside someone else; now almost nobody is.
The town square now has several gathering points across it, and each townsperson keeps to their own.
Every neighbourhood has a corner where its people meet, and people's favourite places are the ones near their homes.
Stall-keepers set up either at the square or at their own market.
People head out for the evening, and to the morning market, at their own time instead of all on the hour.
In the towns measured, the busiest spot in the evening went from 30-64 people (all around one point of the square) to 6-17.
A townsperson who stops for you now stays exactly where they stopped.

They belong to the guild of their trade or class: scholars, booksellers' and alchemists' people and mages to the Mages Guild; smiths and fighters to the Fighters Guild; courtiers and knights to the town's knightly order. Each spends an evening at their guild hall twice a week.
Sellswords and adventurers now go to their own guild's hall instead of whichever hall is nearest.

Errands go into a shop more often, and to a shop the person has business at: shopkeepers bank their takings, scholars visit the library and the bookseller, households the general store and the clothier.
The people you find inside a guild hall are now its own guild's members. Daggerfall's guild halls now see 18 visitors a day instead of 12, and its banks 7 instead of 2.
Travellers staying at a tavern, sailors ashore and adventurers who live there each have a room by one of its beds.
You'll find them up in their room in the morning and again before bed. They come down to the common room for breakfast and supper, and sleep out of sight.
A room you rent is never given to a lodger.

Guild members walk the streets in their guild's classes: Mages Guild members in a mage's hooded robes, Fighters Guild members in a warrior's arms and armour, the knights of an order as knights. Priests wear the healer's robes. Adventurers, sellswords and couriers wear their own class all day, not only on their way out of town.

Someone keeping their place on their own appears as one of Daggerfall's own pictures of their kind: an old beggar at their pitch, a merchant, a blacksmith or a porter at their stall, a monk at the temple door in the morning, a lord or a lady at home in the palace. Each kind has several pictures, and the animated ones move as they do in the game.
They become themselves again the moment they walk on or join a conversation. A look never changes while you are watching.
In Daggerfall city, 24 of its 317 people now walk in a class, and 17-28 stand as still pictures by day.
Right-click the Overworld or the world map (V) to place a waypoint. Give it a name and a flag colour, and choose who it is for: you alone, your party or your guild.
Party and guild waypoints are shared with the other members. Only the player who placed one can change it for everyone; anyone can rename or remove one on their own screen.
Follow a waypoint from the Overworld's filters: it stays marked at the edge of the screen with its distance. A waypoint's own menu can also send you travelling there.
Leaving a party or a guild removes its waypoints.
Two speed dials while travelling: the journey's speed and the speed while enemies are near. Both go x5, x10, x20, x30, x40 and x60, and x100 on a road only.
Leaving a road drops a dial at x100 to x60 at once; it does not climb back by itself. Journeys start at x60 - turn the dial up to x100 on a road.
The dials are in every interface: the Overworld's panel, the Enhanced journey bar, and a small speed box with the classic interface and GrimoireUI.
The Overworld's filters now sit in their own box at the bottom left, which folds away and can be moved like the rest of the HUD.
An enemy's health bar no longer shows an empty box under it; the poise bar appears only when there is something to show, and the bar has one shadow instead of two.

With Enhanced Lighting on, shadows no longer blink all at once in some rooms. The shadow cache behind it is now off by default; turn it back on under Enhanced Lighting with "Shadow cache (faster, may flicker)".
Shadows hold steady through a brief hitch instead of flashing.
Fixed a cat meowing many times a second while you looked at certain townspeople (reported in Chesterwark).

Fixed "Protect an Honored Mage" (Mages Guild) online: the three-hour guard could end before the assassins came, leaving the quest impossible to finish. The guard now lasts its full three hours of play, and the attack always comes inside it. A guard that already ended this way stays unfinished.

Steel armour has a new look on the Morrowind body: a full suit of plate - breastplate, pauldrons, gauntlets, greaves, boots and helm - made for the port. It shows on your character in third person, on the paperdoll, on other players, and as your gauntlets in first person.

A new switch under Features > Combat, Steel Helm: Closed (a visor and a blue plume, the default) or Open (a nasal helm with a mail aventail that shows the face). It changes at once, and it is how your game draws every steel helm - yours and other players'.
The grass can now be a meadow made from new hand-drawn sprites: tall and short green tufts, flowering tufts, dry tufts and bushes, mixed across the land.
Every tuft and bush grows to its own size. Whole patches run taller or shorter, so the land no longer looks the same everywhere.
Flowers gather in lush patches and dry grass in poor ones. Bushes turn up here and there, from shin-high to shoulder-high.

The meadow doesn't turn to face you. Each tuft and bush stands on crossed cards like the low-poly trees, so you see it from every side as you walk round it, and a low sun lights one face more than the other.

The meadow follows the ground: its greens take the colour of the grass they grow on, so it fits every climate and season (flowers keep their own colours), and on a hillside each tuft stands on the slope instead of hanging over it.
The meadow sways in the wind the way the trees do. Bushes are stiffer than grass, as the world's bushes are.
The meadow does about the same vertex work as the old pixel tufts.
Crossing into a new part of the map no longer makes all the grass jump to a new pose in the wind. The trees no longer jump there either.
Pixel-style grass tufts no longer swap to different pictures when you cross into a new part of the map.

Grass is now off by default. Turn it on under Settings › Grass with Full, Half or Quarter. If you had it on Full before, it is off after this update until you turn it back on; Half and Quarter are kept.
Grass › Style defaults to Meadow. Pixel (the old tufts) and Smooth are still there.
Wind › Trees sway is now just Sway: it moves the grass as well as the trees, and turning it off holds both still.

Every weapon type now has the same base condition, the Warhammer's 1,600. Daggers, tantos and short bows started at 50 and long bows at 100, so they broke 16 to 32 times sooner than a warhammer of the same metal.
Enchanted weapons gain the most. A Cast-When-Strikes enchantment costs 10 condition a strike, so an iron Worm's Tooth now lasts 160 strikes instead of 5.

A Cast-When-Held enchantment pays its spell's casting cost in condition the first time it is equipped, often over a hundred. That broke an iron dagger, tanto or short bow on the spot. Now the weapon keeps the rest and lasts about four game days.
Bows no longer break after a couple of dozen hits: an iron short bow takes about 800 hits of 20 damage.
Light weapons and bows cost less to keep up, because a repair is priced by the share of condition lost.

Your weapons are updated when you load a save and keep the same percentage of condition. A broken weapon stays broken, and a half-worn dagger is half of its new pool. That covers every weapon your save holds, wherever it is, and a family heirloom paid to an heir. A weapon that comes back from the online market, a guild vault or a trade is updated the first time it takes wear.

When you load, older items get their fixes wherever your save keeps them, not only in your pack, wagon and containers. The fixes: a weapon moves to the new condition pool, an item made with no condition gets one, Roleplay & Realism armour gets back the Brigandine, Fur or Mail word its name lost, old Sigil Stones are named Deadlands Embers, and a rolled jewel stuck on an unwearable Wand becomes an Amulet.

That now includes things set out in your house, quest items, a revenant's takings and a sworn revenant's pack, enemies' and guards' gear, and Project Legacy's bequests and remains. Before, an item in one of those places kept its old record until you carried it back and loaded again.
Project Legacy: an heir's bequest gets the same fixes when it is paid, and a fallen relative's remains get them when you open them.
A rolled Wand you set out in your house becomes an Amulet, but it still looks like a wand where it stands until you pick it up.
Customs now counts gold and letters of credit in a sworn revenant companion's pack, the same as a crew companion's pack. Before, a revenant could carry any amount across uncapped.

A home the Arena moved kept emptying. Homes in Daggerfall city that were moved out of the Arena's way could have their storage emptied at login: every chest, the storage pieces and the things standing in the room. It happened while the account server was failing, as it did through 6 October. The move no longer touches a home its owner already lives in. Items already lost this way are not brought back by this update.
A moved home's crate could stay hidden. The crate of belongings that comes with a moved house now shows up in the new house when the city uses the Beautiful Cities layout.

Towns with three or more bulletin boards no longer show two or three Notice Boards. Each town has one: the board nearest the town's middle. The other boards are Daggerfall's rumour boards again, as they are offline. Bounty Boards are unchanged.
The Notice Board now says "Notice Board" when you point at it.
Notes stand straight, the text is larger, and anything written on the cork sits on a dark panel.
On a phone the tab row scrolls sideways, so Guilds and Seat can be reached.
Tabs show counts: new notes on Notices, and open writs on Work once you've looked at it.
Notices shows town and server news first, then players' notes.
Work shows "Court writs today" at the top instead of under the last card.
Views are grouped: Buy (Materials, Crafted, Auctions, Goods), Sell (Orders, My listings), then History.
Your silver is shown at the top, and listings have column names.
The Weavers' and Apothecaries' counters are folded under one "Suppliers" line.
My listings is split into the List form, your listings, auctions, bids and buy orders. Form fields are labelled (a stall's "Put up a piece" form too), and the List button is full size again.
The Vendors list has the same column names.
The Notice Board's window now downloads in the background after the game starts, so it is usually ready the first time you open it.
The Market starts loading as soon as the board opens.
The Seat tab loads its standings and works at the same time.
Split into panels: the Charter, This week (Muster, Reckoning, Turning), the battle, Standings, Your guild, the holder's orders, the Works and the Chronicle.
Each challenging guild has a bar showing how close it is to claiming the Charter or winning the Right of Siege.
New "How the seat war works" guide: pledging, earning influence, claiming, sieges and holding.

Messages across the board, Market, Work, Vendors and Seat tabs are shorter and plainer. For example, "The counting-house is not answering. The market cannot be read now." is now "The market did not load."

Slurs and crude words are starred out () in chat on every channel, Notice Board notes, guild notes, letters and shared journal pages. The rest of the message stays as written, and ordinary words that only contain a filtered one ("spiced wine", "snigger", "don't get cocky") are left alone.
Notes pinned before this update are starred too when a board is read.
A guild rank name or a ship's name with such a word is refused, and the message names the word.
A custom class name with such a word isn't shown to other players, and a maker's mark with one is left off the item.
A name given with the Item Maker is starred wherever the item is shown.
The inspect card is tidied up: the name always keeps its line, badges sit on their own row under it, and the duel, breach, town and serpent records are compact plaques.
Worn gear is grouped into In hand, Armour, Clothing and Jewellery. A pair, such as two rings, shares one row.
The wallet's sheet is now a ledger: Coin (gold, silver) and In the wallet (letters of credit, Deadlands Embers, Welkynd Shards), with each amount lined up on the right.
The shadow cache is on again by default, so lamp-lit rooms such as taverns, shops and guild halls get their frame rate back.

Fixed the shadow flicker with Enhanced Lighting on Windows: a rapid, strobing flicker on some NVIDIA cards, and on others every shadow in a room blinking at once. It came from how the cached shadows were copied on Direct3D, not from the cache itself.
The "Shadow cache (faster, may flicker)" switch is gone from Enhanced Lighting. It is no longer needed.
Trees, bushes and rocks no longer stand on roads and tracks, and their branches no longer hang over them. This includes the 3D trees from Low Poly Trees.
Herb patches, ore veins on open stone and Motherlodes keep off the roads too.
Forests no longer grow across dirt tracks.
Settings › Clear roadsides (on by default). Off lets them grow up to the edge of the road, as Daggerfall does.

Where two climates meet, the land no longer changes along a straight line. The border wanders and breaks into patches about two hundred metres deep: grass thins out into sand, rock creeps into the woods, snow comes in drifts.
The trees follow the same border. Near it, each tree belongs to the climate of the ground it stands on.
The grass follows it too.
Settings › Blended climates (on by default). Off changes them at a straight edge, as Daggerfall does.
In winter, the trees of a wood are cover the way they are the rest of the year: enemies hide behind the trunk and under the crown.

Big cities no longer drop to a frame or two a second between 4 and 6 in the morning (game time). Every time the game looked at a city watchman who sets out for their post before the day begins, it worked out the whole town's day again from scratch - hundreds of townspeople, every frame. It was worst in the great cities, Daggerfall among them; offline the slowdown kept itself going, and online it came back with every in-game dawn. The people on the street are exactly where they were before.
A port whose harbour lies far from any street no longer searches for its dock four times a second.

Repairs Objects now mends the gear you are wearing. Before, each repair went to the first damaged thing anywhere in your pack: a worn piece of loot, a looted book, spare shoes, even a lit torch's fuel. The armour and weapons you wore were rarely touched. Now it mends the most worn piece you are wearing first. Only when everything you wear is whole does it move on to your pack, again most worn first.

Weapons mend at a dagger's pace. Since every weapon type was given the same condition pool, a repair of 1 point barely moved a weapon. Every weapon now mends 32 points every four game minutes (about every 20 seconds of play), the share a dagger always got: 2% for iron and 0.25% for Daedric. A battered weapon is like new in under three game hours at iron, about eight at Dwarven and about a day at Daedric.
