It no longer refills what a smith won't repair. That means torches, lanterns, candles, arrows, a campfire's fuel, a bedroll's nights and the doses of Waking Salts and Meditation Candles.
Armour, clothing and jewellery still mend Daggerfall's 1 point at a time. So do the uses of classic magic items and artifacts.
Enchanted items still mend only with Allow Magic Repairs, which is on by default and always on online.
It still mends one piece every four game minutes, and only for you.
The grass grows by default again, at Full, in the meadow style.
If you picked Half, Quarter or Off yourself, your choice is kept. If you turned the grass off during the day it was off by default, it is on again: turn it off in Features > Grass.
The grass is cheaper to draw, and looks exactly the same. The biggest gain is on Windows, the desktop app included, and on Macs.
If the outdoors still run slow, Features > Grass > Half halves the grass's cost.

Lamp posts, torches, braziers and the other lights you place in your home's yard now light the ground and walls around them at night, the way the town's street lamps light theirs: the same light (a warm flame with Enhanced Lighting, white without it) and the same flicker, from 17:00 to 08:00, the hours the town's lanterns are lit.
Up to eight lamps light in each yard, the most any Daggerfall town block has. Lamps placed after the eighth stay dark until one of the first eight is taken down.
A lamp you scale up casts a bigger pool of light.
Lamps you placed before this update light up on their own. You don't need to switch anything on.

Mining, Logging, Herbalism (the Basket included), Fishing and Hunting no longer stop for the day. The 60 harvests a day in each profession (120 across your characters), the 40 hauls a day and the 30 hides a day are gone.
Each node can still be worked once a day by each character, so the next harvest is wherever the next node stands.
The chip under the compass shows the day's count without a limit ("Mining 34 - 12 today"), and so does the Professions tab.
Rare hides (tiers 5 and 6): 3 a day for your account.
Veins in dungeons nobody has vouched for: 4 a day for your account.

The two towers in Castle Daggerfall's courtyard are whole again. Every floor, stair, lantern and piece of furniture is where it belongs, the rooms are lit, and the stairwells no longer open onto the void.
Project Legacy: the Family tab's House page can now move your family's seat to the town you are standing in. Press Make <town> the family seat, then press again to confirm.
Your heirs are born in the new seat, your fallen can be laid to rest there, and a family without a home of its own lives there. Your house keeps its name.
When you aren't standing in another town, the House page tells you how to move the seat.
Online, every character now starts Privateer's Hold on their own, with its enemies alive, its doors shut and its loot untouched. Other players are back as soon as you step outside.
If you step out and come back in the same session, the enemies you defeated and the chests you emptied stay that way for up to an hour, as in other dungeons online.
Local chat in the Hold now tells you that nobody can hear you there.

You can no longer climb while you fast travel on the Overworld, whether on a journey or holding the movement keys under the travel view. Walking into a wall at 60x speed no longer farms the Climbing skill, and travellers no longer fall off the rocks along the way.
You can't start a journey while hanging on a wall. Climb down first.
Climbing works as before at walking pace.
WAITS: four long online waits shortened - bank hours, Daedra summoning, the King of Worms' messenger, banishment
The steel plate cuirass now has its skirt, painted with its own texture.
The steel plate no longer T-poses in game. It follows the body's arms and legs.
Attacks now keep up with your attack speed. At high Speed every blow is drawn, and each one connects when its damage does.
Other players' fast attacks play at their pace too.
Casting a spell plays the Morrowind casting animation through to the end, and the spell leaves your hands on the cast's release.
Your weapon leaves your hand while a spell is readied.

With Morrowind data installed, spells use Morrowind's own effects: the glow around the caster and on your hands, the bolt a target spell flies as, the hit on whoever it lands on, and the burst of an area spell. Spells from enemies and other players show the casting glow and the bolt too.
New switch under Features > Combat: Morrowind Spell Effects, on by default.
With Travel Options on, a journey down a steep road follows the road instead of flying off it into a fall.

If the roads arrive after you have loaded in (online, or on a slow connection), whatever lies on the ground stays on it as the ground settles, and so do you. A download of the roads that never answers is tried again instead of leaving you on a roadless world.

Resistance from rolled gear now counts up to 45% per element, and only fills an Aetheric piece's resistance up to that same 45%. Two +25% Fire rings no longer make you immune to fire spells. An Aetheric piece's own resistance, set bonuses, spells, your race and your class still count in full.

Luck now multiplies drop chances (half at Luck 0, half again at Luck 100) instead of adding a flat amount. Low-luck characters can find Legendaries again, and high luck no longer outweighs where you loot.

Clothing can drop as Magic and Rare with lines of its own: standing with a social group, warmth and weatherproofing (for Climates & Calories), Personality, and street skills - footwear leans to movement skills. Warmth and weatherproof lines say "(survival off)" when survival is off.
Superior and Masterwork clothing you make now comes out Magic and Rare, as crafted weapons and armour already did.

Six Legendary garments, each with a power: the Alik'r Wayfarer's Robes (the heat is felt 20 less), the Wrothgar Pass Mantle (the cold is felt 20 less), the Vestments of Stendarr (Restoration spells cost 25% less), the Pilgrim's Sandals (you tire 25% slower, falls hurt half as much), the Silks of Queen Barenziah (+5 standing with every group) and the Shade's Cowl (+25 Stealth while hooded). Rare clothing can take their powers at the Reforge's Imprint.
With the loot rarity setting off, clothing stays exactly as in Daggerfall.

One Rare or Legendary in twelve from a body or a pile is cursed: one extra bonus line and one drawback (a bad reputation, bad reactions, damage or wear in holy places, weaker blows against a kind of foe, or a health leech). A drawback never cancels one of the item's own bonuses. You won't know until it is identified - then the card reads "Cursed Rare".
A temple's Cure Disease priest now offers Lift Curse: the drawback goes, the bonus line stays. It costs a quarter of the item's value, at least 300 gold.
Hone: raise one line within its own range. It always goes up; each hone on an item doubles the next one's price.

Scry: name a kind of foe and the guild marks the nearest dungeon of theirs in your region that isn't on your map yet (3 Welkynd Shards and 500 gold). An unfound Legendary in the Codex points you there.

Sockets: some Rares and Legendaries carry an empty socket. Set one of Daggerfall's eight gems in it for 100 gold for a bonus that depends on the gem and the item; unsetting shatters the gem. A gem you are carrying for a quest is never offered.
Salvage every Magic: one button on the Salvage page, asked first.
Item cards now compare what the item would change against what it would replace: up or down by how much, "new", and the lines you would lose. Resistance lines show how much would count under the cap.
Junk: mark gear as junk from its card, and "Sell junk" at a shop puts every junk piece on the counter in one press. A piece you sell loses its junk mark.
Quick loot has a new "Take gear" setting (All, Magic+, Rare+) for the take-all key. Gold, supplies, quest items and Daggerfall's own magic items are always taken, and junk is always left.
The Welkynd Stone (fills your magicka) and the Varla Stone (restores every enchanted item you wear, magic items' charges included) can turn up in the deepest places.

Towns have all their Notice Boards again. In towns with three or more boards, every board that isn't a Bounty Board opens the Notice Board, shows its "new" count, gets a mark on the town map and, in seat towns, flies a pennant.

A raised hood now shields a vampire from the sun. With the hood of a cloak or robe up, a vampire in daylight keeps the +20 to their stats instead of taking the daytime -20. Bare-headed, the -20 still applies in the sun.
The Carrack (the pirate flagship and the merchant carrack) is a new model, fully textured.
Ten gunports, each with its own shutter, and a gun on a platform behind every port. Two bow chasers and a stern barrel.
A companion through her middle house leads down to her gun deck.
Her wheel and rudder turn together. Her anchor is weighed and let go, and rope ladders hang down her side.
She carries seven lanterns, so a carrack at sea is lit at night.
Her rig: a spritsail, fore and main courses, a main topsail and a lateen mizzen. They trim with the wind like every other ship.
The Large Boat (the pirate sloop and the coasting trader) is a new clinker-built model.
All seven of her sail plans are rebuilt on the new hull.
She steers by a tiller: a raked rudder on her sternpost, with the helmsman on a step at her stern.
Seven swivel guns sit on her gunwale: three a side and one at her bow.
A carrack's broadside still hits as hard as before, now from five guns a side instead of seven.
The pirate sloop now closes to 50 m (it was 55), because the new boat is a taller target.

A beaten revenant of rank 1 or 2 now usually breaks and runs, and it really gets away. Before, every flight was run down and it knelt every time, so killing you was almost the only way a revenant grew stronger. Now escaping is the usual way.
A fleeing foe now sprints at twice its walk, which is faster than a player running at average Speed and Running. A fast runner, a bow or a spell can still bring it down.
Fixed: a foe that broke while circling you used to keep circling instead of running away.
From rank 3 nothing changes: you still break its will to make it kneel.

Low Poly trees no longer hang over roads, tracks or town streets. Each tree is drawn no wider than the room it has from the nearest road, track or street. This includes the trees inside towns, farms and other locations, and the ones beside the paved ring round a town.
Trees still stand exactly where they did. Only the drawn size of a tree that would overhang a path changes. A tree planted right on a path shrinks to a sapling.
This follows the Clear roadsides option, which is on by default.

A raised hood now protects a character whose class has the Damage from Sunlight disadvantage. With the hood up they take no sun damage outdoors by day, can fast travel by day, and arrive in daylight rather than being held until dusk.
Bare-headed, the sun works as before. The travel refusal now also says how to lift it: raise the hood of a cloak or robe.
A hood carried in your pack, not worn, doesn't count.
Your third-person sprite no longer flickers between two directions when you start running or strafing at an angle. It turns once and stays turned.

An attack now plays one swing instead of a swing and a follow-through. Each attack art holds two strokes (a slash then a chop, a sweep then its return), and your attacks alternate between them, one stroke per click. Other players see the same stroke you do.
The "PingPong Offset" setting no longer does anything. Under "Attack Strings", PingPong now plays like None and Mixed like Mirror.

A revenant you beat with a party now always kneels for your judgement (or makes its last stand first). Before, if the fight's ownership passed to a party member (for example, after you died mid-fight), it could die outright with no kill or spare choice and no trophy.

You can now interact with your party members while they are under Chameleon, Shadow or Invisibility, and they can interact with you. The F menu and its plaque, trading, showing a page, spell gifting and the Nearby list all reach a concealed party mate.
Concealed players outside your party stay hidden from all of these, as before.
How concealed players are drawn has not changed. With Enhanced Combat Visuals off, a concealed party mate is still not drawn, but F reaches them where they stand.
Players who first played on the evening of September 24 in the Americas now hold the Founder title. The cutoff now counts the 24th in every time zone, not just UTC.

Played before September 25 on another device or browser? Back up that character to the cloud from your account, or bring it into the realm. Founder is granted automatically if that character was played before the cutoff.

Shift-click an item in your pack to drop it in front of you as itself. Several drops fan out on the ground instead of piling up, and never land behind a wall or on a table above the floor. Locked, bound and pack-only items still refuse to leave, and so do your horse and wagon. With your wagon or a chest open, Shift still stows there.
Each item shows its own picture: its Morrowind model when Morrowind data is attached, its classic picture otherwise. Until its picture arrives, a dropped item keeps its loot bag.
Rarity shows on the ground: Magic-or-better items get an outline in their tier's colour, and Rare-or-better ones stand the same line of light the world boss's spoils do.
Items come to rest against walls rather than through them, stop moving while the game is paused, and ride along with a body on a moving deck.

Settings are under Features > Physical Items by demifiend000: turn it off, choose which kinds of loot spill from bodies, how hard it is thrown, and how big items are. Size and outline changes apply straight away.

The profile that opens from your portrait in the top-right corner has been reorganised. It now opens on your portrait, your name and Renown, the title and glyphs you're wearing, and the character you're playing.

Underneath, it is split into sections: Record (duels, breaches closed, towns defended, serpents slain, silver, each in its own tile, with a bar for the share of duels you've won), Characters (each character's Renown, with a bar showing progress to the next level), Wardrobe and Account.
On a wide screen the sections sit side by side in two columns. On a phone the profile now fills the screen, so the menu no longer shows through behind it.
The Close, Sign out and Change password buttons stay pinned to the bottom of the profile, so you never have to scroll to close it.

The main menu buttons are now carved stone slabs in the Enhanced Plus style, all one width. They turn brass when you hover over them or select them with a gamepad, and they follow your chosen Plus colour theme.
On phones the buttons are a little more compact, so the whole menu now fits above the Screenshots and About buttons.

The website now uses the game's stone and brass. Each section is a carved window with brass corner fittings, and the boxes inside it are stone panels. Play, Install, Discord and the section links are stone buttons that turn brass on hover, and Play is brass all the time.
FIELD BUGS 2026-10-07: the board crash, potion names, fishing, black screenshots, guild halls, skinning indoors
WATER-NEXT + AUDIT WATER-NEXT: town puddles dried, the Enhanced water replaced (translucent, swell, shore foam, ripples), audited and its cost measured
Refining for a craft costs no extra station fee. You pay only the craft's fee.
It never refines a material into a lower tier. It won't burn Ghostwood for Charcoal or cure a Dragonling hide into Hardened Leather; do that by hand.
When you are short of something, the box names the raw good you need (e.g. "short of Iron x2"), not the ingot.
When your Stores have no room for what it would refine, the box says so.
If a refining step is refused, the message names the step where the chain stopped.
Materials you can't make yet are dimmed. Those past your rank say the rank they need ("Daedric - rank 90").
The anvil's Weapons, Armour, Tools and Repair Kits are 39 pieces, not 308 rows behind a metal picker.

The first-make bonus (+500 XP) is now paid once per piece per tier, not once per material. Your first Adamantium, Ebony, Orcish or Warforged Longsword (all tier 6) pays it, and the rest of that tier don't. A Wand pays it once for Ironwood or Ghostwood, and Arrows once for any fletching. Pieces you made before still count.
A merged craft keeps the higher of its two XP totals.

Each rank's choice is the higher craft's where it chose, else the other's. If you chose under both at the same rank, you keep the higher craft's choice and may change it once for free - no Marks, in effect at once.
A merged craft offers four choices at a rank, each named for the craft it acts on.
You may still take two crafts past Journeyman - now two of five.
The stations name the craft: "Building 10" at the workbench and the mason's bench, "Smithing 25" at the jeweller's bench, "Provisioning" at the fire and the alchemy station.

Temper at an anvil (Smithing) or a loom (Outfitting): a weapon, a piece of metal armour, leather armour or clothing, one quality step better - Crude to Standard, Standard to Fine, Fine to Superior. Found or made, as long as it is Rare or below. A found piece counts as Standard.
A temper costs half the piece's recipe's main material, rounded up (a Steel Longsword: 2 Steel Ingots; a Leather Cuirass: 3 Cured Leather), needs that recipe's rank, and pays craft XP.

A tempered piece gains condition and loses a little weight. A crafted piece's record is re-signed at its new quality, so the Market shows what it is - and a Fine crafted piece tempered to Superior gains the Superior's Magic roll.
Legendary, Aetheric, artifact and Sigil pieces can't be tempered, and a Masterwork keeps its maker's quality.

Reforge with Essence: from Enchanting 50, an enchanting station rolls one line of a known Magic piece again for 2 Arcane Essence, a Rare's for 5 - the Mages Guild's Reforge, paid in Essence. Once a piece is reforged, only that line again. No XP.
Take a worn piece off first. A shop's station charges its usual fee.

Repair Kits made at an anvil now come in a quality, like other crafted pieces. A Superior or Masterwork kit mends a weapon or armour up to 90% of its condition; any other kit still stops at 75%. Each use still mends a quarter of the piece's condition.
The kit's card says its quality and how far it mends. A Masterwork kit carries its maker's name.
Kits you already own, and field kits found in loot, work as before.
Town ponds no longer show flat painted squares. Tiles with a small island, a corner of water or a flipped diagonal shoreline now take the new water like the rest of the pond (Enhanced look).
Six lone island tiles in town layouts are now dry ground, and some pond edges the puddle removal had wrongly cleared are back.

Towns no longer sit in pits behind sheer walls of earth. The ground round every city, village and dungeon entrance now flows up to it from the surrounding land, so a town on a hillside sits on a hillside.
Coastal towns no longer stand behind cliffs at the beach line; the strand rises to them gently.
Towns on the coast stand on their own land, not dragged down toward the sea.
Rolling hills across the whole country, gentle in some regions and rolling hard in others, taller on the high ground.
Rivers and streams cut their own valleys: the water lies at the bottom, with the hills rising either side.
Mountains: long ridgelines that hold their line for kilometres, with spurs and smooth valleys.
Mountain woods: foothills, half rolling and half ridges.
The Alik'r: dune seas lying across the wind, a long rise to windward and a steep slip face to lee. Dak'fron has mesas and buttes among its dunes.
Rainforest: karst towers standing over plains. Subtropics: soft, broad domes.
Swamps: near-flat, with shallow hollows and low hummocks.
Haunted woods: broken ground gashed by ravines and studded with crags.
Where climates meet, their lands blend across about a map pixel.
Roads and tracks no longer climb every hill. The hills ease down beside a road, so it runs through a gentle corridor or over a saddle, and the hills rise again beside it.
Every player in a room stands on the same ground, even if a town pack failed to load for one of them.

The new steel armour set now moves with the Morrowind body the way Morrowind's own armour does. The gauntlets stay on your hands, the pauldrons on your shoulders and the greaves and boots on your legs, in every pose, in third person and first person. No more T-posing pieces or gauntlets floating over the helm.
Your companions no longer follow you into the Burning Court. They wait outside and rejoin you when you return, with the health and spells they had.

Look around: selecting Info mode underground lights up, for six seconds, what's near you, in sight and nameable (within 8 m). A secrets tier also shows the hidden movers that only a lever chain reaches.

Lever echoes: a lever that moves something out of sight tells you which way. It marks the spot on the dungeon map until you find it, and the mark glows when you reach it. In Info mode, a lever's plaque says which way its work lies.
The way out: the compass points you back to the entrance along the trail you walked. It takes you down a drop you jumped from, and never back up one you can't climb.
Exact quest guidance (optional): a quest's people and things are marked on the dungeon map and the compass - a finished quest's no longer are.
Detect Treasure now also finds what's hidden in searched objects.
Secret walls are no longer labelled "Door".

Online, every dungeon has its own size - small, medium or large - the same for everyone in it. Dungeons that were already small stay small, and about half of all dungeons are medium. The main story's dungeons and Abyss Dungeons are always large.
Medium Dungeons (offline): a new option builds dungeons at a medium size: two interior blocks closed by six.
Dungeon sizes as online (offline): a new option uses the online sizes offline. A quest keeps the size it was set up at, so quests you started online keep their dungeons at the online sizes.

Online, a dungeon now says what it is - Regular Dungeon, Elite Dungeon or Abyss Dungeon - with its size beside it, as in "Elite Dungeon, Small". It shows on the entrance sign, the overworld name plates and the sighting message, and as a line when you go in; the held map says it for the Bay's own dungeons.
One at a time, where the players are: an Abyss Dungeon - a Hollow of the Hour - rises beside a busy city in the region with the most players online.
Seen and heard of: a column of brass-gold light stands over it from the moment it rises, and the taverns of its city talk of it.

Found: the first player to reach its door finds it, and everyone online hears where - by its city, or its region when no city is near. From then on its ring is on the map, its mark is on the compass, and it has a row in the Timers window and a note on the notice board, until it is gone.

The hardest dungeon in the game: three foes at every spot, each four times as tough and hitting two and a half times as hard, drawn from the strongest monsters there are; six elite foes; half again the loot; and no campfires - the Hour is cold.

The Rift: at an Abyss Dungeon's deepest point stands the Rift - a ring of brass light around a dark membrane, tolling like a bell heard under water. Press it or walk into it. Beside it, a small Return of pale light takes you back to the way in. Once the Remnant has fallen the Rift takes no newcomers, but anyone who already went through can step back in while the Hour collapses.

The Shattered Hour: through the Rift lies the moment the Warp left behind - islands of stone and brass hanging in a void, under a sky of brass aurorae, with the Bay's skylines hanging upside down in it and a clock-face of stars whose hands run backwards. Every player sees the same sky at the same moment. The Hour refuses what the Burning Court refuses: no rest, no saving, no map, no Mark or Recall, no regeneration - and no Levitate. The Rift at its back takes you home to the Hollow.

The Orrery of Endings: the Shattered Hour's first hall holds six Ending-stones - Daggerfall, Sentinel, Wayrest, Orsinium, the Underking and the Blades - each showing an hour of twelve. Turn a stone by its handles (the right turns it forward, the left back), and its hidden gears turn others with it. Six Ledger plaques round the hall say in riddles the hour each stone keeps; the dial in the floor lights a segment for every stone at its true hour - how many, not which. Every turn frays the Hour: at 48 it snaps back, resetting the stones and lashing a quarter of their health from everyone in the hall whose turns did not bring the stones nearer the Concord - whoever was setting them right, or never touched one, is spared. While others are turning, a player who has turned the stones the wrong way six times since the last snap has to wait, and guests count as one player. Set every stone right - the Concord - and a bridge of light opens toward the Unmoored Steps. Every Hollow's puzzle is its own, and everyone in the Hour turns the same stones.

The Unmoored Steps: past the Orrery, a course of platforms over the void in three spans, each begun at a stone checkpoint. The Drift: eight brass platforms swinging side to side - the leap is in the timing, and a platform carries you as it swings. The Beat: platforms that are there only on the Hour's beat (they blink before they go, and the Hour ticks as they come back), and two brass walls to run up. The Crumble: cracked platforms that shudder and give way moments after you land, while the Warp's breath gusts across them - you hear the wind rise a second before each gust. Fall into the void and the Hour casts you back to the span's checkpoint, at the cost of some of your health (never your life). The platforms move the same for every player; a platform you break is broken only for you.

The Brass Remnant: past the Steps, in the arena of the Last Moment, waits what the Warp kept of the Numidium - a brass colossus four times a man's height, its chest a cage around a heart of shattered soul-gem light. Step into the arena and the fight begins for everyone in the Hour at once; it grows tougher with every fighter who joins, by each fighter's own level, and once you've joined, the arena holds you until the fight ends, you die or you take the way home. The Walking Hour: it stamps a shock ring that rolls out across the arena (jump it), sweeps the Hour-Hand - a beam from its chest - across half the arena (outrun it, or put a pillar between you; its top is no shelter), and hurls gears that leave burning brass where they land. The Dragon Break: at 70% it steps outside time and two Echoes of it, gold and silver, take its place - fell them within 15 seconds of each other, or the one left alone rises again. The Last Moment: at 35% it returns, faster, and about once a minute it winds up the Reset - break every Heart that rises around the arena before it lands, or it takes most of everyone's health and heals. Through it all its heart pulses, a little harder each time - never more than three quarters of your health - and fifteen minutes after it wakes the Hour Ends. Its blows show on the arena's floor as they wind up; a blow about to land on you says Move!, with an arrow to the way out of it, or Jump! for the ring. When it falls, a chart ranks everyone's part in the fight and everyone online hears of it.

Each Hollow's marks: every Abyss Dungeon keeps one of six Endings - the element the Remnant fights in, its signature and the light it burns with - and two of nine omens that change the fight (a quarter more health, quicker wind-ups, a shorter Hour, a Pulse that climbs twice as fast...). They're said when it's found, shown on a card at its door and as you step into the Hour, and its blows and burning brass take its element - resist it to blunt them.

Hours broken, Hourbreaker and The Turning Hour: when the Remnant falls, everyone who truly fought it is credited an Hour broken, counted on their account card and on their Inspect card. Each Hour broken has a one-in-four chance to grant the title Hourbreaker and a one-in-eight chance to grant the aura The Turning Hour. Once held, they are yours for good. Online accounts with a username only - a guest's Hour is kept for a week and counted once they add one.

The Brass of Numidium: a new Aetheric set of Dwarven brass - nine pieces, every one at the very top of the Legendary range. Dwemer Brass (2 pieces): +4 to +10 magic and shock resistance. Gearward (4 pieces): the next blow a foe lands on you is 15% to 30% lighter, then the gear winds again. The Hour Turns (6 pieces): a blow that would kill you does not - you are left standing and 15% to 25% of your health returns. Only the Brass Remnant's spoils carry it, one time in three.

The Remnant's spoils: when it falls, everyone who truly fought it sees their own share burst from the cage of its chest and scatter across the arena floor - gold, a Rare piece that is Legendary one time in four, two more pieces Rare or better, one time in three a piece of the Brass of Numidium, and one time in fifty the Hourlock. Your share is yours alone. Whatever is left goes into your pack when you leave the Hour.

The collapse: three minutes after the Remnant falls, the Hour collapses. Everyone still inside the Abyss Dungeon or the Hour is told how long is left. Once the Remnant's body has sunk, a way home of pale light rises where it fell: step into it or press it to leave the Hour for the Abyss Dungeon's door outside.

One life: die in the Shattered Hour and it casts you out for good - you wake before the Abyss Dungeon's door, and its Rift will not take you back. It's your account's one life, on every device and tab. When an Abyss Dungeon ends, anyone still inside it or the Hour is put out at its door.
Its own score: nine songs - the Hollow, the Orrery's hall, the Steps, one for each of the fight's three phases, its last minute, its fall and the collapse - each place's music giving way to the next.

Its voice and its air: the Remnant's steps, wind-ups and blows are heard where they happen; the Hour has its own wind, the ticking of its works, the Orrery's hum, and motes of brass drifting in its light.

Seen: every blow bursts in sparks, shakes the arena and lights the floor; the colossus walks, turns and swings with its whole body; its gears fly and the Hour-Hand's beam sweeps the floor it strikes; title cards mark each turn of the fight.

Its presence: near a standing Abyss Dungeon the land's light and haze lean to brass; at its door a banner names it and how long it has, its marks on a card beside it; its last hour is said to everyone online.

A tab hidden through a landing no longer dodges it, and a frozen page no longer holds a place in the fight; the Hardened Hearts omen and the Hearts' toughness are fair to small parties; the Pulse never lands on top of the Reset.
The fight runs smoother: its frames make next to no garbage, and its effects are built before the first blow lands.
The music no longer cuts out or plays the street's song between the Hollow's and the Hour's; the End sounds once, then tolls; nothing plays war over the dead.

The banner at an Abyss Dungeon's door fits a phone's screen; the title card stays clear of the Remnant's bar; times read the same everywhere ("1d 22h"); its ring's card on the held map can be reached beside its city.
A Resurrect in an ended Abyss Dungeon no longer strands you there; /unstuck in the Hour leaves by the Hour's own way home.
Gilded is the new top of the rarity ladder - above Aetheric, and above even Artifacts - the rarest thing in the game, its name in gold leaf and its frame breathing light in every slot.

A Gilded Thunderlock: what the Warp kept of a Dwemer smith's last commission, gilded in the Hour that never ended. Its lines never vary: +40% damage, +15 Agility, +30 Archery and +10 shock damage a shot - each at the very top of the Legendary range.
The Hour Tolls: every third shot that lands strikes for double, and a foe it fells gives back the pellet that felled it.
Where to find it: the Brass Remnant's spoils, one time in fifty (online).

About twice what any Legendary Thunderlock lands a shot, still the slowest weapon to fire. It can't be broken down, reforged, honed, cursed, socketed or made an heirloom, and in a duel its power sleeps. Its first find joins your codex, at the head of the list.
Shot in the shops: Dwemer Pellets are now sold wherever weapons are - Weapon Smiths, Armorers, General Stores and Pawn Shops - and restocked each day.
Its pictures in every slot: the gun and its pellets show their own art in your pack, on the hotbar and in the quick slots, instead of their initials; a list shows the whole gun.

The Morrowind gun, closed and kicking: the 3D gun has no holes left (you no longer see into its receiver), it kicks back at the shot, and the reload tips the gun down and back up - the breech heard after the bang, never before it.
The Rift is always reachable: the Rift no longer stands in a sealed room with no way in. It now stands at the deepest monster spawn point in the dungeon's inner rooms.
No more flying out of the Hour: leaving the Shattered Hour after its Abyss Dungeon has ended no longer leaves you hanging in the sky above it - you land where you stood outside when you went in.

Companions wait outside: your crew and sworn companions no longer follow you through the Rift. They wait outside the Hour and return to your side when you come back. Stepping through with them says *"Your companions cannot follow you through the Rift."*
On the Overworld view, the dungeons near you - Daggerfall's own, the random dungeons online and a standing Abyss Dungeon - now show their own entrance model, enlarged so you can see them from above.

Stepping through the Rift no longer throws you straight back out of the Shattered Hour. The game was speaking to the Hour's server before the server had finished letting it in, and the server took that as a broken connection and closed the door on you, on almost every try.
A connection that blinks during the boss fight no longer throws you out of the Hour the same way.
Leaving the Shattered Hour, for any reason, now puts you on the ground in front of the Abyss Dungeon's door. It used to put you hundreds of metres in the air above it.
Reload the page. A tab left open from before the last update puts the Rift in its old place.
In winter, outside the deserts, real snow now lies on the ground, deeper in the wild than in towns. It builds up while snow falls and melts back in clear weather.
You, monsters, guards and townsfolk leave tracks in it. Tracks slowly fill back in, faster while it snows, and they are kept in your save.
A fallen enemy leaves a hollow in the snow where it lay.
With Basic Roads, its paths and tracks keep only a thin layer of snow, and its main roads get a bank of snow along their edges.
The winter ground under it has new textures.
Wind now changes from day to day. Trees and plants sway and shiver, some days turn windy or stormy, and gusts come and go with their own sound.
Leaves blow off the trees, and in winter snow blows off the boughs.
The wind waits while the game is paused.
In the deserts by day, the distant land and sky shimmer in the heat: fully under a clear sky, half as much under cloud, fading in after sunrise and out before sunset.
The desert ground has new sand textures with ripples, from Sands of the Alik'r.

All of it is on by default in the enhanced outdoors. Snowfall, Windfall and Heat Haze each have their own switch in Features; the desert sand and the winter ground are packs of their own on the Replacement packs card.
The launcher can now be used with a controller: D-pad or left stick to move, A or Start to press, B to go back.
Add --play to the game's launch options (Playnite, Steam shortcuts, Big Picture) to skip the launcher and go straight into the game.
Updates still arrive: you're told in-game, and they install when you quit.
The launcher still opens when it needs to ask you something: on the first run, or if your Daggerfall folder can't be found.

An auction won in a town whose seat takes a Tithe now closes on time and pays its seller. Before, when the seller's Marks were near the cap, the sale could stick and never close, and twenty such sales held up every auction behind them.
Auctions, guild writs and contracts now settle on time on the service's own clock, even when nobody opens the market or the Work tab.

Your letterbox, the count over a town's Notice Boards and your play time now share one request to the account service instead of three, and the service does about a third less database work for each player. Nothing you see changes.
C now crouches *and* sneaks. While crouched you move at sneaking pace and the stealth checks apply, so enemies are slower to notice you.
Left Alt no longer sneaks. The old standing sneak is still in Controls as an optional key, with no key set by default.
If you had your own key bindings saved, you'll see a one-time on-screen note that Sneak lost its key.
Hold Left Alt to open the wheel: Talk (up), Grab (right), Steal (down), Info (left).
Flick the mouse toward a mode, then let go or click to choose. Move the mouse back to the middle to cancel.
F1 through F4 no longer change modes by default, and no longer open the browser's help or find bar. You can bind the four modes back to any keys in Controls.
On a controller, the d-pad's "next mode" still cycles through the modes.
On a controller, the menu cursor now eases in, speeds up on a long full push, slows over buttons and settles onto the nearest one when you let go.
It works in every menu, on both the Classic and Enhanced skins.
At the main menu the left stick moves the same cursor and A presses what it's on; the d-pad still jumps from button to button.
Don't like it? Settings → Controls → Controller cursor assist → Off gives back Daggerfall's plain fixed-speed cursor.
Clicking with the controller cursor no longer acts like a held-down drag in some windows.
Classic spellcasting now runs at the same pace as the Morrowind animation. The spell leaves your hands at half a second, so players using the Morrowind hands are no longer slower than everyone else.
A new cast can't start until your hands finish the motion. Clicking or recasting during that motion does nothing and costs nothing.
Casting speed now scales with your Speed attribute: up to 25% faster at high Speed, 25% slower at low.
New rarity affix, +N% casting speed, on jewellery and weapons. Everything you wear adds up, capped at 30%. Because it rolls on jewellery, classes that can't wear plate can still get it.
The heart of the Wrothgarian Mountains is now an open PvP zone, marked on the world map with a red border and drifting fog. Wrothgaria itself stays outside it.

Other players in the zone can attack you, except your party, your guild and your duel opponent. That includes its dungeons. Attacking a player inside a city calls the guards, and the zone's guards are ten times as strong.
Foes in the zone are four times as strong, elites and champions included, and travel in packs four times the size.
The zone has four tiers, from the Foothills at its edge to the Heart. Loot rises with each one: +25%, +50%, +75% and +100% (twice the gold, twice the drops, twice the odds of a rare piece).
Click the zone on the world map, or press V while inside it, to open its own map. It shows the tiers, the towns, the dungeons and where you stand.

When you die you keep your potions, torches, campfire kit, food, ammunition and anything that never changes hands. Your bags and your cart's load drop where you fell and stay there for 10 minutes. They are marked so you can find them again, and anyone can take them.
Killed by another player, the killer may also take one piece of your worn gear.
You wait two minutes before you can respawn. You rise in the nearest town outside the zone, and your cart comes with you.

You cannot fast travel into or out of the zone. Inside it a fast journey costs 2,500 to 15,000 gold depending on the tier you arrive in, and you can take one every 10 minutes. Walking on the Overworld map works as always.
In the zone, travel speed is capped at x20 in the wilds and x40 on roads.
The Overworld no longer refuses a walk over mountains.
Other players who are not in your party or guild show as red "Strangers" with no name. You can see them from 1.5 km away, and the closer they get the more they slow your travel.
/unstuck now sends you to the next town when you are outdoors. It has a cooldown. In the zone it works only indoors, takes five minutes and can be cancelled.

Each tier of the zone has two Greater Giants, shown on the zone map where they wander, and everyone in the zone sees the same ones. At half health a Greater Giant calls ten giants to help. Giants never leave the zone.

The zone has its own dungeons, its halls, which change each day. Once you leave a hall you can't go back in for an hour, unless your own remains are still inside; a small lock marks it on the map. Crows circle a hall where a player died.
Banks, house purchases, world events and revenants are restricted inside the zone: only one revenant may walk with you there.
Temples now offer Heal Curse beside Heal Disease.
Resting while poisoned or diseased now warns you first.
Hovering an item in any shop shows the same card as in your inventory.
The stats screen shows your resistances.
Ordinary dungeons outside the zone respawn after 20 minutes, elite dungeons after 40.
Sit at a tavern's card table and play Hold'em. The tavern's regulars take the other chairs, and your character is seated in the chair for everyone to see.
Online, the relay deals: shuffle, hole cards and the seat clock are the relay's, so nobody's client can see another's hand.
Gold tables: buy in with real gold, held in escrow by the account service and paid out on the hand's receipt. Top up between hands.
The cards are physical on the cloth: dealt, fanned, peeked at, chips dragged to bet, the deck riffled.

A two-player collectible game played on the same table: three holdings between you, six turns, hold two of three to win. Units, spells and Daedric Prince cards, each painted in code with the Iliac Bay's own creatures, artifacts and places.
The Card Binder is an item every character carries from creation; it holds your decks. A new Collections tab under Holdings shows the weapon codex and your cards side by side.

A monument to Julian LeFay, one of the creators of Daggerfall, now stands in the middle of Gothway Garden. It has three granite steps, a marble pedestal and a gilt-tipped obelisk. A bronze plaque on each side reads "Julian LeFay, 1965 - 2025, Father of The Elder Scrolls".
Look at the monument to choose Throw flowers or Read the inscription. In Info mode a press reads the inscription.

A thrown flower lands on the monument's steps or at its foot, on your side. Each character keeps its own flowers: up to the 48 newest stay where they landed after you save and load, and the plaque counts how many you have laid.
Townspeople walk around the monument.
Online, your flowers are yours alone. Other players see the monument, but not the flowers you laid.

Zoom the enhanced map out past the Iliac Bay and the whole of Tamriel is on the sheet, drawn in the same hand: the nine provinces and their borders, the capitals, the mountains, the rivers and the seas, with the Bay inside a faint dotted frame and its coast running on into the continent's. Hover beyond the Bay to read the province, a capital or the sea. Nothing beyond the Bay can be travelled to.

Walk off the edge of the Iliac Bay and the land of Tamriel continues under your feet: hills, mountains and coasts under each province's own sky and trees, as far as you care to walk. Empty ground for now - no towns, roads or dungeons stand there yet.
Both are Features rows (Tamriel on the map; Land beyond the Bay), on by default on the enhanced skin.
The land beyond the Bay had pulled the online relay's code into the terrain worker, and the world froze on its first outdoor build. Fixed.
The land beyond the Iliac Bay is now traced from your own game's map of Tamriel (the race screen's picture), so the coast, the provinces and the borders are the ones Daggerfall drew.
The Bay is placed on that map by matching its own coastline, so the join is where the game put it.
The ground past the Bay's edge follows the same traced land.
Every tavern and inn now has its own card table: a green-felt poker table with six stools, standing near the entrance.
Walk up to it and press activate to sit down and play Hold'em with the regulars, or with other players online.
The tavern's ordinary dining tables are no longer card tables.
The land past the Iliac Bay is now the shape Daggerfall's own map paints: one continent with the Imperial Province in the middle, not eight islands.
The Bay sits on it where its coastline matches.
Townsfolk inside a building no longer bunch up by the door. They spread through the whole room and sit at tables set apart, never at a table split by a wall.
Nobody sits in the tavern for hours waiting for lunch.
Everyone in a room sees the same people in the same places, whether or not a door was left open.
The watch posted at a city's gates stops strangers coming in and asks their business. Strangers answer civilly, curtly or with open hostility, and sellswords and sailors are rougher.
Patrols stop strangers on their rounds.
Townsfolk fall out with each other, more often in the evening between drinkers, and the watch breaks it up.
Buyers haggle at stalls, and beggars ask passers-by for a coin.
When someone shouts, the people nearby fall quiet and turn to look.
Small voices fill the street: the night watch calls the hour, with words for the weather; stalls cry their wares; beggars call out; drinkers sing on the way home from the tavern.
Every player in a town sees the same incidents at the same places.
A stranger at the gate names their own home town, and a beggar no longer calls a stranger by name.
Every stranger stopped at a gate is questioned, and a gate stop no longer keeps a visitor from leaving town.
The watch breaks up a quarrel even at a change of shift, and only one of a patrol pair calls the hour.
A beggar no longer pulls a stall keeper away from their stall.
Beggars and stall keepers turn to face whoever they are talking to.
People in an incident greet you again once it's over.
Stall keepers no longer cry their wares before they reach the stall.

The spellbook can no longer be dropped, put in a chest, pile or companion's pack, shift-dropped, or sold at a shop. It still goes into your own wagon. The game tells you: "Your spellbook never leaves you."
In an Enduring family, a vampire, werewolf or wereboar who dies loses no years to Arkay's toll and always rises, even with their span spent. Once cured, the toll applies again from the next death.
A letter of credit is now dropped at a death in the zone, at its full value, like the purse's gold.
The wallet and the Deadlands Embers and Welkynd Shards it holds always stay with you.
Every quest can now be abandoned and later reclaimed. You'll find this in the pause menu's Quests tab.
Abandon asks you to click twice to confirm.
Reclaim takes one click and works from the new Abandoned section.
An abandoned quest is set aside, not lost:
its timer stops;
its items, topics and journal are kept;
its dungeon or building stays reserved for it.
When you reclaim a quest, it picks up where you left it, and the days it spent abandoned don't count against its deadline.
Abandoning a quest frees its quest-giver, so the guild offers you work again.
The game's built-in quests (the main quest's core, the curse and the tutorial) and sea raids can't be abandoned.
A reclaimed quest doesn't rejoin your party's shared progress. Share it again.
Medium dungeons no longer repeat the same layout block twice. Quests already inside a changed dungeon move their targets to match.
Lord K'avar in Privateer's Hold: random quests no longer send you into main-story dungeons. Quests that were already stuck there are moved to a proper dungeon.
Enduring and Bloodlines characters can marry again. Propose marriage was greyed out for every character who should have been allowed to wed.
Mercantile and Personality matter again when selling online. Better skills now get a better price, still within the online limit of half the shop's price.
Fast travel no longer drops you inside a mountain. A landing inside rock now puts you on the nearest open ground.
Enhanced Water can be switched off online. The toggle was locked while playing online.
The bank's ship loan has been removed. Ships are bought outright again. A ship you already bought on credit is unaffected.
The pause menu now has a mailbox: an envelope beside the hourglass (online).
When the developers send you a message, the envelope shows a count, and a line in the world chat tells you post has arrived.
Open a message to read it. If it holds an item, press Claim and the item goes into the pack of the online character you're playing.
Type /mail in chat to open the mailbox from anywhere: outdoors, indoors or underground, on either menu style.
A message whose item you haven't claimed can't be thrown away by mistake.
The thirteen players of the first Abyss Dungeon clear have been honoured:
a new title, Hour's First, drawn in rose gold, pearl and the white of dawn;
a new aura, The First Hour: The Turning Hour's wheel cast in the first dawn's light, with its dial turning forward, the Hour's own mark ablaze, and rays of first light;
The Hourlock, waiting for each of them in the mailbox.
Wear the title and aura from your profile.
With Snowless Swamps and Jungles switched on, swamps and jungles no longer get deep snow on the ground or falling snow in winter.
Deserts no longer get snow drifting in from nearby snowy regions, and the edge of the desert next to a snowy area stays bare. Snow storms that reach the desert now fall as rain.

You can now decorate the ground right outside your own front door. Many desert houses are L-shaped or have an outside stair, and the open ground in front of their doors counted as "inside your house". Spots under your own roof or eaves still count as the house.
Opening the Overworld no longer freezes the game: nearby dungeon models now load one per frame once the view has finished rising.
Long journeys no longer slowly use up video memory. The dungeon models' textures are released when you leave them behind.
Deep snow no longer does its work while the Overworld is open, since none of it is shown there.
Saving is faster in snowy areas: the snow-track data is only recompressed when it has changed. Online, this removes a hitch that happened every two minutes.
Fixed a crash ("Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'velocity')") when another player's ship list changed while you stood on one of their ships.
When a member of your family dies for good, their houses pass to whoever carries the line on - door, bed, chests and furniture as they left them.
Online, a fallen character's home moves to their heir, cupboards included.
If your heir already owns a house in that region, the inherited one waits until they sell theirs.

Card tables locked players out. Each tavern had one table, and whoever sat first decided whether it played for gold or for chips. One realm character staking gold shut every guest out, and one guest playing for chips shut out every realm character.
The red table plays for gold, and only realm characters can stake at it.
Realm characters can now also play for chips at the green table, alongside everyone else.

Whenever a Rare, Legendary, Aetheric, Artifact or Gilded item reaches your pack, wagon or Materials Bag, a banner slides in at the right edge of the screen: the item's picture framed in its tier colour, its tier and pips, its name, and what it is.

It works however the item arrives: loot, boss and raid spoils, quest rewards, crafting, the Sigil Broker, shops, trades, the market, and Iliac cards (shown with their own card face and a count when you get several).
Aetheric, Artifact and Gilded items get a bigger, glowing banner and a fanfare.
Up to three banners show at once, newest on top; more wait their turn, best tier first. They pause while a window is open, so a purchase announces itself when you leave the counter.
Moving items between your pack, wagon and bag, or taking your own things back out of storage, never shows a banner.
A first find for your codex now shows "New to your codex" on its banner instead of a separate line.
The small pickup feed under the crosshair no longer repeats an item its banner is announcing.
Move or hide the banners in the HUD editor (Alt+U): Loot banners.
At the red (gold) table, if the realm can't take your stake, the panel now says why, beside the buy-in. Before, "Deal me in" seemed to do nothing.

Clicking a spot on the Overworld while you're past the edge of the Iliac Bay no longer crashes the game ("RangeError: invalid array length"). The Overworld now plans journeys across the land beyond the Bay.

Online, a player beyond the Bay is no longer invisible. Players there see each other and the players near the edge, and the game no longer drops your connection out there. Logging back in there now works too.
A Dark Brotherhood or Thieves Guild member's hall stays named on the town map and at its door while you have a contract.
Looted weapons, armour, clothing and jewellery can be listed on the market, sold at stalls and traded again.
Motherlodes, veins, boulders, herbs and trees no longer appear inside rocks.
The carriage driver at one gate of each walled city (Shrarton in Tasoparet) now has a face in the talk window.
The casting hands are quick again: a spell leaves your hands 0.2 seconds after you cast it, as it did before the casting speed change.
Spells still can't be spammed. The next cast waits out a short recovery, and your Speed and any "+% casting speed" on your gear shorten it.
The thin dotted line that showed up beside the casting hands on some graphics cards is gone.

If two players' dungeons were built differently (usually one of you on an older version), you now see the host's monsters instead of fighting ones nobody else can see. The game tells you once to reload.
Other players' monsters keep up better while they run, so you're less likely to swing at the air where a monster used to be.
More of another player's summoned and called monsters are shown, including all ten of a Greater Giant's call.
Quest monsters are visible to everyone nearby, and anyone can hit them. When a party member kills one of your quest's monsters, it counts for everyone in the party with that quest.
After you die, your own pile of remains now shows up.
A red "My remains" waypoint marks where your remains lie, on both the Overworld and the world map, and goes away when they do.

The giant angular rock spires from World of Daggerfall's mountains are off by default. The mountain regions get rounded mountains instead. You can turn the spires back on in the mod's settings ("Mountains"); online, the room decides.
Boulders in rock fields no longer hang over slopes with their open undersides showing.
The Discord links on the website, the Terms and Privacy pages, and the desktop launcher now point to our new invite: https://discord.gg/jM2JdwSM8w

The Rift is now a brass astrolabe standing in a cracked crater, turned to face down its hall's longest line. Its gear ticks forward once a second, and its ring of Roman-numeral hours clicks back an hour on every toll.

Its iris shows its state. It opens wide while the Hour can be entered, narrows to a pinhole when it can't, and shuts when the Hour closes. Studs round its rim count down the hours the Hollow has left, and during the collapse they go out one by one.
Through the iris you see the Hour's own sky, with real depth as you move. Gold light drifts in from the rim, and the gear's teeth cast turning spokes of light on the floor.
The Return is a pale stone arch with silver bands and a window home: the sky over the Hollow's city at the world's real hour, with Masser and Secunda at night.
A silver hand-plate on every Return's sill lights up when you aim at it.

Entering the Hour has its own transition: twelve brass blades close over the Rift wherever it is on your screen and lock into a clock face. Its hand sweeps backwards and the broken quarters chime, and if you hold there long enough, the Dragon Break splits the hand and cracks the face. The face then shatters open onto the Threshold.
Leaving by the way back or the Return, the clock is silver and still cracked. Taking the way home, the crack mends as it shuts. Being thrown out by force shatters the face into falling pieces.
If your system is set to reduce motion, the face holds still and fades in and out instead.
When you arrive in the Hour, the way back breathes out a spray of brass sparks and its ring turns once.
The light has been redone, so floors read as stone and brass instead of one amber glow. The Threshold is paved with the Bay's cobbles around a compass rose.

The islands hang in the void on jagged rock spires, with half-buried gears and chains swaying on the clock's tick. Distant islands drift slowly below. Far beneath the course, the Works turn: four vast gears, black against the furnace glow, a tooth at a time.

The sky is hand-painted: dithered bands of void, single-pixel stars, aurorae, a great clock face drawn in stars with its numerals and the six Endings as constellations, and the Bay's cities hanging upside down with their windows lit. Its hands run on the Hour's clock.
The way back looks into the hall you came from: dark coursed stone lit gold from the front. Its rings turn forward, and it casts the Hour's only cool light.

The arena tells you the fight through its floor. Eight fissures flood green each time a Mantella Pulse lands. The rim's numerals light one by one through the Reset and the last two burn ember. When the Hour ends, everything turns red. The sky's clock follows along.
The Stomp's ring now rises as a low wall of brass light you can see to jump. While the fight holds you in the arena, a gold curtain rises at its rim.

The arena's four pillars are clock-towers now. Their dials' hands follow the Remnant (the Echoes in the Dragon Break, the way home once it falls), and a lantern burns in each cage. A brass mark on the floor shows where the Remnant and each Echo stand, and the arena's lamps dim as the Reset gathers.

The Brass Remnant has been rebuilt from riveted brass plate. It has a domed helm crowned with seven broken clock hands, bell pauldrons, an open ribcage around a cut soul-gem heart, knee and elbow gears, organ-pipe vents, and a right forearm that is the Hour-Hand itself. Its heart lights the arena in its Ending's colour and beats faster as the next Pulse nears.

The Remnant shows what it's about to do. The part about to strike heats up: its raised foot before a Stomp, its blade before the Hour-Hand, its fist before a Volley, its ribs before a Pulse, its heart before the Reset.

A great dial on its back keeps the fight's time: it ticks backwards, runs down a stun, and spins back to twelve on the Reset. In the Dragon Break, the surviving Echo's dial counts down its partner's window. Lamps on its ribs count the Hearts still standing.
When it falls, its heart tears out and rises before going dark, and the dial breaks free and rolls away.

Where it falls, the way home assembles inside a column of pale light: the jambs rise out of the floor, the arch swings shut, and the keystone clock drops into place. In the Hour it stands half again as large, with a silver beacon over it, tall for its first ten seconds and then low.

Every step shows what it will do next. Beat plates are clock faces whose hand runs down to the moment they vanish, and they dissolve in pixels instead of blinking out. Drift steps hang from pendulums. Risers climb on gear racks.
Crumble stones crack in stages under your feet, fall in pieces, and fly back together when they return.
A vane on the last island swings toward the next gust a second before it hits.
Waystones mark where the void will send you back, and a golden burst plays in reverse when it does. Faint outlines show where vanished steps will return.
The six stones are rebuilt: carved shafts with their sign, a dial in a bezel, and a gear on top that turns with the hand. The bezel glows gold while a stone turns and ember when your turn is refused.

Banners hang from each stone, lecterns hold the plaques' ledgers, and the floor's dial is raised in brass, its lit plates glowing like soul gems. Tabs round the rim count the fray and pulse near the end.
Six rings turn slowly overhead, shivering as the Hour frays. At the Concord they swing flat, the gem flares, and the bridge lays itself in twelve plates.
Changing weapons or casting on an ally right after a connection blip no longer throws you out of the Hour. Neither does entering the Hour, which a party-status message used to trigger every time.
Hiding the tab no longer dodges the Pulse, the Reset or the End.
A fighter whose connection dropped while a fight was lost can rejoin the next fight instead of being stuck.
You can no longer set a Mark inside an Abyss Dungeon.
Stepping into the Rift now works on slow machines and across a hitch.
Pressing near the Rift no longer grabs it when you're aiming at a body or the floor.
The Return and the landing back from the Hour no longer stand on or next to the Rift in small rooms.
The Rift is sized to fit its hall and no longer pokes through pillars or ceilings.
Abyss Dungeons no longer appear on beaches or with their end underwater.
A refused or failed step through the Rift leaves you in front of the Hollow's door instead of in its middle.
An open door no longer moves where the Rift stands from one player to the next.
The Remnant no longer grunts while it's outside time, a Stomp lands as one thud instead of two, and the Hour's distant sounds stop when you leave.
Coming back to the tab no longer plays every Heart that broke while you were away all at once.
The Brass of Numidium's powers play the right sounds.

The fight's title cards only show near the arena. Interrupted lines are repeated. The Hour's messages wait while a window is open, sit above the arrival and damage cards, and no longer wrap to four lines on phones.
The Remnant's health bar uses the Hour's own colours.
After the Concord, a stone's plaque says "The Concord holds." instead of offering a turn.
The large boat no longer shares its textures with the Shattered Hour.
The Rift's and the Return's textures sit where they belong: the Return's stone and dial were drawing in the Rift's brass, and four of the ring's numerals showed the wrong picture.
Levitate no longer works in the Shattered Hour. The Steps are walked, not flown.
You can no longer walk onto the Concord's bridge before it has finished laying.
The Drift's pendulum rods hang beside its platform instead of through anyone standing at its edge.
The sky and the arena no longer turn red before a fight has started.
The way back no longer rings a bell every time you arrive, and its light stays on the island instead of spilling into the void.
The arrival sparks wait until the step-through animation finishes, and play on every arrival, not only the first.
The Hollow and the Hour run with less memory churn: the Rift, the sky, the Orrery's hands and the Hour's sounds no longer allocate every frame.
Settings and Features are now one screen, in tabs: Graphics, Gameplay, Combat, World, Interface, Audio, Controls, Accessibility, Mods & files.
Graphics opens on a quality preset: Low, Medium, High or Ultra.
One search across every tab. Filter by what you changed, Enhanced, Mods or Daggerfall Unity.
Each tab can restore its own defaults. "Reset everything to defaults" resets every setting and mod.
Mods & files lists every mod and takes you to its options.
Less text. Press a row's name to read more about it.
Quick-loading (F11) after dying in town no longer leaves the death screen up.
Face mods (Paperdoll Enhanced) draw faces at their proper size.
Updated steel armour model: wider breastplate shoulders, larger pauldrons, and the waist band is its own piece.
The steel helm (closed and open) now sits properly on your head. Before, the top of your head poked through the closed helm.
Morrowind models (your body, arms, armour, weapons and item pictures) now use smooth shading instead of a faceted look.
The Oblivion Gate is a new, handcrafted model: two clawed pillars under a heavy lintel, ringed with burning spines.
Its stone is cracked basalt veined with fire. The frame around the portal smoulders by night, and the spines burn toward their points.
The portal's fire now fills the gate's opening right to the stone, and it meets the ground even on a slope.
The gate rises fully out of the ground, with no piece of it showing early on a hillside.
Anyone caught inside the stone as the gate finishes rising is set down safely in front of it, wherever they stood. Players standing in the doorway or beside the gate's feet are no longer moved.
The portal on the bridge is gone. You step out of a gate of fire that closes behind you, and it opens again when another player arrives (including someone coming back in).
The way home opens where the Warden falls, as before, and now closes as the court comes apart.
Until he falls, the only ways out are death and the Wrath. /unstuck no longer works inside the court.
If the fight stops answering (a full or stalled room), you are returned to Tamriel after 20 seconds instead of being stranded.
Iliac Hand at the tavern table. Sit at a card table and choose Play Iliac Hand to play the collectible card game with a deck from your Card Binder.

Offline, against the tavern's regulars. Each regular has a temper (careful, reckless or sly) and a deck to match the tavern: a village's regulars play close to the starter deck, and a city's carry a Daedric Prince.

Play for fun, or for keeps: each side stakes a card and the loser hands it over. Your staked card is set aside when the game is dealt and returned if you win or draw. A regular pays out one card a day.
Online, against another player at the same table. The relay deals and keeps every hand hidden.
Ranked, for realm characters on a registered account. Results count on a season board (the arena's seasons and ratings), and the season's top player wears the new Iliac Champion title.
Where cards come from:
A slain creature sometimes drops its own card (a rat drops a Rat). Titled foes drop theirs twice as often.
A finished guild, temple or knightly-order quest pays one of that guild's cards about one time in three. A higher rank pays a better card.
Card Packs are sold at Enhanced taverns' counters and card tables. Each holds five cards, the last rare or better.
Three new boss cards: the Oblivion Gate's Warden, Sethrakul, and the Abyss Dungeon's Brass Remnant. The set is now 85 cards.
At the Hold'em table:
Press your cards and pull down to squeeze them.
Click your cards to check, or push them up the screen to fold on your turn.
Other players seated at a card table now sit in their chairs instead of standing in them.

Realm customs counts cards. An offline character entering the realm can bring cards worth the starter deck (285) plus 150 per level. Customs keeps the rest back, dearest first, and tells you how many stayed behind. Sealed packs and cards set out as decor count too.
Iliac Hand's panel can be played with the keyboard.
Tavern card tables no longer stand across doorways; they keep a walking lane clear.
Ghost and other flying companions no longer climb into the ceiling while following, and their health bar shows again.
Your PvP remains stay marked on the map if the game crashes or closes before you reach them.
Firefox for Android: tapping the screen no longer opens the pause menu.
The Stores page now lists looted, shop-bought or traded materials as "unstorable" and explains why they can't go in.

Every save the realm takes from an online character is now read by the server, not only the first. It checks that every item you hold is one the game can actually make, that your level matches what your character card shows, and that your gold, attributes and skills are within the game's limits.

Nothing you play is ever lost to this. If something looks wrong, the save is still kept, and only trading is frozen: the market (listings, purchases, auctions, crafted pieces and your Stores), trades between players, guild vaults and treasuries, rent and card-table stakes. You'll see a message naming the item when that happens, and another when trading opens again.
If the same valuable item turns up on two characters, the character that showed it second is the one checked; the original owner keeps theirs and can still sell it.
Enchanted items brought into the realm from a classic Daggerfall save through customs stay yours, but can't be traded or sold in the realm.

The server now records how fast each character's wealth grows against time actually played. For the first week it only measures; after that, wealth that grows faster than play could earn it will freeze trading until play catches up.

Items handed to you by other players (chests, bodies, shops) are now checked the same way. An impossible item is left out on its own, so an honest chest or body is never lost because of one bad piece.
Items in for repair could be refused when passed between players; that's fixed.

Every crafting station now uses the materials in your Materials Bag and pack, not just your Stores: the anvil, forge, workbench, loom, mason's bench, cook fire, jeweller's bench, alchemy and enchanting stations, and tempering.
That includes materials you looted, bought at a shop, were traded, or took out of your Stores before the bag existed. Before, these showed (0) at a station and crafting said you didn't have enough.
A craft that needs refining first (ore to ingots, logs to charcoal) plans that from your bag too.
When a station takes something from your pack, any of it you didn't gather or take out of your Stores is kept as "from your pack". You'll see it on the Stores page.
Goods from your pack can only be used at a crafting station, or taken back out into your pack. They can't be delivered to writs, put in the guild Stores or sold for silver.
A piece crafted from them sells on the market for gold only, the same as any piece from your pack.
Mountain and Mountain Woods veins can now be Silver on ground few players have mined. Before, that ground gave only Iron in the Mountains (and Iron, Copper or Lead in the Mountain Woods).
Gold, Platinum, Mithril and a region's own ore still appear only once three different players (each account at least a week old) have gathered on that ground. The Mining page now says so.
New setting: Settings → Interface → Maps → Map text and icons - Auto, or 0.75× to 2×.

The map of Tamriel beyond the Iliac Bay is traced more faithfully: provinces meet at their borders instead of across thin channels of sea, specks of paint are no longer drawn as tiny lakes, coastlines are smooth, the continent lines up with the Bay's own coast, and the made-up rivers that ran out to sea are gone. The land past the Bay no longer has sea running down its borders either.

New setting: Settings → Interface → Character sheet → Every faction's standing (off by default). With it on, the Standing page lists your reputation with every guild, temple, knightly order, kingdom, witches' coven, vampire clan and Daedric Prince - including a guild you've left or been expelled from.

Beautiful Villages: in Akatosh's temple villages (Gentle Redeemer of Akatosh in Wayrest among them) one house stood buried inside a hill. It now stands on open ground nearby, and a quest that sends you there (such as An Item On Loan) leads to it.
Ebony armour now has its own full set on the Morrowind-style body: breastplate with tassets, pauldrons, gauntlets, greaves, boots and helm, each with its own painted texture.
Mithril and Adamantium still wear the Morrowind ebony look.
Casual and Formal Cloaks are now real cloaks, worn over your armour instead of a full robe that hid it.
The cloak moves with your body: it hangs from the shoulders and swings with your legs as you walk.
Each dye has its own colour. Aquamarine wears the blue and Yellow the light brown.
The cloak is smooth over the shoulders.
Its inventory icon shows the cloak itself.
Greatswords and bows worn on the back sit over the cloak and stay visible.
Swords, daggers and crossbows at the hip hang under it.
Stowed weapons follow the cloak as you walk, run and lean, so they no longer cut through it.
Sitting at a card table, the cloak hangs behind you instead of folding under your legs.
Online, your reputation with all twenty-two guilds, temples and knightly orders is kept by the realm, not your save. It moves only for things the realm saw you do.
Reputation can rise by up to 15 a day with each guild. Anything past that isn't lost: it's paid out on the days after.
Ranks 0 to 7 work exactly as in Daggerfall, earned with reputation and skill. Ranks 8 and 9 are now seats (see below).
Each chapter posts hall writs on its town's Notice Board, under the Work tab. They ask for the kinds of materials that guild works with.
A hall writ pays like a Court writ, plus +2 reputation with the guild. Hall writs and Court writs share your three writs a day.
Members also get their own writ each day, one per guild, which earns Merit for the chapter.
The Thieves Guild's and the Dark Brotherhood's writs are shown to their members alone.
Slaying a gate's guardian or defending a raided town earns +1 reputation with each guild you belong to that keeps a chapter there.
A chapter's receipt writ gives +2 more for your first such deed of the day in that region.
Merit is what members earn for their chapter: 100 for a member's own writ (only units you gathered yourself count, not bought ones), and a share of 50 for each receipt.
You can earn up to 600 Merit a week at a chapter. You start earning it after a week in the guild.
Every week at the Turning, each chapter's Strength (0 to 100, starting at 50) rises with its members' Merit and slips when they neglect it. At each Season's end it settles halfway back toward 50.
A chapter's Strength sets its standing:
Failing (0–19): training and spells a quarter dearer, a poorer shelf, fewer writs.
Steady (20–69): Daggerfall's own prices and shelf.
Thriving (70–89) and Ascendant (90–100): training and spells a tenth cheaper, a richer shelf, more writs.
The Notice Board shows each chapter's standing ("The chapter of the Fighters Guild here is Thriving").
Each chapter has one Master (rank 9) and three officers (rank 8). The seats go to the members who earned the most Merit there over the last four weeks, and are settled at each week's Turning.
To hold a seat you need 80 reputation, fourteen days in the guild, an account at least a week old, and rank 7 earned the usual way.
A sitting holder keeps the seat on a tie. A seat no one has earned stands empty.
At its own chapter's halls a seat gives you rank 8 or 9: its title, services and quests.
Titles on your name: Master, Officer, and Former Master for the rest of the Season you lost the seat in. These appear once titles are switched on.
A Master names the chapter's Focus each week: the kind of material its hall writs ask for more of.
The Hall of Records keeps each region's Chronicle: every seat that changed hands, every Season's ending and every patron. Open it from the Notice Board or at a seat's palace.
The first book on every guild hall's shelf is now the hall's roll: its chapter's standing, its Master and its officers.
A thriving chapter's hall is busier. Its members gather there more evenings each week, and a failing hall stands half empty.
Townsfolk talk about their chapters, whether they're failing, thriving, or caught up in a Season's trouble.
Calm: a quiet Season.

Schism: two of the hall's people stand for different doctrines: cheaper training, a deeper shelf, or more writs. Members back a side, and the side whose backers earned more Merit wins. Its doctrine holds for the next Season. A guild is only offered doctrines its hall can actually provide.
Succession: the hall's head steps down. The Master names an heir from three candidates by the Season's third week; with no Master, the top backer's choice stands.

Crackdown: the watch hunts the chapter. Members' own writs earn half again Merit. A chapter that ends the Season under 30 Strength has its halls shut for the next Season: no services, no writs, an empty hall. You can still talk there, get your rank review, and receive free healing or recharge.

Rivalry: two rival chapters in one region race for Merit, and the winner takes 10 Strength from the loser. The rivals are the Fighters Guild and the Thieves Guild; the Dark Brotherhood against the temples of Arkay and Stendarr and every knightly order; and the Mages Guild against the Temple of Julianos.
Decline: the chapter loses 2 Strength a week unless its members earn twice the usual target.
Ascendancy: the halls' training and spells are a further tenth off, and the Master is a High Master for the Season.
A Master who holds the seat for an entire Season earns Season Master ("Master of the Mages Guild, Daggerfall, Season 3") for good.
The Notice Board and the hall's roll tell each chapter's Season. Members can back their side right from the board.
A player guild's guildmaster can bid silver from the guild's treasury to become a chapter's patron for the next Season. Bids start at 1,000, are sealed, and can be raised but never lowered.
When the Season opens, the highest bid wins and is spent. Every other bid goes back to its guild's treasury.
A patron's banners hang beside the chapter's halls, and its members pay the Thriving price there whatever the chapter's standing. The Chronicle remembers who held it.
Patronage buys no influence over the seats. The Thieves Guild's and Dark Brotherhood's chapters take no patrons.
The Thieves Guild's and the Dark Brotherhood's chapters, writs, Seasons and seats are shown to their members alone. Nothing public says where they keep their halls.

The relay passes on each player's movement faster when many players are together: with 200 players in one spot a movement update costs 47 µs instead of 82, and 50 instead of 96 at 256. Everyone receives exactly the same updates as before. Deploying it disconnects every player once.

Online, the frame no longer stalls while the living world works out its travellers' roads. They used to be planned two a frame, and every trip near you was planned again each frame until they were all done. Now a frame plans as many as fit in 2 ms. In the measured town, the frame with nobody else around went from 36.5 ms to 19.4 ms.
The sun's shadows check each object once instead of once per shadow layer: about 0.6 ms a frame saved in a town by day, and the same shadows as before.
The movable HUD checks its layout four times a second instead of about eight.

Cast-When-Held gear no longer breaks from re-equipping. Putting a piece back on within six hours of its spell's last casting costs no condition, and the equip cost can never take a piece below 1 condition. Wear while worn still uses it up over time.
