A Bloodline is never locked out after a failed heir's birth online. The Online page now lists each of your houses whose Succession is waiting, with a "Carry on as" button for every living member.
Your own remains in the Wrothgarian zone now show up. Walking back to your pile from the next cell over no longer loses it, and taking from it works from either side of the cell border.
Duels are now judged by the server. Every hit and spell is checked against the weapon you hold and the gear your character really has, and the server decides when a duel ends.
Your health bar in a duel is the duel's own vitality. Your real health is never touched, so nobody drops to 1 HP and nobody needs healing afterwards.
Both duellists' bars now show as soon as the bout starts, not only after the first hit.
Wins and losses are recorded from the server's result. Clients can no longer report results themselves.
Fights in the zone are judged by the server the same way duels are. Your vitality in a fight shows on the battle readout.

Your vitality goes back to full only after 30 seconds with nobody hitting you, spent in the zone. Stepping out of the zone and back in no longer heals you, and neither does walking into the next area.
A fallen player stays down for the full two minutes. Nobody can rise where they fell straight away.
When you fall to another player, the server takes what you drop from your saved character and puts it in your remains. You no longer hand it over from your own game.
If your pack holds more than your remains can carry, the gold and your most valuable pieces go into the remains first, and the rest stays with you.
The piece your killer picks off your body now arrives in their pack by itself once your remains appear.
If the fallen player never settles their death within 30 seconds, the killer's game does it for them, and lays the remains where the body fell.
A crafted piece you pick back up from your own remains can still be worn, but it can't be traded or sold any more.
Party members, and anyone who left your party in the last ten minutes, still can't hurt you there. The server now enforces this too.
Every damaging spell cast at another player is capped by the server: at most three in five seconds, each to its limit.
A Royal Tourney bout is blows only. Spells cast in a bout no longer land.

The world events channel now announces Abyss Dungeons: when one rises (never where - it still has to be found), when someone finds it and in which region, when the Hour is broken and by whom, and when a found one fades unbroken.
The rise and the find ping the world events role, so you hear when there is one to hunt and when its Rift is open.
Steel and Ebony pauldrons now fully cover the upper arm - no more skin showing through.
The closed Steel helm and the Ebony helm sit lower, where they were designed to, and the Ebony helm's mail coif covers the neck again.
The Small Cart is now drawn as the new Wagon Cart.
Two new wagons are for sale at General Stores:
The Open Wagon (900 gold) carries 1500 kg and has four seats in the back.
The Caravan (2500 gold) carries 2000 kg and you can step inside it.
If you own more than one wagon, you drive the best one, and your wagon store holds what that wagon holds.
Wagon wheels now turn as the wagon moves and turn back when you reverse. Four-wheelers steer on their front axle.
You can't sell, trade, list, or put in a guild vault a wagon you're driving while its store holds goods.
Online, you can choose Ask to ride on another player's Open Wagon. The owner gets an Accept/Decline strip.
Once seated, you go where the wagon goes, fast travel included, with no fare.
Jump gets you down.
Your companions take the seats no player is using.
Riders and companions are drawn in the wagon in the Overworld too.
Inside, the caravan is a room of its own, shaped like the caravan. Use it like a house:
Place decor.
Craft at stations.
Store things.
Rest.
Paint your wagons for free, any time. You can paint the outside of every wagon, and the caravan's walls, floor and ceiling.
Online, set Who may enter, like an online home: Only me, My party, My guild or Anyone. Visitors see what you've placed.
A save or Recall made inside a caravan that can't be re-entered now puts you outside its rear door.
From the street, house windows show a room behind the glass. At night some rooms are lit and some are dark.
From inside a house or your caravan, windows show the real street outside, at the current time of day, in the current weather, with the sea where there is one.
Hold to keep shooting. With *Draw And Release Bows* off, holding attack now fires again each time the bow is ready, at the same rate as before. You no longer need to spam-click.
No more double shots. Under the Morrowind bow, a click while the bow was still being drawn could fire two arrows from one draw, then a draw with no arrow. Each click is now one draw and one arrow.
The arrow leaves on the release. Arrows no longer fly off at the start of the draw or halfway through it.

The Morrowind bow draws properly. The nocked arrow now travels to the string and is drawn back, and the bow's limbs and string bend with the draw. Before, the bow stayed rigid and the arrow sat in its resting spot.
Weapons now carry sockets you can see: round wells under the item's picture on its card, and small pips along the top of its tile in your pack.

A weapon's size sets how many sockets it can have: one on a short blade (dagger, tanto, shortsword, wakizashi), two on a one-handed weapon, three on a two-handed weapon, a bow or the Thunderlock. Armour and jewellery keep their single socket.
Socketed weapons drop far more often. Magic weapons can now have one socket. Rare and Legendary weapons can roll extra sockets, up to their size.

Set gems yourself, right in your pack. Click an empty socket to pick a gem from your pack, or open a gem's card and choose Set in.... Setting a gem is free (the gem is spent), and you can do it on a weapon you're wearing.
Click a filled socket twice to shatter its gem. To get a gem back whole, go to the Mages Guild's Reforge, which extracts it for gold based on the gem's grade.
A piece that holds a gem is never salvaged (extract or unset the gem first), and a set gem adds its own worth to the piece's price.

Each of the eight classic gems now comes in five grades: Chipped, Flawed, regular, Flawless and Perfect. The better the grade, the stronger the bonus. Socketed in a weapon, a gem adds fire or frost damage, life leech, extra damage or an attribute; in armour or jewellery it adds a resistance or an attribute.
Gems now drop from bodies, dungeon treasure and tavern or guild caches. Deeper, deadlier places drop better grades.

World bosses drop gems. The Oblivion Gate's Warden drops one, Sethrakul drops one to every player who dealt their share of the damage, and the Brass Remnant drops two. All are Flawless or Perfect, and the bosses' weapons and armour can now come socketed.

Fair stacking: a weapon's gems of the same kind together give at most one Rare line's worth (for example +6 Fire damage at most). Mixing gem kinds pays more than doubling up, and the item card shows when a weapon hits that limit.

Monsters are now tougher depending on where you meet them, using the same grading that decides how good a place's loot is. Mines, natural caves, cemeteries and towns add nothing. In a Crypt the strongest foes have up to a third more health, in a Vampire Haunt up to 70% more, and in a Dragon's Den or the Volcanic Caves up to double health, hitting up to 25% harder and with more skill.
The wilderness is a little tougher by day and more so at night.
The weaker the creature, the less it gains: rats, bats and imps gain nothing. Offline, turning off Loot rarity turns this off too.
With the Physical Combat and Armor Overhaul on (the default), an enemy's weapon skill now helps it hit exactly as much as yours helps you. Its critical strikes land as often and hit as hard as yours.

A weapon in top condition no longer strikes up to 30% harder, and fresh armour no longer lets 15% less damage through, unless you turn on the overhaul's Equipment Damage Enhanced module (Settings > Combat > Rules & armour > Physical Combat And Armor Overhaul). That module wears gear down fast enough to make the bonus something you earn by maintaining your gear. Worn gear still hits weaker and blocks less, as before.

Elite enemies now appear offline while Loot rarity is on: about one foe in twenty in the wilds, and sometimes one in a dungeon. An elite is never a creature below level 3, and offline a level-1 or level-2 character meets no elite among a dungeon's bandits and knights.

Enhanced AI is now on by default offline, as it already was online. You can switch back to the classic enemy AI in Settings > Combat > Enemies (Enhanced AI). If you had pressed All off in the features list, it stays off.

Dying offline now costs gold. When Project Legacy raises you after a death, you lose a tenth of the gold you carry, as online. Gold in the bank is safe. The death screen shows the amount and now says Rise instead of "End the journey".

Dying offline now costs gold. When Project Legacy raises you after a death, you lose a tenth of the gold you carry, as online. Gold in the bank is safe. The death screen shows the amount and now says Rise instead of "End the journey".
Every city and town now has a Stable and a Wagon Yard. They are open-air yards on the town's open ground, clear of homes, guild halls and roads.
The Stable sells horses and buys them back.
The Wagon Yard sells the Small Cart, the Open Wagon and the Caravan, and buys any of them back.
Each yard has its own keeper, named for the town, and a signboard. Horses and wagons stand on show, and pressing one opens the yard's stock.
General Stores no longer sell or buy horses, carts or wagons.
The Open Wagon now costs 9000 gold and the Caravan 25000. Wagons bought before the change stay valid everywhere.
Every yard charges the same price in every region, and its keepers can't be stolen from.
Yards keep clear of the boulders, stalls, walls and crop fields the town mods add, and of the spots where travellers arrive.
You can see a town's yards through the windows of nearby houses.
On the Open Wagon and the Caravan you now sit on the driver's bench with the reins in hand.
Both now need a team of two horses. Buy the second one at a Stable. The Small Cart still takes one horse.
The horses are harnessed with traces and reins that sag and swing as the wagon moves.
You can zoom out to third person while driving from the bench, on the Open Wagon as well as the Caravan, and you stay in third person after fast travel or a teleport.
Your parked wagon now blocks you instead of letting you walk through it.
If you're left with one horse for a two-horse wagon, you can ride that horse again.
Wagons are no longer oversized in the Overworld.
Summoning a wagon no longer traps you under it.
Other players driving a bench wagon are drawn sitting on their bench.

Clicking Take bounty again and again now takes the board's notices in order, top to bottom. Before, the notice you had just taken stayed open with Give up under your cursor, so quick clicks took the top bounty and gave it straight back.
After your last take, the notice shows a short line instead of buttons; pick it on the left to share it or give it up. In a party, a stray click there no longer shares the bounty with everyone.
Give up now asks for a second click ("Click again to give up") and sits on the left of the notice.
The board keeps one size, so the Take button stays where it is while the list grows.

The Enhanced world map now opens on you, as if you had pressed Find me: it glides to where you stand and the red cross blinks over you. Opening it from the journal still shows the quest's place, and a journey under way, a teleport and a carriage or ship driver's map open as before. The classic map opens as it always has.

Towns in Hammerfell's regions are now walked by Redguards. Before, Sentinel, the Dragontail Mountains and other towns outside the desert had Breton and Nord townsfolk with Redguard names. Residents there keep their names but get Redguard looks, and so do the townsfolk inside houses (with Roleplay & Realism's Variant Residents on, as it is by default).

Damned weapons: one cursed Legendary weapon in four is now *Damned*. Its curse line rolls at the very top of its range, but it costs you 8 health on every hit, and no temple can lift the curse. Unequip it and the bleeding stops: take it out for a boss, then put it away.
In arena bouts, an enchantment's own bite (a Damned blade's, or any Health Leech weapon's) no longer kills you; it leaves you at 1 health like every other blow there.
The server now checks the boss's attacks itself. Your game still shows each hit, but the server also works out, from where you were standing, which of the boss's blows reached you.

The server keeps its own count of each fighter's health in these fights, and of each ship's hull against the serpent. Your game tells it your health as it changes, and potions, healing spells and repairs count as long as they stay within a set amount over time. Healing from your allies' spells doesn't use up that amount.
If you sail off to repair your ship and come back to the serpent, the server counts your hull fresh.

For now the server only records this. Nobody is knocked down or wrecked by it, and fights play exactly as before. Once a week of fights shows how much healing honest players really use, staff will switch it on.
When it is switched on, a fighter the server counts as fallen will fall in their own game too. In the Abyss Dungeon that uses up your one life, and at sea it wrecks your ship.

The server always gives you the benefit of the doubt. It only counts a blow if you were well inside the attack's area both just before and just after it landed, and it never counts elemental damage (fire, frost, shock, poison or magic), since your own resistances can block it.

Third person now works properly when you drive the Open Wagon or the Caravan from its bench. Before, the camera jammed into your character's head. Now it swings up over the wagon's roof, where you can zoom out and look down at your driver, the team and the road.
Both town maps now show each town's Stable and Wagon Yard: their ground in the shop colour, with their names written on.
The Overworld marks each Stable with a horseshoe and each Wagon Yard with a wheel, with their names. They hide with the Towns filter.
Ask anyone "Where is..." and you'll find new Stables and Wagon yards lists. Townsfolk give directions or mark them on your map, as they do for any shop.
Towns full of furnished yards are cheaper to draw. Yard pieces behind you are no longer drawn, and many copies of the same placed piece no longer force extra shadow work every frame.
The stables and wagon yards in every town you can see are no longer drawn when they are behind you or far out of view.
Collision no longer gets more expensive as you raise the view distance. Movement for you and every nearby foe costs about the same at Ultra as at Low, including while new land is loading in.
A lamp's shadow no longer redraws all six of its sides when someone walks past it. It redraws only the sides they are in front of.
Other players' name tags are cheaper for the browser to move when you turn the camera in a crowd.
The game's main per-frame loop now runs as optimized code in the browser.

Reconnecting after a server update asks less of the account service. When the world chat was too busy to let you straight in, your game used to ask for a fresh sign-in token on every retry. Now it reuses the one it already has.
The account service can now answer sign-in token requests from Cloudflare's database read replicas.
The world chat server does less work for each player who joins or leaves, and that work grows far less with the number of players online.
The World tab's "Online" count now stays accurate once more than 512 players are in the world chat. It used to creep upward.
A World tab closed because you went online on another device no longer shows the old count over an empty list.

With the Morrowind body on, the people and creatures around you stand in Morrowind bodies too. This covers dungeon and wilderness foes, the city watch, townsfolk walking the streets, people in buildings and dungeons, quest givers, the keepers of the Stables and Wagon Yards, ship crews, siege fighters, road parties, and the Oblivion Gate's boss and his host.
Foes wear the armour and carry the weapons they rolled. Each has a race and face of their own.
Online, everyone sees a foe as its owner does: the same race, face, armour and weapon. In a dungeon, each player's copy of a foe carries that player's own loot, and wears it.

Townsfolk are dressed by their station: priests in robes, nobles in formal wear, merchants, scholars, and the town's guards in steel. In a living town, people wear what their sprite shows: the watch his uniform on duty, a guild's members and priests their class's gear.
Foes swing, flinch when struck and fall when they die. Their tells show on the body too: the wind-up glint, the elite glow, the hit flash and the dissolve.
A body is drawn at its sprite's size: elites stand larger, and the wild zone's giants tower over you. The dead lie where their corpse lies, on a moving deck too.

Creatures use Morrowind's creatures where Daggerfall's have a match (rats, skeletons, daedra and more). Those with no match keep their classic sprite, as do flyers and swimmers with no Morrowind match that flies or swims.
The Daedra Seducer keeps her disguise until she transforms.
Ghosts and wraiths are Morrowind's ancestor ghost, seen through. Vampires wear their race's vampire face, werewolves stand as Bloodmoon's wolf, and orcs are Orcs.
Bodies are drawn for the nearest people only, within one budget for the whole frame. Everyone farther away keeps the classic sprite, and so does everyone seen from the travel view.
Third-person Morrowind bodies, yours included, are now skinned on the graphics card instead of the CPU.
A new Morrowind People setting (Settings > Combat > With Morrowind data): Off, Near (the default, up to 24 bodies) or All (up to 48).

New travellers set out from the towns: farmers leading a pack horse to market day, hunters heading into the wild, patrols of knights walking a round between a city and its region's towns, nobles travelling between courts with their retainers, and minstrels going to play another town's tavern for the evening.
Bigger towns now send out more pedlars, pilgrims and couriers.

Parties at night now stop at a roadside inn when one is close ahead. Otherwise they make camp, and every camp has a fire. Parties that meet on the road greet each other once in passing, warn each other of trouble behind them, and share a camp when they stop near each other.
Roads a patrol has walked recently see half the trouble. A patrol knight who sees a wanted criminal draws on them, even one the knight is on good terms with.

A merchant's caravan now travels with a horse and wagon (two wagons from a great house's city), with its guards walking in front and behind. A noble's procession brings a baggage wagon, and pedlars and farmers lead a pack horse.
The wagons' wheels turn as they roll. At camp the wagons are parked around the fire with their horses unhitched. Seen from the travel map, a caravan's mark is a wagon.
Trade with them: talk to a caravan's merchant, a farmer or a pedlar on the road to buy and sell. Each one keeps a shop's stock and has a limited purse for the trip, and gives friends 10% off.

Hire on as a guard: a merchant's caravan offers you a contract from the day before it sets out until it arrives. Stay within 300 m of it until it reaches its town to be paid by the day, plus more for each foe you beat. Fall behind for more than an hour, let the merchant die, or rob or kill any of them yourself, and you're not paid. If outlaws rob the caravan on the way, you're still paid for getting its people through. Offline, outdoors and with no enemies near, you can travel on with them, skipping ahead to their next stop.

Rob them: beat every guard of a caravan yourself and it surrenders. Its goods and purse are yours to take. But any survivor who reaches a town reports you: theft, pickpocketing and murder on the road are now charged as crimes in the region where they happened. Leave no witnesses and nobody hears about it.
Each region now has bands of outlaws (up to four), named, with a hideout off a road between two of its towns. A band holds up the parties too weak to fight it off and keeps what it took.

Find a hideout and you'll see the camp: tents, a fire, the band, and a chest of what they've stolen. Kill every one of them to rout the band. Step away and come back, and the ones you've already killed stay down; an outlaw chasing you doesn't vanish because you ran. The people it robbed will be grateful, and the region's towns will talk about it. A new band moves in later.
Travellers warn you about camps near the road they're on. A band you've heard of is marked on the travel map as a rumoured hideout, near it but never exactly on it.

Adventurers now travel together in named companies, such as "The Lantern Company", and dive dungeons more often as a group. Pilgrims going the same way on the same day travel as a band, and each region keeps its own holy day when pilgrims set out for its temple towns.
A company introduces itself by name. Your chronicle's People page lists the companies of the people you know.
A company works its way through a dungeon stop by stop, block by block. If you meet them, they're wherever their route has brought them. You may hear fighting ahead before you see them.
Talk to them to have them join you, lead on to their next stop, or part ways. Badly hurt members fall back, and a beaten company heads for the exit.

Offline, for a day after a company passes through, the monsters at the places they reached lie dead with their packs emptied and the treasure there is picked over. Quest monsters and items, fixed monsters and fixed treasure are never touched. Online, the room's dungeon is unchanged.
A rival company that isn't friendly won't like you taking treasure it was heading for.

A trader you've hired in a home that's open to the public now sells to the town's people, not only to players. Every hour, the town's people may buy a piece you've listed, at your price. The lower your price against what the piece is worth, the more likely it is to sell. A piece priced above 60% of its worth never sells to them, and a piece is never worth more to them than its own price.
Pieces you bought at a shop counter online never sell to townspeople: they buy what you found, looted or made.

A town's traders sell at most four pieces an hour between them. Each seller sells at most two an hour and 20,000 gold a day. Market tax and fees apply as for a sale to a player. Quest items and keepsakes never sell this way, and a crafted piece sells for no more than a found one.
You'll see the buyer walk in to your house a little later. Some townspeople just come in to look. Your Vendor page shows who bought what: "Sold to Ada Lark of Wayrest".
News now travels between towns: travellers bring what their home town knew when they set out, and couriers bring news from one town further.
Your reputation travels too. Strangers who have heard of your deeds (good or bad) may greet you by them. Hearsay alone never makes anyone your friend or your enemy.

Books and potion recipes no longer jump to a much higher price after passing between players online (through a shared container or a shop's shelf in a room), which let them sell back for more than they cost.

Magic, Rare and Legendary weapons can now drop with a technique: a special attack with its own key. By default that is the mouse's back side button, and you can rebind it under Controls → Combat. Unarmed fighters find their techniques on Gauntlets. Phones get a "Tech" button you can add to a touch corner, and controllers can put it on the d-pad.
Bows: *Volley*: aim a circle and six arrows rain down on it. *Piercing Shot*: one fast arrow that passes through up to five foes. The Dwarven Thunderlock can carry Piercing Shot.
Long blades: *Leap Strike*: leap onto a foe up to 9 m away and hit everything around where you land. *Whirlwind*: hit everything around you.
Short blades: *Shadowstep*: dash behind a foe and strike. *Lunge*: dash forward and hit everything you pass.
Axes: *Cleave*: a wide sweep. *Headsman's Chop*: hits harder the more wounded the foe is.
Blunt weapons: *Ground Slam*: hit everything around you. *Skull Crack*: one heavy, accurate blow.
Bare hands: *Flying Kick*: leap and strike. *Haymaker*: one heavy, accurate punch.

Hold the key to aim. A blue marker on the ground shows where a Volley will land or where a leap will end, and it turns red when the spot is out of reach. Let go to fire. A quick tap fires at once where you are looking. Techniques that don't need aiming go off as soon as you press.
Under a low ceiling a leap flies a lower arc. If no arc fits, you get "No room to leap."
The key does nothing while a window is open (a conversation, the pack, a menu).
An unidentified piece's technique works, but it is called "Your technique" until you identify it.
Every technique costs fatigue and has a cooldown. The Enhanced HUD shows a chip with the seconds left, and the message line tells you when it is ready again.
Damage still comes from Daggerfall's own formula. A technique multiplies a normal hit, so a miss is still a miss. The +N% on the item raises that multiplier.

Techniques are disabled in duels and player-vs-player bouts, and they never hit another player. A technique that hits all around you only hits an ally or a peaceful creature where a normal swing would have.
Techniques need the loot ladder. With the ladder off, none drop and the key tells you why.
The Reforge shows what a technique does under its line, so you can see it before you reforge or hone it.

A technique now has its own section on the Enhanced item card, the way set pieces and sigils do. Its header shows its own glyph (three blue strike marks), the technique's name and your roll (+23% [15-30]). Under that is what it does, then a footer with your key, whether you hold to aim or just press, the fatigue cost and the cooldown. The shop's hover card shows the same section.
The key shown is the one that actually works: your primary or secondary binding, or the controller button's name (A, Square, RB…) while you're playing on a controller.
The section is compact, so item cards still fit without scrolling. On a crowded card it drops the "hold to aim" hint first, then the footer. The Info box always shows everything.

The Info box shows the same section in full, with the word *Technique* over the name, and adds two lines: how your roll raises the technique's own blow (+23% rolled (15-30) on its 140% blow: 172% of a plain blow.), and how to use the key. If no key is bound, it tells you to bind *Weapon technique* in Controls.
In a duel the section greys out and says why.
The HUD chip uses the same glyph, so the chip and the card are clearly the same thing. It says "unbound" if no key is bound, and it hides during a duel, like set-power chips.
The classic tooltip, the Reforge and the player-to-player trade window still show a technique as two lines.
Leap Strike / Flying Kick: the view widens as you leave the ground. You land with a hard dip and a thud, and a shock ring with thrown stone spreads to the technique's reach.
Ground Slam: the weapon rises, then the view slams down for the heaviest shake of all. Two shock rings race out across the floor with the most stone and sparks.
Whirlwind: the view leans into the spin, and sparks are flung round a ring at its 3 m, carried the way the blade goes.
Cleave: the view winds up leaning one way and lands leaning the other, and a fan of sparks follows the arc.
Skull Crack / Headsman's Chop / Haymaker: a star of light and a spray of sparks where the blow lands. The Chop adds a ring under it, the Haymaker a ring standing in the air.
Shadowstep: a quick high whisk and a ring of rising light where you vanish, and a star where you strike.
Lunge: a trail of sparks down the lane you ran.
Piercing Shot: the bow kicks the view up, flares, and lays a tracer of sparks down your aim, stopping at the first thing in its way.
Volley: each of the six arrows lands with a puff of stone exactly where and when it hits the ground (on slopes too), and a ring closes over the circle with the last one.

Technique camera motion (Settings → Accessibility → Motion): Full, 75%, Half, Low or Off. It scales the view's movement, the shake and the hands' dip. At Off the screen doesn't move; the sparks and sounds stay. Better Ambience's own shake switch and limit still apply. The sounds follow Sound Enhancements.
The game also does less work every frame than before: polling a bound key no longer builds a list for every binding each time it's asked.

Other players' horses and wagons more than 400 m away are no longer updated or drawn. A town full of parked wagons no longer slows the game down wherever you are in its area. They reappear where they stand as you come near.

Wagons, carts, harnesses and tents that are off screen are no longer drawn. This covers your own and other players' wagons, the caravans and pack teams on the roads, your cart, camp tents and outlaw hideouts. If one is just off screen, its shadow still falls into view.
The game no longer fails to start with "boot failed: cannot access ... before initialization". It happened when starting near a port town, or with the travel map's dungeon lists in play.

When many players sign in at once, such as right after an update, you now wait in a short line instead of getting a "server" error. The game tells you that you're in line; try again in a few seconds and you keep your place.

Towns, woods and streets cost less to draw. Every patch of trees, plants and lamps used to carry its own small buffer, so drawing it needed a costly state switch first, nearly a thousand times a frame. Still flats now share large buffers, which cuts those switches almost in half, and the picture is the same, triangle for triangle. Measured in the real game at night, the town's frame takes about 14% less main-thread time.

Night-time towns make less garbage. Each lantern's shadow matrices are worked out in place instead of being rebuilt every frame, and the shadow pass stopped creating temporary numbers for every lantern and tree pair. That means fewer garbage-collector pauses, which show up as stutter.
Towns by a harbour are much cheaper. Moored ships no longer rebuild every part every frame, which cost up to 7 ms a frame near a port.
Busy servers stutter less. Other players' name tags, footsteps and sprites make far less garbage, and their sprite art loads in idle time instead of all at once when you turn toward a crowd.
The first spell, the first fight and the first trip to the coast or the sea no longer stall while their shaders compile. Those shaders are now built in the background.
The sky skips drawing stars during the day, when they can't be seen.
On laptops with two graphics cards, the game now asks for the faster one.
With Eye of the Beholder in first person, looking up no longer shows your own body. It now follows the mod's visibility setting, which by default casts your shadow but is never seen.

Main menu > Overhauls > UI has a fourth look, DFO Grimoire: everything Enhanced Plus does (the hotbar, camps and tents, the rest, the maps, trading and every online panel) dressed in GrimoireUI's parchment, wood, red-and-gold presses, glass vials and lettering.
The vitals are GrimoireUI's three vials, upright in the corner in Daggerfall's order or lying in a row under the hotbar.
The card has its own choices, each applied at once: Pages (cream page or tan scroll), Backdrop (the desk or the map), Vitals (upright or in a row) and Spellbook (the DFO book or GrimoireUI's own).
The front door stands on a detailed desk, as large as the screen allows, and every wooden board uses a soft desk wood.
Rarity, set and sigil names are inked deeper on the page so they stay readable.
The compass can be turned over in the HUD editor (Alt+U): a new turn-over press sits beside the X.
Main menu clicks now play the in-game click sound once your game data is loaded.
Letters of credit say what they're worth in the player-trade info box and hover.
The Daggerfall Online logo is repaired: the torn rows through "DAGGERFALL" and "The Elder Scrolls" are mended, and the clipped tops of its letters are closed.

Towns and forests draw with far fewer graphics state switches. The shared buffers that hold trees, plants and lamps now grow to fit a large town, and each kind of flat stays together, so drawing a street jumps between buffers far less often. Measured in the real game at night, a town's frame takes about 14% less main-thread time than before this change, and about a quarter less than before the previous one. Nothing looks different.

The account service was being slowed down by the Notice Board's trader directory, which every player standing in a town reads. That read now looks only at the traders of its own region, so sign-ins, saves and everything else on the account service should stop failing under load.
Other players far away are no longer drawn. Before, everyone up to about 3 km away was animated and drawn every frame, even when they were a pixel or two tall.
The new Draw distance setting on the Other players card chooses how far out other players are drawn: 150 m, 300 m (the default), 600 m, or Everyone.
Your party, and the player you're dueling, always show at any distance.
At the default 300 m you still see anyone close enough to hit you with an arrow or a spell. The 150 m option can hide a distant archer.
Near the edge between two map areas, each nearby player's position used to reach you two to four times. Now it mostly arrives once, which cuts network traffic and CPU in busy towns.
Other players move as smoothly as before.
The Small Cart's boards and stakes now run square to its box. They used to sit about 10° off, most visibly with a horse in the shafts.
The Caravan's side windows are now centred: one in the middle of each half of the side, and midway between the trim lines. From inside, the windows still line up with the outside.
Leave a wagon parked on a road in a city, hamlet or village for 10 minutes and a guard comes for it.
A town holds four parked wagons. When a fifth arrives, the one parked longest is thrown out first. Each player counts once per town: park a second wagon of your own there and that one goes first.
The guard walks up, lifts the wagon (horses and all) over their head, and throws it out of town. It tumbles through the air and lands about 40 m past the town's edge.
Nothing is lost. The wagon keeps its cargo, its paint and its horse. Walk out to fetch it, or summon it. Summon it while the guard is still carrying it and the throw stops there.
The wagon usually lands on a side of town that keeps it in the same area. In the biggest cities it lands just over the edge of the map square, and appears once you walk out to it.
You're told when the watch throws your wagon. If you weren't nearby, you're told the next time you're back near it.
Everyone nearby sees the throw. A caravan the watch threw can still be visited where it lands.
If you're riding in the back of someone's wagon when the guard lifts it, you're set down first.
A horse left on its own is never thrown. Only wagons and carts are. A horse standing beside the wagon goes with it; one you rode off and left elsewhere stays where you left it.
Offline, the 10-minute road rule still applies. The clock is kept in your save, so a wagon left on a road and loaded later is thrown as soon as you're outdoors.

From high ground the sea no longer fades into a pale band of fog that ends in a hard square edge with a darker plane behind it. It now runs on through the haze to the horizon in one piece, and the far sea reflects the sky the way the near water does.
The far sea now uses the same colour, light and sun glints as the water near you, so the two meet without a line.
No extra cost: nothing new is drawn. The far horizon that was already there now shows the sea correctly, and it now skips shading the parts hidden behind nearer ground.

Walk up to another player's home and its door now offers Vote up and Vote down. Once you've voted, that row becomes "Take back your vote up" (or down). On a touch screen, on the Classic interface, or with World Tooltips off, click the door in Info mode to vote.

Each account has one vote per home. You can't vote on your own home, your own guild's hall, or a house given by a Knightly Order. You need to have had a username and password for at least a week to vote, and you can cast up to 30 votes an hour. Taking a vote back is always allowed.

If a home's votes add up to less than zero, other players see it as Daggerfall built it: no placed decorations inside, nothing outside, and the town's own paint. A hired trader with goods on sale stays open for business. The owner, and a hall's guild members, still see everything. Nothing is deleted, and the decorations come back once the total is back to zero or above.
Once a home has votes, its door shows the total. Its owner is told, at the door or in the Info box, when the decorations are hidden.
If you voted on a guild hall before joining that guild, you can still take that vote back.
People you place with the decorator (the Vendors list), inside or in a yard, can no longer be resized. Smaller and Bigger are gone for them.

People placed earlier at another size now stand at their normal size. Moving one sets it to normal size. One that was enlarged gives back half the price difference, as shrinking any piece does; one that was shrunk costs nothing to move.
Thorns now pay back at most 10 damage per blow, down from 25. 25 was nearly two full sword swings returned every time a foe hit you, so standing still in front of an Ancient Lich could kill it.
Thorns never deal the killing blow. They can wear a foe down to its last point of health, but you have to finish it yourself.
Your existing thorns gear keeps every line it rolled.
Same rule: it still returns its share of each blow, but it never takes a foe's last point of health.
New Rare armour no longer rolls Cast When Held: Troll's Blood. It gave permanent regeneration on a piece that smiths can repair, so it never wore out.
Pieces you already own keep it and stay valid online. The Mages Guild item maker still sells it at Daggerfall's own price.

The graded gems you set into sockets (Chipped, Flawed, Flawless and Perfect stones, plus plain ones found the same way) now drop about a third as often from bodies, dungeon piles and tavern or guild markers. A mid-level foe drops one about once every 33 kills instead of once every 12. In the deepest dungeons and from boss-level foes, a gem drops once every 20 sources instead of once every 7.
A gem's grade still depends on where you find it, so a deep source still gives the Flawless and Perfect stones.
No change to the gems world bosses drop, the gems shops sell, Daggerfall's own gem drops, or the gems you mine.

Lamp shadows in towns at night take less work. When nothing near a lamp has moved, it reuses last frame's answer about which nearby plants and trees can cast into it. The shadows are exactly the same.
Distant small flats are skipped before the game checks whether they are on screen, not after.
The glow pass skips flats that have no glow before checking whether they are on screen.

Towns use less graphics memory. The large shared buffers for trees, plants and lamps now share one index buffer, where each had its own copy. That saves about 6 MB per buffer, and opening a new one no longer causes a short hitch.

With Enhanced Lighting on, taverns, shops, homes and guild halls are no longer lit evenly from wall to wall. A building's own lamps burn at half their old strength, so their light falls in warm pools with darker corners between them.
Candles and other plain white lamps indoors now burn with the same warm flame colour as the street lanterns.
Your eyes no longer brighten a dim room as much. Interiors stay moody instead of drifting toward grey.
Gold tables refused every buy-in with "You have too many stakes waiting to be settled", on every character. You can buy in now. No gold was ever taken by the refusal.
A refused stake shows as a warning, a stake being asked shows as a wait, and your turn is highlighted.
Quick buttons set your stake: Min and Max for the buy-in, and ½ pot and Pot for a raise. They only move the slider; you still press Deal me in or Raise.
The slider shows its amount with its unit (gold or chips).
A − button in the panel's title hides the seats and the log so you can see the table. The message and the buttons stay.
The log shows one line per event, and the newest line is always visible.
A key you have set but not confirmed says "Not saved yet - press Confirm." on its row.
The top of the page counts your unsaved changes and highlights Confirm.
The Confirm bar no longer hides behind the Settings search bar.
On a phone, the Confirm bar no longer covers the row you are binding.
Recall, unstuck and other teleports from a ship's helm no longer leave you stuck in the void. You leave the helm the way fast travel does, and a boat you can pack goes back into your pack.
A soul-trapped Dragonling now gives -5000 enchantment points as Soul Bound. Before, only the rare quest Dragonling did; the ones you meet in the world gave 0.
This update restarts the multiplayer server once: everyone online is disconnected for a moment and reconnects on their own.

After a server update, everyone online no longer reconnects in the same instant. Each game now waits a moment, longer the more players are online, so the account service is not overwhelmed. Rejoining the world chat takes no longer than before, but your own area may take a few extra seconds to reappear.
Games in a crowded town send less: a player with no enemies, camps, horses or boats around no longer repeats "nothing here" to everyone every two seconds.
Asking for a sign-in token costs the account service fewer database reads.
The account, realm, heartbeat and profession reads a game keeps asking can be answered by read copies of the database, so they need not queue behind everyone's saves.

After the next server update, crowded towns cost the server far less: other players' movements reach you in small bundles twenty times a second instead of one message per player per step, and the world chat's list of who joined and left arrives once a second.
After the next server update, an area next to a duel, a Wrothgarian zone fight or a sea serpent fight says so, and your game sends it every step while it does.

After the next server update, the world chat is no longer one server for everyone: players are spread over sixteen by account, so it holds many more at once. The World tab still shows how many are online and, while that is no more than 512, lists them all.
After the next server update, type /find <name> (or /who <name>) to find anyone online by name. The Guild tab lists your guildmates online wherever they are.
After the next server update, each region's chat is split four ways the same way, so a crowded start region lets everyone in faster. The Region tab still lists everyone in the region.

After the next server update, a full town, building or dungeon no longer turns you away: you join another copy of the same place (up to eight), and a party out in the open world joins its leader's copy. A sea serpent, a raid, a circle-rite and the card tables stay with the main copy of a place.

After the next server update, a world boss's court no longer turns players away when it is full: a newcomer joins a copy of the court and can fight the same boss for the same rewards, beside the players in that copy.

The Renown you earn now reaches the server every few minutes instead of every minute, which saves the server a great deal of work. Your bar still shows what you earned at once (the faint part fills in when it is counted), and a level-up and the hour's limit are still reported within the minute.
Once you have earned all the Renown an hour allows, nothing more is collected until the next hour, since the server would not count it anyway. Your weapon's sigil already stopped drinking then.
With Morrowind models on, a road caravan's campfire showed as a dead body. It's a fire again.
Your inventory's Cart slot showed "Small Cart" if you still owned your old cart after buying a Caravan. It now shows the wagon you actually drive.
A realm trade of an item you looted in the last couple of minutes could fail with "The realm could not find the goods offered". It goes through now.
You can jump while Slowfall is active. The jump is normal height and you come down at Slowfall's speed. You still can't jump in mid-air.
Legendary items no longer lose condition when you equip them. The Aegis of Dawn used to lose about a third of its condition the first time you put it on. Other magic items still pay their usual cost.

Property lines are shared with your neighbours. The ground between two houses is now split down the middle. You can no longer decorate in front of a neighbour's door, and your own door step is yours. The marked edge on the ground hasn't changed shape yet.

No single enemy blow can kill you from full health. It leaves you at 1 HP instead, and the next hit can still kill. Falls, spells, traps and world-boss attacks are unchanged. Your set's death saves (Unbroken, the Hour Turns) aren't used up on these blows, so they're still there for the next one.

If you own boats from Come Sail Away, towns no longer lose frames for every boat you've placed, wherever it's moored. A fleet parked in a far-off port used to cost frames even in a town deep inland. Other players' boats near you cost less too.
The sea's helm and broadside panels no longer do work every frame while you're ashore.

A tavern's card tables no longer stand in corridors, doorways or the mouth of an opening. At The Gold Dungeon in Menakat the table stood in the one corridor joining the inn's two halves and shut the back half off; at The Dancing Castle in Pilliweyn the red gold table stood across the hall's way east. Both are fixed, and so is every other tavern laid out like them.

A tavern with no floor for a table that is out of the way now has no card table (about one tavern in ten), and some keep only the green chips table where they had both. Almost every table that stays stands exactly where it stood.
Foes' ground telegraphs, like a revenant's blast circle, now always draw on top of deep snow. Before, the snow buried them outdoors in winter. Your own technique marks are fixed the same way.
If you would rather not have deep snow at all, turn it off at Settings › Graphics › Sky, water & weather › Snowfall by demifiend000. Searching the settings for "deep snow" also finds it.

In a trade with another player, each letter of credit now shows its worth on its own row ("Worth 12,500 gold"). That covers your pack, your offer and theirs, and works on touch without hovering or clicking. The item card shows it too, as Worth.
Copper, Silver, Platinum, Moonstone, Dwarven Scrap, Mithril, Adamantium, Ebony and Orichalcum veins each have their own colour now. Lead and Lodestone keep their classic look.
Online, point at open ground on the world map to see a card listing:
the ores its veins can be;
what its dungeons' deep veins hold;
its kingdom's own ore (Daggerfall's Moonstone, Sentinel's Ebony, Wayrest's Mithril, and so on);
whether that ground is witnessed yet.

Gold, Platinum, Mithril, Ebony and a kingdom's own ore only appear on ground that three different players have gathered on (each account at least a week old). That's because the servers can't check which land a player claims to be standing on. The card shows which ores are waiting on that for each place. The Mining page now points to it.
Sethrakul's waters now stay open until it dives. The 08:00 storm no longer locks ships out, so latecomers and friends sailing out to help can still join.
The serpent has a sixth less health, so fights end sooner. Two ships at average gunnery now win every time, in about 8½ minutes.
One ship alone still can't bring it down.
Inside its waters a gale fills your sails from every direction. No more beating upwind at half speed.
Your ship also turns 1½ times faster while you're in it.
Its blows throw your ship half as far and tear half as much canvas. You won't be pushed out of the fight and left unable to sail back.
Sethrakul is much thicker now (1.6 times its old girth), so slow cannonballs fired with lag still land.
Players standing on someone else's ship can hurt the serpent with their own bows and attack spells.
In the serpent's waters ships have a wide invisible buffer around them and bounce off each other, instead of colliding and passing through.
Rewards no longer depend on being near the serpent when it dies.
Dealing a real part of the damage (several volleys that land) now earns a hoard. Spending a quarter of the fight within range does too, where half was needed before.
When the serpent falls, party members of any ship that dealt heavy damage also get a hoard, as long as they came to the fight.

With a spell readied, your casting hands are now raised and ready on screen until you cast. This is jefetienne's Readied Spellcasting Hands 1.3, ported 1:1. Self-only spells raise nothing because they cast at once. It's on by default and you can turn it off under Features -> Combat.

The chat has a search bar above the player list (over the conversation on narrow screens). Type part of a name, or # and a tag, to see every tab's lines from or about that player. The player list filters to match.
Type /search <name> in the chat field to search, and /search on its own to clear it. /find and /who still look up who is online anywhere in the world.
Text on the parchment is readable again: the Social panel, letters, the guild page and fields you type in are now in the page's ink.
The stray ruled lines are gone from the talk window, Professions and Master Skills.
Enemy and boss health bars scale with your screen resolution. They no longer drain or sit on a board, and they stretch cleanly when made longer in the HUD editor (Alt+U).
In the HUD editor (Alt+U), the length handle now follows your pointer, and resizing a piece no longer pushes it off the screen.
In the in-game book, a setting's description opens as a scroll beside the book instead of covering the list. The Controls header no longer hides the rows while you scroll.
In the decorations menu you can now see which tabs and filters are selected.
The world and town maps have their Find me button back. It is still hidden on the dungeon's hand-drawn map.
Spamming the hotbar no longer makes the game stutter.
You can type in the quest journal's note field on the classic and Grimoire UIs again. It now opens as the game's standard text-entry box.

Pressing your home's enchanting station now asks what you want: Daggerfall's item maker (Make Magic Items) or Disenchant. Disenchant opens your Stores page, scrolled to the Enchanting Station section, where a crafted piece comes apart into Arcane Essence.
The alchemy station works the same way: Make Potions, or Brew on your Stores page.
Offline, both stations open Daggerfall's maker as before.

The Members page of the Guild tab now shows whether each member is online, the same way the Friends list does: a green dot while they're playing, and "Online" or "Last online 3 h ago" under their rank.
A member counts as online while they're in the world (within ten minutes of their last check-in), and the time keeps updating while the page is open.
The old tutorial is gone. New characters get a short welcome tour: moving and climbing, using things, the HUD, and the menu and saving.
Any key a tutorial mentions is the key you have bound right now, named the way it appears on your keyboard.
The first time you reach something new, a short note explains it. About 56 systems have one, including:
Each note shows once. Click or press a key to close it.
Notes won't close from a key you're already holding.
Notes wait until the pause menu and loading screens are gone.
A Tutorials tab in the pause menu and a Tutorials button on the main menu hold all 68 notes, in 13 sections.
You can search the notes, and unread ones are marked.
You can turn popups off, show them all again, or mark everything read.

Other players no longer look like they're floating above the ground or sunk into it. Their height was being rounded to the nearest metre on its way to you, so depending on where they stood they could be up to half a metre off the ground.
In dungeons, towns and buildings, other players no longer move in one-metre jumps.
This update restarts the online server once, so everyone online is disconnected briefly and reconnects.

Members has a new folded list, "What each rank may do". It shows every rank's powers in your guild's own rank names, each rank on top of the one below, and what a rank may not do: Officers and the Guildmaster don't fill their own guild's writs or get paid by its contracts. A Member and a Recruit hold the same powers, and the list now says so.
Treasury now says which of the gold can buy a hall, or a new name or tag: only gold your realm characters put in.

The silver ledger now says which way each line went. A Tribute, an upkeep or a claim fee reads "paid ...", where it used to read "put in". A line the guild made itself, such as a Sellsword hired or a Charter's upkeep, now reads as the guild's ("The guild hired a Sellsword for 1,500 silver").

Settings lists everything that still stands in the way of disbanding, before you press: gold, the hall, the vault, guild Stores, open writs or contracts, a Charter, a battle, and silver your own account has no room to take. Disband waits on it and says why, and so does Leave for a guildmaster alone in the guild. You no longer clear one thing, press, and only then hear about the next. Opening Settings checks the list again.
Overview says where the rest of your guild is run: seats and sieges from a seat town's Notice Board, writs and contracts from the Work tab.
No guild yet? The tab now says, in two lines, what a guild is for.
Silver is called silver everywhere: a siege's Honour, a struck Charter's refund and the daily reset said "Marks".
A vassal's 5% to its liege is its "fealty share", so "Tribute" means only what a guild pays at the seat it pledged.
Your guild's heraldry is its "arms" everywhere, as on the Arms page.
A shot that misses now stays in the wall, floor, tree or ground it hit. You can take it back like any other pile: the plaque reads "Arrow", and quick loot takes it in one press.
Up to 40 stay in one place, and the oldest goes first. They're gone once you leave the area.
Conjured arrows still vanish. Arrows shot in an arena bout are still refunded by the healers instead of sticking.
An arrow that hits an enemy now survives half the time and can be looted from the body.
Arrows no longer count toward a normal enemy's three-item drop limit. That limit was throwing them away first, which is why bodies almost never gave arrows back.
Use Twigs, a Pine Branch or a Wood Bundle from your inventory (Use mode) to fletch arrows: 2, 4 and 10 arrows each. This works online and offline.
Weapon Smiths now always keep 50-100 arrows on the counter. Armorers and General Stores keep 14-29, and Pawn Shops 7-14. Better shops keep more.
Daggerfall Online is now DFO Online, with a new logo on the intro, the main menu, the menu's masthead, the website and the desktop launcher.
The website, the desktop app, its installer and the home-screen app all carry the new name. The home-screen label reads DFO.

Settings and menus now say "the original game" or "classic" where they used to name it. For example, "Off uses the classic weather". The leveling choice and the classic start are titled Classic, and the third view-distance step reads Classic (3).
Screenshots and saved loading shots are now named dfo-..., and the saves you export are DFO-Online-Saves.zip.
The downloads are named DFO-Online-... from this update on. Your copy finds its update as usual, whatever it was called when you installed it.

On a Mac: the new version installs as DFO Online beside your old Daggerfall Online app instead of replacing it. Once DFO Online opens, drag the old app to the Bin. Your saves, settings and game folder stay where they are.
On Windows: if you pinned the app to your taskbar or Start menu, you may need to pin it again under its new name.
The Terms of Service and the Privacy Policy now name DFO Online. Nothing else in them changed, and no one is asked to agree again.
Going all in and losing at an online Hold'em table no longer crashes the game. The hand that broke you now plays out on the table before you're stood up.
With All pressed, the 3D dungeon map now draws every ramp in full. Daggerfall's standard ramps used to be cut off at the floor below.
Kills you make after a raid's fight drifts past the edge of town now count, as long as you're still on the town's map square.
Dying, fast travelling, Recall or /unstuck in the middle of a raid no longer stops raiders from coming when you return.
The raid card on the map shows the town's real count against its real target (anywhere from 15 to 25), not only your own kills.
The loot list on a body or pile now scrolls. The mouse wheel (or the pad) reaches every item, not only the first six, and the list shows how many items are above and below.
People placed by a quest now show their name when you look at them, like everyone else in the room.
When the realm refuses a trade because a character is under review, it now says whose character it is: yours, with the reason, or the other player's.
EG0 + AUDIT EG0 + EG0b + AUDIT EG II: Elite Gates - the Elite Breach and the Battlespire's torn halls, designed, audited and polished
Re-casting an effect that is already on you or a target now resets it to that cast's full duration. It no longer adds the new duration on top, and a shorter re-cast never cuts a longer one short.

This applies to buffs and debuffs alike. That covers Shield, Fortify, Regenerate, Levitate, Light, Detect, the resistances and the rest; Paralyze, Silence, Continuous Damage and Soul Trap; a party member's spells on you; and a torch's fire on a foe.
Re-casting Regenerate or a Continuous Damage effect on its last round still gives the full number of ticks a fresh cast would.
Buffs banked before this update keep their time and run out normally. You can also end them yourself from the buff icons.
When a window is open, F11 (Quick Load) now works only from the death screen. Loading from under your pack, a loot window or a sell counter could duplicate what that window was holding.
Any load closes every open window before the save is read, including windows left waiting behind the death screen.

Shops pay for a crafted Superior or Masterwork piece what they pay for the plain piece its recipe makes. The quality's magic or rare lines are power, not resale value: the piece keeps them, and keeps its worth to other players.
Patrons follow the same rule for crafted pieces. Found magic and rare items are priced as before.
The keyed shelf now prices a sale exactly as the trade window does, and no longer buys conjured (Create Item) pieces.

A character whose trade is on hold can no longer move its crafted pieces through another character, by listing, auctioning, filling a commission or disenchanting. Its Stores also cannot go into a guild's Stores or fill a guild writ.
Other players' yard decorations no longer draw across the whole map. Their small pictures (flowers, signs, crates) had no distance limit at all; now they stop where the models stop.
Tiny yard pieces stop drawing once they would be only a few pixels tall, so a busy street of furnished yards costs much less.
New option: Settings → Other players → Yard decorations: Off, 75 m, 150 m or 300 m (the default, as before). Your own yard always shows. If towns run slowly for you, try 150 m or Off.
Yard pieces still standing above the 4 m height limit (built before the limit existed) have been removed. No gold is refunded for them.
A username can no longer be an email address. If you already signed up with one, you still sign in with it, but other players now see your generated name instead of your address.
The board's Seat tab no longer gets stuck on "The standings did not load." once many guilds have pledged.
The weekly Turning hands out Charters again. A guild that earned a seat last week is given it the first time anyone reads a seat after this update.
Caravans and travellers now keep to the right of the road, so parties that meet pass side by side instead of walking through each other's wagons. Two caravans heading the same way walk abreast.
A wagon now follows its horse round a bend instead of swinging round all at once.
At a shared camp, every caravan's wagons park round one fire without standing in each other, and each horse is tied alongside its cart.
In a roadside hold-up, fighters and bandits no longer stand inside the wagons and horses.
A roadside fight you walk up to no longer ends by itself, killing the caravan's guards and counting as a win you never fought.
A merchant whose caravan will meet trouble now offers to hire you, and the missing offer no longer gives that away.
Remains found in a dungeon are no longer laid again after you save and load inside it.
Townsfolk walking into a shop are inside as soon as they reach the door.
In town, people no longer stand inside one another in a three-person conversation.
The weekly seat Turning can no longer swamp the servers. Only one request at a time settles the week; everyone else's seat board answers immediately.

If you act at a seat (pledge, Tribute, a lever) in the moment the week is turning, you're told "The week is turning at the seats. Try again in a moment." The act is never applied to a half-turned week.

Port towns now have a shipyard on their seaward edge, its back to the water. The shipmaster sells every ship Come Sail Away builds, from the Rowboat to the Carrack and the Large Galley, and buys your ships back. One window holds everything you do with a ship at a port:

Ships for sale: each hull's size, crew, guns and price. Buying asks you to confirm. The Rowboat goes into your pack as parts (if you can carry them). Every other ship's deed goes into your Fleet, and she is laid up at that port: the window turns to Your fleet, where Bring her here brings her round to the quay.

Your fleet: where each ship lies, what she's worth and what the shipmaster will pay. You can bring her here, lay her up, rename her or sell her. Selling asks you to confirm, and a big sale is paid as a letter of credit if the coin would be too heavy.
Shipwright and Refits: repairs, provisions and the four refit lines for any ship of yours at that port or laid up. These need Naval Combat on.

The shipmaster won't buy a ship with cargo in her hold, anything in her cabin (in its chests or on its floor), or her crew ashore with you, and he won't buy a ship that came into the realm through customs: she stays yours. When a ship is sold, her cabin's furniture is sold too, and half its value goes to the bank, as with a house.

Inside every shipyard, the crewmaster has six named sailors looking for a berth each day. Each one has a class, a grade from Green to Veteran, a trade (First Mate, Bosun, Gunner, Carpenter, Lookout, Cook, Deckhand, or a Bard) and a signing fee. You choose which ship they join and at what post.

A ship comes with her whole crew, so on a full deck a recruit signs on in place of a hand you pick. A hire that adds men to her crew costs what the shipwright would charge for them, if that's more than the fee. You can pay hands off from the same page: if her crew still fills her deck, the window names who steps up, and you can't pay off her last hand. Hiring and paying off need Naval Combat on and can't happen during a fight.

Port towns have a lighthouse: a whitewashed stone tower with red bands, a gallery and a lantern room, and the keeper's cottage beside it. While the town's lanterns are lit (5 pm to 8 am) its lamp lights the harbour, and two beams sweep a full circle, over the sea and the town. Online, everyone sees the beams in the same place.

Talk to the lightkeeper (or press the door) to climb up to the gallery: you go up on foot, not at a ship's helm and not with enemies about. You can't fall or climb off the gallery. The hatch takes you back down.

Every quay has been overhauled: cross-braced piles, timbers under the decks, fender piles and iron ladders down into the water, cleats and coils of rope by the bollards, a cargo crane on each harbour's main quay, and lamp posts along the long jetties.

Townsfolk can now tell you where to find the shipyard, the crew hall, the lighthouse and the docks. The shipyard and the lighthouse are marked on the town map; for the crew hall and the docks, townsfolk give you directions. On the Overworld the shipyard, the lighthouse and the docks show as an anchor, a tower and a bollard.
General Stores and Pawn Shops no longer sell or buy ship deeds and parts. Ships are bought and sold at the shipyards.

The tutorial's Sailing page now sends you to the shipyards, Shipwrights is now Shipyards (the shipmaster, the crew hall and the shipwright), and there's a new Lighthouses page. The empty Fleet page and Come Sail Away's setting now point you to the shipyards too.
A ship sold while you were placing her could be placed and sold again.
A double click could buy two ships.
Paying off a hand could put a stranger on deck, and hiring could raise a wreck back afloat.
Hiring and paying off could push a ship's morale past its limit.
The crew page didn't show which hands were ashore with you.
Climbing or jumping on the lighthouse gallery could take you over the railing.
Coming down the lighthouse stair could leave you stuck in the door's step.
The lighthouse lamp was blocked by its own glass, so it barely lit anything with Enhanced Lighting.
The lighthouse sometimes stood right beside the shipyard instead of along the shore.
A lake behind a port town could be taken for the sea.
Selling a ship lost whatever lay on her cabin floor.
Flickering roofs, beams and posts on the shipyard and the lighthouse, and props poking through each other.
Ports, lighthouses and quays run lighter: the lighthouse lights cost nothing per frame, the port's textures load over a few frames, and the quays' hidden timbers are left out of collision.
Every hand now earns rank from the fights and boardings they have been through: Green, Seasoned, Veteran, Old Salt.

The six posts aboard each do something, and do more the longer their holder has served. The Gunner speeds the reload, the Carpenter the mending, the Lookout lets you see further, the Cook keeps spirits up, the Bosun adds way under sail, and the First Mate brings extra hands over the rail (never more than your crew has men for).
A companion who sails with you works his post while you're at the helm.
A new hand takes whichever post is emptiest, so a fallen Cook is replaced before you get a third Bosun. You can still reassign posts on the Fleet page.
The new Captain tab in Holdings keeps your log: leagues sailed, ships sunk, taken and beaten off, contracts done, your best prize and the plunder you hauled.

You also build standing with each crown, from Unsworn to Admiral. Each rank brings perks in that crown's harbours: a discount at the shipwright, better-paid and more contracts, a letter of marque for sale (Privateer), the Admiralty's carrack for sale and seasoned hires (Commodore), and the navy always coming to your aid against pirates (Admiral). A captain whose notoriety runs too high in a crown's waters gets none of them there.
Beating off a pirate boarding now pays. The pirate is beaten then: taking or sinking her afterwards is logged but not paid again.
A letter of marque makes a rival crown's merchantmen and navy lawful prize in your crown's eyes. The rival still calls it piracy.
Far from every port, pirates are more common, bolder and bigger, and every hold and floating cask is richer. The helm plate tells you when you're in the deep.
Ship names no longer float over every sail. A ship you haven't identified is just her hull, such as "a sloop" or "a two-master", and her card says nothing else about her: no colours, no damage.
You learn her colours by sailing close, from your Lookout's call, when her guns turn on you, or through the spyglass.

Press K aboard to raise the glass and use the mouse wheel to zoom (x2, x4, x8). Hold it on a ship to read her name and colours. Hold it on her up close to see her guns, crew, damage and cargo. The glass can't see ships behind land, or dark ships far off at night.
Some wary pirates sail under false colours, passing for a merchantman of their own size with a trader's name. The glass can see through them, and they run up the black flag when they come for you.

On a controller, the d-pad press you give the Spyglass works at the helm too, and the right stick's click zooms while the glass is up. On a touch screen, the Glass button sits at the helm and as a corner-button choice, and the glass has its own Magnify and Lower buttons.

Every port's shipwright window now has a Harbourmaster tab with the day's contracts, while your ship lies at that port's quay. Bounties on a named pirate, hunts in the crown's waters, cargo to carry to another port, a wreck's casks to raise, and Admiralty surveys of ships through the spyglass.

Contracts pay by your level and rank and run to a deadline. Finishing one raises your standing with the crown; failing or giving one up lowers it. You can hold three at a time, and the Captain tab lists them. Each kill or survey counts toward one contract.
The bounty's pirate is waiting in the waters named on the contract. If someone else sinks her first, the bounty is void, with no loss of standing. A wreck's casks float up when you reach its mark.

An Exchange tab buys and sells eight goods of the Bay: wine, grain, wool, iron, spices, silk, silver and ivory. Each crown's ports make some goods cheaply and pay well for others, every port has a twist of its own, and prices drift from day to day. Each port only deals in so much of a good each day.
Goods load into and out of the hold of the ship at the quay. A full hold slows her. The exchange tells you how much more she can carry and won't sell her so much she can't move.
Shops don't buy the exchange's goods. Sell them at an exchange.

Pirates you sink or take sometimes carry a treasure chart, more often in the deep waters and most flagships. Read it from your inventory to mark its cache, then sail to the spot and the cache floats up beside you: gold and a strongbox's worth of loot. A cache you've already raised stays raised.

Sail far out on the open Abecean, west of the Bay's mouth and well away from any land, and you're asked whether to sail on into the open sea. Three days later your ship comes out off Veilhaven, the first port past the Veil, with her crew and her hold aboard. Sail back into the Veil, at the sea's eastern edge, to be asked the way home. If an enemy is close or another player is aboard, you're told so, and asked again once the deck is clear.

Past the Veil lies an endless sea of isles, the same for every player. Port isles have a town and a freeport quay, ruins have a dungeon to delve, wild isles bear exotic goods, and bare rocks are just rocks.

The farther west you sail, through the Shallows, the Reaches, the Deep Aether and the Abyss, the deadlier the corsairs and the richer every hold. Ruins in the Deep Aether and the Abyss are Elite dungeons.

No crown's law reaches past the Veil. There's no navy to call on, and nothing you sink there counts as a crime. Corsairs and the isles' traders sail under the sea's own names, and a corsair's papers sometimes chart her waters for you.

Exotic goods: ether-amber, starglass and voidsilk are made on the isles and wanted in every port of the Bay, and the isles pay well for the Bay's goods. Sail close to a wild isle and casks of its good float out alongside your ship; its strand fills again seven days after you first gather it.

Six legendary ships haunt the depths, each with her own terror and a purse on her head: Sorrow's Wake, The Drowned Queen, Ninefold Hunger, The Lantern-Eater, The Pale Regent and The Starless. A freeport's harbourmaster will tell you where each was last seen. Sink one for her purse and a name with every crown, though a month later the sea raises her again.

The Chart of the Etheric Sea: past the Veil, the travel map key opens your chart of the isles you've sighted, the depths, the Veil and the legends' haunts you've heard of. Drag to pan; zoom with the wheel, a pinch or the chart's own buttons; point at or tap an isle to name it. Isles are charted as you sight them, and a freeport sells a chart of its waters.

The Veil holds the Bay's magic back: Recall, guild teleports, portal stones and a party's travel to its leader don't cross it, and your Fleet can't summon or send a ship across. Sail her yourself. Fall past the Veil and you wake at the nearest port isle.
The light past the Veil is cold and violet.
The crossing out is part of the enhanced game and online play. The classic game keeps Daggerfall's own sea, though a captain already past the Veil can always sail home.
A herb patch, vein, boulder or tree now goes the moment you finish working it, instead of waiting for the server to answer. If the server refuses the harvest, the node comes back.
Your goods, XP and rank-ups arrive faster after each harvest.
The market loads noticeably faster, especially when switching views and after buying.
A view you opened in the last minute shows straight away, without a "Reading the market..." flash.

The desktop app finds and installs updates again. No new desktop release had been published since 0.1.8020, so the launcher had nothing to offer. The next release after this merge brings in everything merged since then.
A new What this is panel sits at the top. It says what a seat is in two sentences, plus your next step: join a guild, pledge here, ask an Officer, or earn influence.
If your guild can pledge here, the Pledge button is right beside that line. Deadlines show how long is left.
How the seat war works is now at the top. It starts open if your guild isn't in this region's war yet.

Words on this board explains every term the tab uses: Charter, influence, Muster, Reckoning, Turning, Right of Siege, Defence, Standing, Tithe, Edict, Tribute, Sellsword, the Works, Fealty and Pacts, Seasons and Tides.
You see the explanation even when the standings are still loading or closed to you.

How chapters work sits above the chapter cards on the Work tab. It covers what a chapter is and how you belong to one, Merit, Strength, the bands, the Master's and council chairs, Seasons and patrons. Every number comes from the game's own rules.
It starts open until you have earned your first Merit.
The Family tab has a fourth page, How it works. It covers:
death under your house's rules and the toll you chose;
who carries the line on, and what they inherit;
heirlooms and remains;
marriage and children;
playing another family member;
what the marks on the tree mean.
The family tree links to it: "New to the family? How it works".
Long names on the tree now wrap onto two lines instead of being cut off. Hover a name to see it in full.
Talking to a Living World resident now shows how they regard you, under their name. It shows Friend, Known, Enemy or Hostile, a bar from −100 to +100, and the number.
Press it to see what the number means and what raises or lowers it.
This works for residents in the street, at home, on the road and in the deep.
Someone who won't talk to you now says where you stand, e.g. "Mara turns away from you. (Enemy, −52)".
On the classic skin, the talk window is the original game's and does not show the badge.
The Notice Board's text is a step larger, and the Family tab's tree, card and labels are larger too.
On a phone, the fold headers are bigger to tap.

Windows inside buildings are now see-through. From a house, tavern, shop, guild hall or temple you see the real street, sky and weather through the panes, and the window's lead lattice and frame stay in place. This needs Settings > Graphics > Real windows set to Full, which is the default on High and Ultra.

The Standing page now lists your reputation with every guild, temple, knightly order, kingdom, coven, vampire clan and Daedric Prince by default, not only the ones you belong to. If you turned "Every faction's standing" off (Settings > Interface > Character sheet), it stays off.
Stables now sell Sacks of Oats and Wagon Yards now sell Wagon Repair Kits online too. Until now they were only sold offline.

A worn-out wagon never becomes unusable. At its worst it is Failing: its team pulls it more slowly, but you can still drive it, hitch it, have it follow you and take it on journeys. A Wagon Yard or a repair kit brings its speed back.
A wagon that was already broken down in your save is now Failing, so you can drive it again.
Horses never die. A horse left unfed goes hungry and then starves. It gets weaker and won't gallop, but it stays yours, and one meal puts it right.
The Chapters from "The Chapters" update are now open to everyone. They had been switched on for developers only.
Guild chapters, hall writs and your own chapter writ now appear on the Notice Board's Work tab.
Boards fill in town by town: a town's chapters appear once three players have visited its guild halls.

Docks no longer cross each other. In harbours round a cape or a bay's horn, two piers could meet over the water in an X; Penwall Derry was one. A pier now ends where it meets its neighbour's, and no berth is placed with its quay over another's.
Fixed a phantom room tab in two-storey homes, often "Room 3". It sat in the gap between the floors, and picking it sent the decorating camera into the walls.
If your trading is held over an item, a refused trade now names that item instead of "something".
The hold notice now warns that each hold counts: the third time, trading stays frozen until staff have looked, even after the item is gone.
If a hold stays after the item is gone, the game now tells you it is waiting on staff review instead of saying nothing.
The sea west of the Bay is water again. You can swim there, Buoyancy works, and you can get back to your ship. Before, you stood on a seabed under the surface.
A torch, lantern or Candle spell underwater no longer whites out the screen. It gives a soft glow and still lights what's near you.
Lights in heavy fog and sandstorms glow a little less, for the same reason.
Rain and snow no longer get choppy after the game has been left open for many hours.

The Greater Giant in the open zone drops its proper loot again: two elite-table drops (magic and common pieces, a chance at rare or legendary, and gold by level). Before this fix it only dropped an ordinary giant's purse.
The Greater Giant now hits every player at four times damage. Before, it did that only to the player whose game spawned it. Everyone else took hits like an ordinary zone giant.

A quest monster, item or person could be placed outside its dungeon if the dungeon was built at a different size from the one the quest was set up on.
