One example was the mummy for Dust of Restful Death in Ruins of Old Barbara's Place. Now, each time a dungeon loads, anything on a spot that doesn't exist is moved to a valid spot inside. To fix a quest that's already stuck, leave the dungeon and walk back in, or reload.
Riding with the Morrowind models in third person no longer paints Daggerfall's 2D horse head and neck over the screen. You see only your character on the 3D horse.
New Text font setting under Overhauls > UI (for Enhanced Plus and DFO Grimoire), with five choices: Game, Sans, Monospace, Dyslexic (OpenDyslexic) or My font.
My font takes the name of a font installed on your computer. List my fonts shows them in browsers that support it.
The change applies at once. OpenDyslexic downloads only if you choose it.
Every channel has its own colour:
World is white, Region green, Guild purple, Local grey, Party teal, Language rose.
Each tab shows a colour square.
Turn this off in Settings > Gameplay > Other players > Chat colours by channel.
Player names have their own colour, separate from their words: strangers brass (red on Grimoire), you pale gold, party members green, friends blue.
Language channels, in 15 languages:
/lang de joins one, /lang off leaves it, /lang lists them all, and /lc <text> speaks there.
You can also choose one in Settings > Gameplay > Other players > Language channel.
A Lang tab appears while you're in one.
@mentions: a line with @YourName is highlighted in gold, shows over the world from any tab, and plays a chime. Turn the chime off with Chime when someone @mentions you.
On DFO Grimoire, a chat tab's unread count is a seal beside its name: red, or gold when it holds a mention.
Inventory: the worn sets lines (e.g. Dagon's Brand 7/9) sit under the paperdoll only, so the item box keeps its full height.
Pause menu: the right-hand page is centred instead of pushed far to the right.
Scry (Reforge):
The price no longer runs over the Scry button, so you can read it and buy again.
On Grimoire each family's name is in the book's red, and the reason you can't afford it is in soft ink.
Rows: hovered and chosen rows are washed a shade darker instead of getting a red bar. The dashed boxes round empty lists are gone.
Faint text is darkened just enough to read.

Port town lighthouses were built like lighthouses from a much later age: whitewash and red stripes, a glass lantern room, a copper dome. They are now beacon towers of the Iliac Bay: bare grey stone with a battlemented parapet round the gallery, an open stone lantern of eight arches under a steep slate roof, and a fire burning in an iron brazier inside.
The beacon is lit from dusk to dawn. The flames rise in the brazier at nightfall and its sweeping beams still reach far out to sea. By day its coals smoulder.
Windows on the lighthouse and the shipyard office now have small leaded panes.

Looking toward a far-off ship used to show her card, with her type and how far off she was, before you had identified her at all. You could spot and range ships without ever raising the spyglass. Now a ship you have not made out shows no card, whether you are simply looking at her or have your broadside laid on her.
To make her out, come within plain sight of her, let your Lookout call her colours, or hold your spyglass on her. Then her card shows as before.

Raising the spyglass at the helm used to fill most of the view with your own masts, sails and crew. The glass now looks past your own ship: while it is raised, her rigging and hands drop out of the view.
Every ship beyond yours stays in view and can be studied with the glass, even one lying close alongside.
Looking straight along the deck toward the bow of a very long ship, such as the Large Galley, part of her bow can still show.

Ships sailing around other players far across the map are no longer built and animated on your screen. They come into view, fading in as any ship does, well before the haze would let you see them. On a busy server this gave back about a third of each frame: one player went from 38-45 FPS to 103-150 FPS.

With Morrowind data attached, townsfolk, guards, shopkeepers, foes, travellers and the figures you place now cast the shadow of their own Morrowind body (its shape, its pose, its clothes) instead of the old Daggerfall sprite's outline on the wall behind them.
Someone just out of view still throws their shadow into it, as the old sprites did.
A foe burning away, or a companion stepping through a portal, loses their shadow once more of them is gone than whole, as the old sprites did.
In a room with many lamps, such as a guild hall, people standing still cast a shadow from every lamp, not only from the nearest twelve.
Your own body, other players' bodies and your household's do not cast a shadow yet.

Townsfolk, shopkeepers, guild members, nobles and priests are dressed from a wardrobe of their own: tops, breeches, skirts, robes and cloaks, each drawn as one of Morrowind's own garments of its kind, in their kind's colours. Their station sets how fine the clothes are, on Morrowind's ladder from common up to exquisite.
A noble never wears common clothes, a farmhand never wears silk, and a dyed garment keeps its colour.

Heads and hairs are now paired freely, from every pairing of the heads and hairs your Morrowind data offers a race at character creation (before, there were ten). Together with their clothes, this makes two people who look alike rare.
Who wears what is sharper:
A knightly order's people wear full plate of one metal by rank: iron and steel at the bottom, up to dwarven, orcish and ebony.
A fighters' guild's people wear whatever armour came to hand.
The Dark Brotherhood dress in dark clothes.
The street's walkers keep the cut their sprite shows: robes, a skirt or breeches.
Khajiit and Argonians go barefoot and bareheaded, as Morrowind dresses them.
A person you place as a decoration in your home or your yard now stands in a Morrowind body too, dressed for who the figure is and of the region's race.
You can now ride in third person with the Morrowind body. Zoom out with the wheel or the view toggle as you would on foot.
In first person, you look down over the 3D horse's neck instead of the old riding sprite.
Other riders on the Morrowind body, Horse Cart and Cargo's horses (standing, following, parked and pulling) and the road's wagon teams are all 3D horses too.
The 3D horse wears the same coat, pattern, legs and markings as your sprite horse, and each flank has markings of its own.

Gallop on its breath. Hold Run on horseback to gallop. Your horse spends its breath instead of your fatigue. When it runs out the horse is winded and won't gallop until it has caught its breath. A horse bar appears on the HUD while you ride.

Feed it to grow your bond. Feed your horse oats (sold at the Stable) or give it an apple as a treat. Every meal grows your bond, from Wary up to Kindred, and a stronger bond makes every stat better, up to +20.

Keep it fed. A hungry horse is weaker. A starving one won't gallop, and your bond slowly fades. A horse never dies of hunger. A horse sent to the stable is fed there, and one left waiting in the wild grazes. On long journeys and rests, your horse eats oats you carry in your pack or wagon.
More than one horse. The Stable page (Holdings tab) shows every horse you own, with its stats, bond, hunger and breath. Feed any of them, or pick which one you ride.
Mend it at a Wagon Yard. The wagonwright now has a Mend option. If your wagon isn't with you, they'll go out to it for a little more.
Patch it in the field with a Wagon Repair Kit (sold at the Wagon Yard). Each kit takes an hour and mends a quarter, up to 60%, enough to limp a broken wagon into town.
Smiths and the Repairs Objects enchantment don't repair wagons or horses.
See how your horse is doing: its breath, its hunger (with how many hours of food it has left) and its bond, plus your gait and speed. On a wagon it also shows the wagon's condition and its load.
Do it from the panel: Feed oats, give an Apple, use a Repair kit, open the wagon's Cargo, open the Stable page, switch the View, or Dismount, all without a menu or a key.
Teams count: on a wagon, the hunger shown is your team's hungriest horse, and Feed goes to that horse.
Greyed out means not now: a button you can't use yet is greyed out, and hovering it says why (no oats, full, out of reach).
Free the mouse (Y) to click the buttons, or tap them on a phone.
Each horse's bond is a bar now, with the points left to its next level.
A fed horse says how many hours of food it has left, and a winded horse says so.
Hover a stat to see where it comes from: what the horse was born with, its bond bonus and any hunger penalty.
The wagon's condition bar is coloured by its state, and the card shows what a Wagon Yard charges to mend it.
Seat boards, market sales and courier deliveries no longer slow the whole account service down in regions where a guild holds a Charter.
The curse's +40 Strength, Agility, Endurance and Speed and +30 to its seven skills now apply only in beast form. In human form you are your own character again. The beast itself is unchanged.
Changing form fully heals you once a day. Changing back, or changing again with Hircine's Ring, no longer heals.
The beast's claws count as silver against creatures that need a better metal. A Lich or an Ancient Lich now takes reduced damage from claws, the same as from a silver weapon.
A raised hood still protects you from the sun's penalty, but no longer gives the night's +20 in daylight. Indoors, underground and at night you keep the full +20.
Rare weapons can no longer roll Vampiric Effect (heal all the damage you deal). Weapons that already have it keep it.
Life leech from a weapon's lines and gems together is capped at 10% of each hit.
Hist-Sap (the Mark of the Hist) now regenerates 1% a round (2% under half health), down from 2% (4%).
Open Hand (the Gauntlets of the Rose): the second bare-handed hit now deals half damage.
Melee and ranged attacks now share the same damage ceiling as spells: at most 180 damage in any 5 seconds, counting blows and casts together.
Fixed: in arena bouts, hits from one side of your opponent always counted as backstabs (triple damage), whichever way they faced. Backstabs no longer happen against players.
With Morrowind models on, other characters and horses no longer shrink when the camera is high above them, or grow back as it comes down. They stay the right size wherever the camera is.

A house's decorations are now hidden from other players only when its votes reach -5 or lower. Before, a single vote down (-1) hid them. A house at -1 to -4 stays fully visible, so people can see it and vote it up.

If you take the overhead lantern (or any other built-in piece) out of your caravan, visitors no longer see it or its light. Visitors see the change the next time you stand in your caravan while online.
Decorations set against a wall now sit in front of it instead of sinking into it, at any size and with the grid on. The grid now snaps along the wall.
A shop, temple or tavern next to your house no longer claims half your yard. The ground between two houses is still split down the middle.
Grass no longer draws over a portal's vortex. Veiled foes and ghosts are fixed the same way.
Caravans and other road parties now set off from outside the city walls instead of walking through them.
Ore veins are clearly different colours: Moonstone a pale blue, Lodestone rust red, Copper orange, and so on. A boulder no longer looks like Lodestone.
Morrowind-style NPCs whose helmet fails to load now show their head instead of a stump of neck.
At high travel speeds (×100) your character, the ring under them and the route line now move smoothly instead of stuttering.
Your speed no longer drops to ×60 for the rest of a trip after a small gap in the road. Leaving the road still slows you to ×60, but your chosen speed comes back as soon as you're on a road again.
The ring under you is smaller and centred on your feet, with a dark rim so it shows up on snow and sand.
The route is now a trail of gold dots fixed to the ground, evenly spaced all the way to the horizon.
The spot you clicked is marked with a gold X instead of a circle. A journey to a town ends in a slightly larger X.
Map dots and diamonds are now symbols, in the same colours as before:
roaming monster bands: a skull
dungeons: a stone arch (red if undiscovered, brass if found)
party members and other players: a person (two people for a crowd)
pilgrims and pedlars: a backpack
gathering nodes: a pickaxe (Mining), a pine (Logging), a leaf (Herbalism), a paw print (Hunting) and a fish (Fishing)
Quest monsters now appear only for the quest's owner and the owner's party, in dungeons, buildings and outdoors. This covers side quests and the main quest.
Other players can't see them, can't hit them, and won't be attacked by them. Party members holding the same quest still get kill credit.
A player standing next to you may see you fighting something they can't see.

Quick loot shows each item's rarity: a coloured gem before the name and a soft band of that colour under the row (blue Magic, gold Rare, orange Legendary, pale blue Aetheric, purple Artifact, gold-leaf Gilded). Enhanced Plus and DFO Grimoire.
Chat tabs scroll sideways with the mouse wheel. The edge with more tabs fades, and a clicked tab scrolls fully into view.

DFO Grimoire's Tab dial now uses Daggerfall's own icons: your character's face for Skills, the HUD star for Magic, the sack for Inventory and the scroll for Map. To bring back the old paintings, go to Settings → Overhauls → DFO Grimoire → "Tab dial".
Online, a magic school past 100 no longer makes spells nearly free. Before, a mastered school with gear on top pushed a spell's cost below zero, so everything cast for 5 magicka, Area buffs included.
Past 100 each point still makes spells cheaper. A school at 200 casts at half what it costs at 100.
The spell maker no longer shows negative costs.

Companions no longer get in the way. When one stands between you and a body, a loot pile, your ship's helm, a door or a container within reach, clicking uses that object instead of opening their inventory. With nothing usable behind them, clicking still opens their pack, and the on-screen label shows which one a click will use.

With Morrowind data attached, crew companions and sworn revenants keep their own race, face and clothes through every door, dungeon and reload, and other players see them the same way. A revenant is the same person every time it returns.
Passing the mantle online can no longer overwrite a sibling with the new heir's name and class.
Heirs resumed from the Online page now start at the family seat instead of Privateer's Hold.
A home you own on a farm or manor can now be made your family seat, and family members met there begin their story there.

Classic Daggerfall magic items (guild-shop and Item Maker pieces, like a "Blazing Holy Dagger of Fireballs") now appear on the Salvage page marked "Classic magic" and explain why they give no shards, instead of silently missing.

After crossing the Veil, a ship too heavily loaded to move now says so ("You're going to need a bigger boat"), where the crossing banner used to hide it. Everything you carry, gold and wagon included, counts against a ship's hold.
The horses that stand in towns, at World of Daggerfall's bandit camps and forts, and in the Stables now stand as the 3D horse when Morrowind data is attached (the nearest eight within 60 m).

People who used to stay as sprites now stand in Morrowind bodies: a town's figures that belong to no faction, World of Daggerfall's dock people, the captives, merchants and prisoners its markers place, and the crews on Come Sail Away's boats.
Past the body range, Daggerfall's own sprites still stand, as they do for the walkers. Other animals, children, vampires' people and Daedra Princes keep their sprites.

Privateer's Hold is no longer a private copy for each character. It is a shared dungeon like every other: its enemies, doors, levers and loot are the same for everyone inside, and you can see, chat and party with other players there.

Once you leave Privateer's Hold online, you can't go back in. Its door, a Recall to a spot marked inside it, and a quest that would send you there all say "You cannot go back into Privateer's Hold." A Recall or quest arrival lands you outside instead.
You still start a new game inside the Hold, and a character saved inside it still loads back in.
Offline, nothing changes.

Furniture Stores now show in the shop colour on both town maps. They used to be drawn as houses. Like every other shop, a store is named on the map once you have been inside or someone has marked it for you.
You can now ask townspeople where they are. The Where-is list has a new "Furniture stores" group.

Every city and town now has a Joinery beside its Stables and Wagon Yard, as long as the town has room for one. It is a carpenter's open-air yard: a shingled workshop, a timber rack, a log pile, sawhorses and a chopping block, with a table, chairs and a bench on show by the gate.

Its workbench is a Carpentry station. Talk to the carpenter, or use the sign or the bench, to open your Stores page at The Workbench. A craft or a saw costs 50 gold, the same as at a Furniture Store's bench. Carpentry is done online, as before.
Linen for beds is still sold only at Furniture Stores.
To find a Joinery, ask townspeople under "Carpenters", look on either town map, or look for the saw mark on the Overworld map.

Entering the world freezes for less. The game no longer stalls while it works out where every town's pilgrims go for their holy days, or while it picks the day's elite halls in the Wrothgarian zone. The pilgrimages and halls are the same, but the frozen screen is seconds shorter.
The map opens without the long freeze. Opening the map for the first time in a session took 6.7 s on a desktop and now takes 0.7 s.

Far-off ships no longer weigh on your frame rate. Ships far out at sea, including the ones other players leave behind when they log off, no longer keep a full animated hull hundreds of kilometres away, and they make decisions less often while nobody can see them. Their voyages, fights and damage carry on as before. With such a fleet in the world, one player's frame rate went from 37 back to 90 FPS.
Smoother walking in the overworld. Ships, their map lookups and wagon harness ropes do the same work for less effort and less memory garbage: 79 -> 93 FPS walking the coast.
Horse coats no longer stutter. Meeting a horse with a new coat on the road no longer freezes the game for a moment. Its coat is painted a few pictures at a time instead of all forty at once.
Parked carts cost less. A parked team's harness stops recomputing its ropes while nothing moves.
Desktop app: smoother frames. The app no longer reads your account and settings files from disk every frame. It keeps them in memory, as the browser does: about 86 -> 110 FPS in a town.

Player yards now take far fewer draw calls. Each yard's 3D pieces are drawn together, and its repeated sprites (the same plant, the same statue) are drawn as one. Where decorated yards are in view, a town makes about 17-18% fewer draw calls a frame. This helps most where each draw call is expensive: the browser version and weaker CPUs and drivers.

Mastering Destruction now makes your damage spells hit harder. Online, a mastered Destruction past 100 adds to your Damage Health and Continuous Damage spells as it climbs - 1% for each point of its effective value past 100, +40% when mastered to 200. Until now those points only made spells cheaper, while the same mastery made dungeon foes tougher. Gear that raises Destruction still makes spells cheaper, as before; the extra damage comes from the mastery itself.

Spells now count the foe you are fighting when they train a mastered school. Past 100, a skill learns from tough foes, but only a weapon blow ever told it who you were fighting. A spell landing on a foe (or a foe's spell landing on you) now does too, so blasting a tough foe trains your school as fast as fighting it with a weapon. A cast never trains slower than it did before.
Potency, a new line on jewellery and weapons: +3% to +15% spell damage. Everything you wear adds up to at most +30%.
Wellspring, a new line on jewellery: 2% to 10% of your magicka back when you kill a foe, at most 10% a kill from everything you wear.
The Eye of Magnus (amulet) - *Magnus's Gaze*: your Destruction spells meet a saving throw 15 lower. A foe immune to the element stays immune.
The Ring of Artaeum (ring) - *Wellspring of Artaeum*: 1% of your magicka returns every magic round, 2% while you are under half.
Shalidor's Brand (broadsword, saber or longsword) - *Arcane Surge*: while you wield it, your Destruction spells strike 25% harder while your magicka is above three quarters.
Spell damage from loot is capped at +50% all together. None of the new spell damage reaches a fight against another player.

The beast's claws no longer count as silver. Creatures that need a better metal to hurt, such as a Lich or an Ancient Lich, take full damage from claws again, as they did before the last balance update.

Your gauntlets now strengthen your claws. In beast form, plate gauntlets add their metal's damage bonus to every claw hit, in every fight, duels and sieges included. It's the same bonus a weapon of that metal gets: Elven +1, Dwarven +2, Mithril and Adamantium +3, Ebony +4, Orcish +5, Daedric +6. Your hit chance doesn't change.

Leather and chain gauntlets add nothing. So do brigandine gloves, which count as leather, and broken gauntlets. No gauntlets ever make your claws weaker. Put them on before you change, because the beast can't open its pack.
Loading a save while in beast form no longer leaves the loaded character treated as a beast until the game is restarted. Before, townspeople wouldn't stop for them, as they don't stop for a beast.
Elite enemies no longer appear in the wilds or rise from searched graves until your character reaches Renown 5.

Revenants wait for Renown 10. Below it, no foe becomes a revenant or breaks and runs to become one, and none comes back for you. Any revenants you already have are held: the Revenants page marks each one Held and says when it will come.
Revenants come back a little less often: a revenant that is due now takes 2 in 5 encounter chances instead of 1 in 2.

Most menus that talk to the server should load much faster: the Guild tab, the market, the notice board's Seat tab, letters, your account card and signing in. The account server had been running on the other side of the world from its database, so each request crossed the Pacific once for every database question it asked. It now runs next to the database.
Joining the world, the chat's player list and the friends list should come up sooner after you sign in, because each connection waits on the account server for its pass.

Your profile card has a new Name in game choice in its Account section: Account name or Character name. With Character name, other players see the name of the character you are playing: over your head, in chat and in the online list.
The change shows within moments in every room you are in. You don't need to change area or sign in again.

If your character's name can't be shown online, other players see your account name instead, and the chat tells you why, once. This happens when the name is longer than 24 characters, uses accented letters or symbols, is caught by the name filter, looks like an email address, or is another player's username.
A letter sent from your friends list now reaches that friend even when they go by their character's name.
Answering a notice-board duel finds its author even when they go by their character's name.
Titles no longer appear in chat. Guild tags and glyphs still show after names, and your title still shows over your head and on your Inspect card.

Online, a letter of credit can't be put into a chest, a cupboard or a body any more. A shared container is everyone's, so the letter stays in your pack. To give one to another player, hand it over in a trade.
Your own storage (your house's cupboards, your ship's chest), a pile you dropped yourself and your wagon still take letters. Offline nothing changes.
Outside a trade, a letter of credit never reaches you through another player's game. That covers a shared chest, a body they let you loot, and a foe's pack handed to you.

A letter of credit that was already lying in a shared chest or on a body when this update arrived is gone from it. Anyone could take it from there before, and the game can't tell it from a forged one.
An item that reaches you through another player's game (a chest, a body, a shelf) can't carry a higher price than an honest item of its kind could.
The gear a fallen player leaves in the wilds holds only things that can be worn.

A purse, a letter of credit or a pile of gold holding more than 2,147,483,647 gold (more than Daggerfall itself can count) is now flagged as tampered. That character can't trade, sell or send gold to other players until the problem is gone or staff clear it.

When a monster attacks you in town, the town guard still comes to help. They used to disappear on the spot about ten seconds after the fight ended, even while you were looking at them. Now they walk off instead. A guard only leaves the world once he is far away or behind you, the same rule that hides townspeople coming and going.

If another monster turns up while the guards are walking off, the same guards turn back to the fight instead of a fresh squad appearing. A guard attacked on his way out defends himself before carrying on. Commit a crime and they come for you, as before.
Your horse now walks by default. Hold Run (Shift unless you rebound it) to gallop, the same way you walk and run on foot.
The gallop is as fast as before and still spends your horse's breath. A winded or starving horse walks even with Run held, until it can gallop again.
In towns your horse walks, because Roleplay & Realism doesn't allow galloping there. To gallop in towns too, turn on its Galloping In Towns option (under Enhanced Riding).
A walking horse looks and sounds like one: a slower clop, a slower nod of its head in first person, and a trot rather than a gallop on the 3D horse. The saddle panel says Walking.
With Horse care turned off in Settings > Features, or on the classic interface, horses ride as they always did.

Walking past a spawned or Elite dungeon no longer starts its despawn timer. The timer (7 in-game days, about 14 real hours online) now starts only when someone enters the dungeon. A dungeon nobody goes into stays where it is.
A dungeon that has despawned now comes back 24 real hours later: the same dungeon in the same spot, with fresh timers. Regions that were emptied out repopulate.
Your character's save no longer keeps despawned dungeons gone forever. Players who walked an area weeks ago now see the same dungeons as everyone else.
Wild Zone halls no longer vanish partway through their day after someone has been inside one.
Quest enemies, like the Fighters Guild's rats, now appear in shops, not only in houses.
"Open a Chest" and other quests whose shop is in another town now show that town in the quest list, on the travel map and on the compass.
A home's chests no longer lose their contents when furniture fails to load; anything without a chest or box to go in is set down at your feet.
The Gauntlets of the Rose's second hit now lands on the Oblivion Gate's boss.
Motherlodes appear on the compass from their warning onward, in their own colour, drawn over nearby veins.
Windows no longer show the street where your building's own wall stands.
Fixed Morrowind models (you, NPCs, enemies, horses) turning invisible until restart.
Swing Weapon bound to Left Click (with mouse activate unbound) now survives a restart.

Inland water banks (ponds, moats, rivers, streams, town canals) no longer show flat blue blotches on the grass beside the water. The shore's painted water now sits under the riverbed, and the strip just past the water's edge reads as dark wet mud.
Standing on a bank, you can no longer see under the water's surface. The water's edge now meets the ground instead of floating over a dip.
Climates & Calories has a fourth setting, Boons, between Off and Casual, and Boons is now the default. If you never picked a setting you play Boons; Off, Hard or Boons, if you chose one, is kept.
Boons takes nothing away. Keeping your character fed, watered and rested earns bonuses instead:
Well fed: +5 Strength, +5 Endurance
Quenched: +5 Agility, +5 Speed
Well rested: +5 Intelligence, +5 Willpower. Sleeping in a bed or by a fire banks rest, up to 12 hours, and you spend it while awake.
Thriving (all three at once): +5 Luck
Hearth: standing by a lit fire gives stamina back.
Boons show as green tiles on the status strip. Nothing turns red in Boons except a drink's effect.
On the Status page, the hours of rest you have banked are a line of their own ("Rested for another 12 hours."), so the classic status box no longer grows wider for them.
Online, the tile that counts down until you can sleep through a night again is called "Next night" (it was "Rested", easily mistaken for Well rested).

A temperature plate sits at the right end of the compass (Enhanced HUD): your felt temperature, its word, and a scale from deadly cold to scorching. It stays on the screen at every HUD scale and on phones, clear of the FPS counter, the enemy health bar, the arena session button and the travel pace box. It can be moved and hidden on its own, and it still shows when the compass is hidden. "Temperature on the HUD" in the Climates & Calories settings turns it off.

The Enhanced inventory shows your felt temperature beside your armour rating. An item's card says what wearing it, or taking it off, would do to your temperature. An unidentified item's comparison no longer counts powers you can't see yet.
The Stats side lists everything that makes up your temperature, and the Status page shows the number.

Red now means the setting you play on charges you for it, and amber means you feel it but it costs nothing. In Hard every need that costs is red; being wet is amber in every setting. Each level is also said in words, not by colour alone.
Resist Fire no longer makes a blizzard colder, and Resist Frost no longer makes the desert hotter. Underground, resistances now act on the dungeon's own air.
Swimming on the surface soaks you a little at a time; only going under soaks you at once. A short river swim no longer leaves you drenched for hours.
Rain and snow soak you at the original mod's rates. A cloak keeps snow off, and a hood keeps rain off.
Robes and cloaks keep the sun off your armour. Surcoats and straps no longer do, because they are worn under it.
Underground, clothes, metal armour and food follow the dungeon's air, not the weather above it.
Warm weather now takes effect on your clothing and a hood's shade gradually. A slightly warmer day no longer reads much colder.
Indoors, a warmer street no longer reads colder inside.
Having a drink to hand cools you down to 9 degrees at most, instead of dropping you to 0.
Cold metal armour chills you a degree less, as in the original mod.
The temperature number and its word always agree. The breakdown's "Bare skin" row is now called "Heat loss".
The open sea is no longer as warm as a beach. A winter crossing is cold now.
Offline, a long rest or a fast-travel journey feels each hour as it passes, including the minute you arrive. Nights are cold, noons warm, and the sun shines only by day.
A long journey no longer keeps the weather you set out in all the way: the road is felt under a fair sky.
In a castle, the Stats breakdown names the row "Castle walls" instead of "Underground".
Hard: a long fast-travel journey can no longer collapse you from exhaustion over and over on the way, or kill you in the minute you land.
Collapsing from exhaustion now counts as an hour's sleep on the ground.
You can no longer save partway through a fast-travel journey ("You cannot save now."); the online checkpoint waits until you arrive.
Leaving prison, you start fed, watered and rested, not starving, soaked and exhausted.
A vampire who is cured is no longer instantly starving and exhausted. In beast form, a werewolf neither hungers nor thirsts.
Stamina no longer stays above its maximum after a boon or a Fortify ends.
Survival messages no longer repeat when you step in and out of a fire's reach, and loading a game no longer repeats them all.
Bare feet are hurt by the weather's own heat or cold, before your clothes count, measured against your current Endurance, so Fortify Endurance helps. They are no longer hurt underground.
Resting at your own burnt-out Campfire relights it if it has fuel. A worn-out tent no longer claims to stoke its fire.
Sleeping in your tent keeps the rain and snow off, and armour no longer rusts while you rest or under a roof.
A cold camp no longer offers Cook.
Resting at a brazier or fire bowl needs you within the fire's reach. From further away you are told to move closer, instead of getting a rough night's rest.
A campfire on a ship's deck no longer counts as a fire while the ship is out of sight.
Food that spoils in your pack shows its spoiled name and picture. Putrid food says it cannot be eaten.
New characters start with the original mod's Formal cloak, hood up, and Shoes, both well worn.
An empty waterskin from a shop is called "Empty Waterskin".
Tavern menus follow the original mod's regional menus, prices and holiday free drinks.
A meal you order when you are nearly full is served whole and leaves you fed.
A soft drink refreshes you (+5 stamina); an alcoholic drink restores stamina and magicka.
Online, passing out drunk wakes you at the next dawn under the sky everyone shares.
Your Boons and other buffs count properly in duels, sieges and the Royal Tourney. Before, your own attributes and Luck were counted against you.

When you climb or hang from a ledge in first person (classic view), your hands now stay on the wall. Turn your view and they slide across with the stone; look up and they go down the wall with it. They no longer turn with the screen.
The two fists grip further apart, about shoulder width.

When you look away from the wall to find your next jump, the arm that reaches out is now the one on the side you look: your right arm from the right when you look right, your left arm from the left when you look left. Only that arm stays fixed to the screen. Its hand lets go of the wall, and the other hand keeps its hold.
With the Morrowind model in first person, your arms now grip the wall while you climb even with your weapon sheathed. Before this, the screen showed nothing unless a weapon was drawn.
Weapon Widget's bob and sway no longer push the Morrowind hands off the stone while they climb.
Your horse no longer has to walk in towns. It still walks by default, and holding Run gallops it anywhere, in town or out, as long as it has the breath. This applies online too.
Watch where you gallop in town: riding into someone at a gallop tramples them. That's a crime, and the guards will come.

On a handheld held sideways, like the ASUS ROG Xbox Ally X, the front door's logo no longer fills the screen. The menu now keeps its two columns: the sections down the side and the open page using the full height. Settings, Load, Online and the rest can be read and used again. A narrowed browser window on a desktop gets the same layout.

Settings > Interface > Language now offers 13 languages besides English: Bulgarian, Czech, Danish, French, German, Indonesian, Italian, Korean, Norwegian, Portuguese (Brazil), Romanian, Russian and Spanish. The choice applies at once and is remembered. If your browser reads one of them first, the game offers it to you once, in that language.

These translations cover the game's own menus and screens: the front door and Settings, the pause window, the death screens, the account and online messages, the Professions and Stores pages and every crafting station, the Features screen and every mod's settings. They are machine translated, and the game says so. A fix from a speaker is welcome. More languages are on the way.

Under the Language row, Translation pack installs a Daggerfall Unity translation (a folder or its .zip) from your own files. Nothing is uploaded. A pack translates Daggerfall's own text too: dialogue, quests, books, and the names of places, enemies, items and spells. It also works for a language not in the list yet. The French pack's grammar works.
The classic windows now draw any script: Cyrillic, Greek, Vietnamese, Chinese, Japanese and Korean. Before, anything past plain English letters came out as question marks.
The About pane credits each language's translation.

Players, NPCs and horses no longer turn invisible online with Morrowind models. If one Morrowind body in view got a bad position (for example from another player's glitched position update), every Morrowind body drawn after it vanished and your own could show the wrong picture, until that player left or you restarted. Now only that one body is affected: it stays at its last good position, and everyone else keeps drawing.

Pleading guilty no longer loops. The first time you went to court, the Crime tutorial page opened on top of the plea. Clicking Guilty or Not Guilty while the page was showing answered the plea underneath it, and the plea box then kept coming back: every click pleaded again, took the fine again and halved the sentence again. Now the plea waits until you've read the page. Click anywhere or press any key to close the page, then plead once.
You can now rise into the Overworld while sailing the Eltheric Ocean, as you can in the Iliac Bay. Open your chart (the map key) and press Overworld (O), or press O while the chart is open.

From the Overworld, click the sea to sail there at the helm, or click a port or ruin you have charted to travel to it. Charted ports further off are shown at the edge of the screen with their distance. Ruins appear as they do in the Bay: a "?" until you have charted or found them.
An island you chart (by sight, a harbourmaster's chart or a corsair's papers) shows on the Overworld at once, without moving first.
A fast journey past the Veil now slows while the land ahead is still loading, so you no longer outrun the world.

Enemy bands now roam the Eltheric isles, and with Naval Combat on, pirate raiders sail its open sea. The Overworld shows both as it does in the Bay. They chase you the same way, and your journey slows as they close in.

A raider past the Veil comes as one of the Eltheric's own corsairs, a ship you fight at sea: the sea's names, the black flag, and a hold as rich as the waters she sails. For a newer captain, the deeper the water, the bigger the ship she may be.
Online, other players now see a band or raider chasing you past the Veil.

The sea past the Veil is now called the Eltheric Ocean, its proper name. It used to be called the "Etheric Sea". The chart, the harbourmasters, the crossing, your captain's log and the legends now all use the new name.

The water past the Veil used to be only a stride deep, with the seabed just under the surface. It now has a real seabed: shallow by each island's shore, then dropping to the open ocean floor about two hundred metres down, as deep as the Iliac Bay's open sea.
You can swim, dive and surface there as you do in the Bay. The seafloor's plants, fish, creatures and sunken loot now appear past the Veil too.
The ocean holes (the pits down into drowned dungeons) still appear only in the Iliac Bay.

Herbs, trees, ore veins and boulders on the islands past the Veil can now be gathered. They used to stand there but answered "There is nothing here to gather". Fishing in the Eltheric Ocean now works too.
Gathering there works as it does in the Bay: each spot gives its full finds only once three players (with accounts at least a week old) have gathered there.
Motherlodes still rise only in the Iliac Bay, where the Watch can see you strike them.
The chart's names are now in the game's own enhanced font. They used to be drawn in a fallback serif.
Names are drawn after every island marker, with a dark outline, so a marker can no longer cover a name.
Each name sits on whichever side of its island is clear. Names and haunt labels no longer stand over each other, and your ship's label takes the clearest spot.
A depth ruler runs along the top of the chart. It names each stretch of water in view that has room for its name: the Shallows, the Reaches, the Deep Aether, the Abyss, the Veil and the world's edge.
The scale bar now sits in the key below the chart, so it no longer hides islands.

The chart's words follow the language you chose, in each fully translated language. The sea's own names (the Eltheric Ocean, its depths, its island types and compass directions) are still in English for now.
Each island type has its own shape as well as its own colour:
a port is round with a harbour dot
a ruin is a diamond
a wild isle is a peak
a bare rock is a cross
Zoom in and larger islands show their real size around the icon. Veilhaven is ringed in gold.
A key under the chart explains every icon.

Each depth band is its own shade of water, lightest by the Veil and darkest in the Abyss. A league grid replaces the old background stars, which didn't move when you dragged the map. The edge of the world is marked.

A legend's haunt is a red-washed square while she sails, and hatched grey while she lies sunk. When enough of the square is in view, her name and status ("Her haunt", "Sunk - she will rise again") sit in a corner of it, chosen to hide as few islands as possible. When you're zoomed far out, her name alone stands above the square.
Your ship is a white arrow in a brass ring, marked on the ruler too. When she's off-screen, an arrow at the chart's edge points to her and says how far away she is.
Point at or tap an island to ring it, draw a bearing line to it from your ship, and show a card with its name, type and distance.

The chart now fits the screen at any size. On a phone held sideways, the key, the zoom buttons and Ship are no longer pushed off the bottom. On a phone held upright, the chart's title wraps instead of being cut off.
Naming an island no longer makes the chart jump.
The chart no longer gets stuck in a fallback font if it opens before the game's fonts finish loading.
On phones the Close and zoom buttons keep their size, and the zoom buttons grey out at the closest and farthest zoom.
Your Ship can no longer be boarded from past the Veil. Boarding it there carried you to the Iliac Bay without the crossing. Leaving it still takes you back to where you boarded.

The furniture catalogue, the pieces in your room, the built-in pieces and your own things are now laid out as picture tiles. Each tile shows the piece's own 3D model, its name and price, plus badges for what it does (holds things, gives light, crafting station). A Pictures / List switch brings the old lines back.
Every tab, type, size and filter has its own icon. Filters sit under named rows (Sort, Type, Size, Show only), and on phones they fold behind one Filters button that shows how many are set.
A placed piece's buttons are grouped by what they do (Arrange, Light and storage, Crafting station). Remove stands alone, marked as the costly one.
The placing bar is now icon buttons, with a Keys button that shows the controls only when you ask. On a portrait phone the bar spans the full screen width.
Every shelf item shows its price before you click it. A List / Pictures switch shows both sides as item tiles.

Your side is labelled "Your pack". The footer shows "To pay" (or "You get") and "Your gold" as separate figures. A magic-only counter is titled "Sell magic items", and Steal sits apart from the other buttons.

The Stores page opens with a row of station tiles marked Here or Away. A station you are away from stays folded until you tap its tile. Smelting, other workings and patterns appear as cards instead of long lines.
Materials and items on the Stores page, the Notice Board's Market and Vendors, and the Vendor page show the game's own item pictures.
A button you can't use yet now explains why when you press it, instead of sitting greyed out with no reason.
Shipmaster cards show each ship's own 3D picture. The Reforge, shipyard and naval-yard pages and a merchant's options each have their own icon.
Panel previews (bank, decorator) no longer show the world behind their background.
On landscape phones, the decorator's catalogue is no longer squeezed to a sliver.
The shop header no longer squashes the shop's name on a phone.

It rains about half as often. A woodland spring used to be wet a third of the time; now it's about one hour in six. The hours it no longer rains are that region's usual dry weather: sun, cloud, the grey deck and fog.

Rain now comes in every strength. Each rain front has its own: about a third are a light sprinkle from edge to middle, most are a steady shower, and only about a quarter build to a downpour at their heart. Walking into a front still starts light at its edge.
Thunderstorms are still downpours, but they come half as often.

The journal (the L key) now has an Abandon button on every quest except the main story's. Click it twice to set the quest aside. The quest keeps everything it had and stops running until you take it back up. Reclaim it from the pause menu's Quests tab, where it waits under Abandoned.
The main story's quests show no Abandon in the journal. Bounties and revenant hunts keep their own Abandon, as before.
Surface veins now show on your compass from 500 m (was 200). Dungeon veins stay at 200 m.
On the Overworld, each nearby vein is marked on its own and named by its ore ("Silver Vein"), instead of one "Mining ×N" group.
Gems still come a tenth more often.
Dungeon veins yield double (was +50%).
Every vein in the dungeon shows on your compass, wherever you stand in it.
The day's Motherlodes are marked on your map and the Overworld from the start of the day. Each mark shows its ore and, until it rises, when it rises ("Tue 13:00", on your own clock).
Warnings still come 30 minutes ahead.
Your own word vouches for unwitnessed ground, so your surface veins there can be any of that land's ores. A region's own ore (Mithril, Orichalcum and the rest) still needs witnesses.
Quarrying still yields Cut Stone directly. If you chose Stonebreaker, you are now a Surveyor.
Dungeon veins no longer sink halfway into the wall. They sit on the floor at the wall's foot.

The harbourmaster's cargo contracts now send you only to port towns on the sea. They used to name tombs, farms, inns, temples, manors and ruins (most cargoes went to one), and region capitals far inland where no ship can reach.
A harbourmaster's board now stands only in a port town, never at a tomb's or a farm's shore.
A cargo you already hold for such a place is cancelled with a notice ("Contract void - ... No ship can make port there."), and your standing with the crown is unchanged.
Felling a tree: the axe's swing and its bite into the trunk (a Clean Cut rings fuller), the tree groaning when it starts to give, its crash as it lands, and the logs gathered up.
Mining: the pick striking rock, the ring of a strike on the glint, and rubble as a vein or boulder gives out.
Herbs and the Basket: leaves rustling as you kneel, the herb pulling free (or bruising), and the Basket's find.
Skinning: the knife's strokes climbing along the line, a tear when it slips, and the pelt peeling free.
Net fishing: the throw, the splash where the net lands, the water by the floats while you wait, the tug, the catch fighting as you haul, and the net coming in.
Your goods going into the bag, a clean finish's chime, and a chime for a new rank.
An axe or pick blow now sounds the moment the tool hits, not when you press the button. Its sound, its weight and its chunks all land together, at any frame rate.
Each sound comes from where it happens: the tree, the vein, or where your net landed.

The tool stays in your hand through your last swing, and the tree starts to fall (or the vein crumbles) as that last blow lands, instead of the moment you press. Starting on the next tree or vein straight away doesn't cut that last blow short.

On the Enhanced skin, each axe or pick blow dips your view and your hands slightly as it lands, a little deeper for a Clean Cut or a strike on the glint, and always lighter than a weapon technique's hit.
It follows Technique camera motion (Settings > Accessibility > Motion), so you can turn it down or off there. It never plays when your system asks for reduced motion.
A vein or a Motherlode cracks as you work it, and so does a boulder's loose stone: the cracks spread out from its middle with each blow until it breaks.
Every blow knocks chunks of ore loose toward you. They land on the ground where they fall, slopes included, lie there a moment and sink away. The blow that breaks the vein sheds the most.
If you stop before it breaks, the cracks close up again. Like the vein itself, the cracks are yours alone.

Other players now see you at work. Every body type shows your tool swinging. Class sprites also show you kneeling and throwing your net, Eye Of The Beholder sprites show the throw, and Morrowind bodies crouch where you kneel.

They hear it too, from where you are working: each chop and strike as it lands, the herb pulled, the knife, the net thrown and landing, the water while it waits, the tug and the haul. A blow you take back with Escape isn't heard.
The still paperdoll (shown while a sprite loads, or with other players' class sprites turned off) doesn't show it, but you still hear it.
The Attack sounds switch for other players now covers their gathering sounds too.
The new sounds are part of Enhanced sounds on the Features screen. With it off, or on the Classic skin, gathering plays Daggerfall's own sounds as before, now timed to the blows.
The veins, boulders, herbs and trees around you no longer blink out for a frame when you finish gathering one of them or when the day turns.

The Hold'em and Iliac Hand panels at tavern tables now use the Enhanced Plus stone-and-brass look and the game's pixel font, matching every other window. The classic skin gets the same look for these panels.

Under the DFO Grimoire dress, every mark on the card tables shows in the dress's own colours: your seat, whose turn it is, the winner, who holds each holding, the power that is ahead, and the holding you are aiming at.

Iliac Hand's panel gets the fold button Hold'em's already had, which tucks the table's words away so you can watch the cards on the cloth. Both folds now say what they do: "Collapse the panel" and "Expand the panel".
Both panels fit on any phone screen, upright or sideways, and scroll inside it when the table is full.
The turn is a track of six marks, and your magicka is a row of gems; the magicka your staged plays will spend shows dimmed.
Your opponent's hand shows as card backs beside their deck count, with a mark once they have committed their turn.

Each holding sits under its own painted location card: their cards above, yours below, empty places for the room left on each side, and each side's power next to its name, with the side that is ahead lit. Cards never cover one another, even on a phone.
Your hand sits in a tray, painted as the cards themselves, with the card you have picked raised in brass. A card you play face down shows veiled.
Online, the board appears once the game is dealt.

A game ends with a banner ("Victory", "Defeat", "A draw" or "No contest"); if you are watching, the log line says how it ended. The log keeps one line for each thing that happens, the newest always in view.
When you play by keyboard, the focus stays on the panel, so Space never makes your character jump up from the table in the middle of a game.
The Cards page's switch, filters, deck list and deck name use the same look.

A chosen, hovered or keyboard-selected tile is marked again on every page that uses tiles. Buttons that cost you something (Concede, Scuttle, Steal and the like) now change when you hover them or reach them with the keyboard.

The new table's words, and Hold'em's fold, are translated into all 13 complete languages. The magicka label uses Daggerfall Unity's own text, like the vitals bar, so it follows an installed Daggerfall Unity language pack.

The remains of your house's fallen now appear where they fell: a body you can see, with a line of light over it, in dungeons and out in the open. Press it like any body to take back their bones, their heirloom and their share of the purse. Before this, nothing was drawn at all, and underground the remains only opened if you happened to stand within a few paces of the exact spot.

The remains appear only in the dungeon your relative actually fell in. Spawned ruins, wilderness halls and the Arena's undercroft no longer show another dungeon's remains. A dungeon laid out at a different size (Smaller Dungeons) shows them only at the size it had when they fell.

Remains no longer stay shut because of an enemy back in the street. Whether you are "in a fight" is now judged where you actually are (the dungeon or building you're in), not by monsters you left outside. A duel, your own arena bout, or a hostile ship within reach now counts as a fight too. All of this also applies to Play as, Pass the mantle and weddings.
Putting the bones back into the remains no longer leaves the death quest stuck. They lie there again, still yours to carry.
Fixed a brief stutter when walking into a new area with Project Legacy on.
When the servers are under heavy load, your game now waits longer between tries to load a town's homes, instead of asking again every 10 seconds. That helps the servers recover sooner.
Loading a town's homes now costs the servers half as many database requests.

When the servers are overloaded, your game now holds off on loading homes, yards, seats, traders, guild invitations, Marks and your save list, and asks again a little later, waiting longer the longer the overload lasts. Your actions (buying, crafting, saving, claiming) still go through as before.
The servers also turn those requests away for a moment when they're overloaded, so they recover faster even before you update.

A door another player locked with a Lock spell is no longer locked for you. Shop and inn doors in Daggerfall that trapped players inside (Lock Level 40+) open again, including copies your save had already kept.
A door's label now names the building that door opens. The Issaqumbaa tavern is no longer labelled "Residence" or offered for sale.
Houses built on grassy hills (for example at some Temples of Kynareth) no longer float over the slope. The hill now reaches under the whole house.
When a party member's progress on a shared quest reveals a place on their map, it now appears on yours too. If your copy already says "Not on your map yet", use Settings > Repair active quests.
The Lost Child: answering "No" by mistake no longer locks the quest. Click the child again and you are asked again, including on a save already stuck after a "No".

Running out of fatigue with enemies nearby no longer kills you outright at full health. Each time you hit empty you lose a tenth of your health and see "You are too exhausted to fight - get clear and rest!".

The Mace of Molag Bal works. Draining a foe's strength now raises yours past 100, as described. Spell points it drains count once even on two quick hits, and the bonus ends when you take the Mace off.

Crafted Superior and Masterwork pieces can now roll the special lines loot can: focus, cast speed, potency and wellspring on jewelry, and the weapon and armour equivalents. Pieces crafted before stay as they were.
A writ's card now tells you how many of the material you hold that it can't take, and why: only gathered or silver-bought materials fill writs. Before, it said "0 held" with no reason.
The Oblivion Gate boss's own mark and his host's paths no longer shade large areas of empty ground. The ground markings in a boss AoE frame cost about a quarter less to draw.
Master two schools of magic and you can choose a specialisation: fifteen of them, one for every pair of schools. The choice is permanent, like a mastery.
Each specialisation has its own passive and a signature spell. The Mages Guild sells that spell only to its own specialists, and it does something extra when they cast it.

You are asked once, the first time two of your schools are mastered. If more than one specialisation is open to you, you are told which, and you choose on your skill screen. After that, choose any time from your skill screen: the Specialisation card on the Master Skills page (enhanced), or the S row on the skill pages (classic).

Battlemage (Alteration + Destruction): Spellsteel, Aegis Bolt. Trickster (Alteration + Illusion): Slip Away, Fleeting Hold. Riftwalker (Alteration + Mysticism): Between Moments, Rift Lance. Warden (Alteration + Restoration): Steadfast, Living Aegis. Wardwright (Alteration + Thaumaturgy): Attuned Wards, Prismatic Ward. Shadowcaster (Destruction + Illusion): Unseen Strike, Shadow Bolt. Spellbreaker (Destruction + Mysticism): Sunder, Unravel. Bloodmage (Destruction + Restoration): Sanguine Tide, Blood Boil. Elementalist (Destruction + Thaumaturgy): Conflux, Chain Lightning. Seer (Illusion + Mysticism): Foresight, Psychic Lance. Lightbringer (Illusion + Restoration): Dawn's Ward, Dawnbolt. Enchanter (Illusion + Thaumaturgy): Glamour, Beguile. Necromancer (Mysticism + Restoration): Death's Due, Siphon Life. Soulbinder (Mysticism + Thaumaturgy): Soul Well, Soul Lance. Hierophant (Restoration + Thaumaturgy): Absolution, Sanctify.

A signature spell is priced and trained by your specialisation's two schools, so a Necromancer's Siphon Life costs what their Restoration says, not their Destruction. That stays true while you mentor a lower party.
Chain Lightning and Rift Lance never arc onto your allies, onto foes you have calmed, or through walls.
Signature spells show their names in your language.
Specialisations work wherever Master Skills is on. They do nothing in duels and other refereed fights, and nothing against other players.
Online, every mastered school past 100 now strengthens its own spells, not just their price. The bonus is 1% per effective point, up to +40% at 200, the same rule as Destruction's damage.
Restoration: your heals heal more.
Alteration: your Shield holds more.
Illusion: your invisibility, chameleon and shadow last longer.
Thaumaturgy: your Spell Reflection and Spell Resistance hold more often.
Mysticism: your Silence, Dispel and Soul Trap take hold more often.

The account server has been overloaded since this afternoon, so town seats, homes, the market and other online menus have been slow to load or failing. The heaviest read, the town seats list, no longer runs on the main database, which should bring them back.

Town homes, home rooms and decorations, gathering nodes, traders, Marks, guild invites, lineages, unions, cloud saves and the Arena board now load from read copies of the account database, not the one main database everyone was queued on. Menus should stop timing out and load much faster.

Town seats are now worked out once a minute for the whole server, not by every server process on every request. The seats list, Watch claims, Levies, Tithes and sieges load faster and put far less strain on the database.

Restart a quest. A stuck quest can now be restarted from its first step: press Restart twice in the pause window's Quests tab or in the chronicle (main-story steps included). The quest picks fresh places, and its old items, links and topics are cleared.
A party member's kill no longer steals yours. Killing your own copy of a main-story foe (like the Dust of Restful Death's mummy) is no longer counted because a party member killed theirs.
Quest markers in small and medium buildings sit inside the building, and quest foes no longer stand on top of a hall's ceiling.
When a quest's foe falls you are told (HUD, chat and the classic line), and a quest box ignores presses for a moment so it isn't clicked away by accident.
An abandoned quest's item can be dropped from your pack, and it is handed back if you reclaim the quest.
The chat roster search now finds every known player, not just the first page.
Clicking in the world no longer stutters.
A found dungeon shows as a dungeon on the Overworld grid.
Compass marks draw over the Grimoire frame.
The installed-font picker is a scrolling, filterable list.
Eight recovery codes instead of one. New accounts get a set of 8 recovery codes. Each code works once, if you forget your password.

See your codes in your profile. The Account section shows how many recovery codes you have left. Make new codes gives you a fresh set: type your password and one of your current codes. Your old codes stop working.
Copy or save them. When codes are shown you can Copy them or Save as a file (dfo-recovery-codes-<username>.txt).
Never left with none. Using a code spends only that code. Using your last one gives you a fresh 8.
Safer: someone who learns your password alone can't replace your codes, so your codes can always take your account back.
The codes screen can't be closed by accident (no Close, Escape or tap outside) until you confirm you've written them down.
Carpentry crash. Using a Joinery's workbench, or opening Esc → Stores afterwards, no longer crashes the game.
Inn beds. Beds in dormitory-style inn rooms (and ship bunks) offer Rest and Loiter again.

Crew morale at the shipwright. Once the crew has had the day's grog, the shipwright now shows their real spirits (e.g. "low") and says "Tomorrow". It no longer claims spirits are "as high as they go".

Repairs Objects. The enchantment repairs your gear again when you wear a Cast When Held or Item Deteriorates piece. That piece used to take every repair and undo it in the same moment; it is now repaired last.

Paying the watch's fine now mends your name. Paying on the spot raises your standing in that region by 5, up to the point where the watch stops recognising you. Before, a paid fine only bought a day without stops, so the watch kept charging the same fine.
Life leech says whose blows it heals on. The line now reads "N% life leech on this weapon's own blows". An off-hand weapon's leech applies only when you fight with that hand (switch with H).
REVIVE: a death taken back holds, and the operator's Realm revive run

Stutter in cities. Arriving in a large city, or walking out of a building in one, no longer freezes the game for several seconds. It was worst in Firefox. Thanks to ghandhikus for finding and fixing it.

The first seconds after entering the world stutter less. The horses' coats on the road's wagons are painted in under half the time, so the frame rate settles sooner. Every coat looks exactly as before. Thanks to joaomdb3.
With Morrowind attached, Breton men now wear three new heads and three new hairs - nine faces between them - on townspeople, NPCs and a Breton player alike.
Each of the ten Breton portraits at character creation shows the face most like it; portrait 6 wears the eyepatch.
If the new heads fail to load, Breton men show Morrowind's own Breton faces instead of appearing without a head.

Eleven of Daggerfall's townspeople now wear their own 3D outfits on the Morrowind body, in their picture's colours: all four Redguard men, all four Nord men, two Breton men and the hooded Redguard woman. Up close, a walker wears what their picture shows from afar.
Hoods sit over the hair, and sleeves, hems and boots move with the body.
Legs stay inside skirts, robes, kilts and the hooded dress as townspeople walk, and tunics no longer pinch in at the sides when they stand.
If an outfit fails to load, the person is drawn without it and with no missing body parts; a woman wears her modest shirt while Show Nudity is off.
Townspeople without an outfit yet (two of the Breton men's pictures, and every woman's but the hooded Redguard's) keep their varied wardrobe.
The cape on the Morrowind body now hangs from the chest alone and moves only with it, as one stiff sheet. Walking, swinging your arms and sitting no longer bend it.
Leaning back swings the whole cape with the chest.
The Dragontail and Wrothgarian Mountains are taller and sharper: pointed peaks up to 400 m over the ridges, where they were 200 m and rounded, on ridges 40% taller.
The mountain woods around them keep their rounded hills.

New setting: Billboard Look (Settings > Combat > With Morrowind data, off by default). On, Morrowind bodies and horses stand upright like the classic sprites, so they look shorter when the camera is above them, as they did before they started leaning toward the camera. Off, they keep their true height from every angle.

Loading an online character into the world takes about 3 seconds less. The game now asks the server for your family, your character list, the towns' homes and the homes of the towns you arrive in all at once, while it reads the world, instead of waiting on each in turn. Thanks to joaomdb3.

Ships, wagons and town buildings now use Daggerfall's own textures. This covers the galleon, the carrack and the large boat; the Wagon Cart, the Open Wagon, the Caravan and the caravan's room; the Stable, the Wagon Yard and the Joinery; the shipyard and the lighthouse; the stone of the Julian LeFay monument; and the tapestries, banners and rugs in towns. Each texture is read from your own Daggerfall files. The ships wear the same textures as Come Sail Away's ships.
Wagon paints are now Daggerfall's colours, fabrics, woods, rugs, tiles and night sky. Every paint still applies.

Windows are see-through. The caravan's windows and the stern windows of the galleon and the carrack are Daggerfall's leaded window, and you can see through the glass between the leads. The ships' stern windows no longer glow at night.
Signboards. STABLES, WAGONS, JOINERY, SHIPS and CREW are lettered on Daggerfall planks. The Joinery's sign also carries Daggerfall's axe-and-sword shop sign.
The lighthouse beacon now burns with Daggerfall's own brazier fire.

The ships' stern windows glow at night again. By day you can still see through the galleon's stern windows into her great cabin, and through the carrack's transom windows. When the lanterns are lit, the glass closes and glows warm, as it did before. The caravan's windows stay see-through day and night.
Trade — buy, sell and swap with players anywhere. /trade (or /tr) says a line there.
LFG — find a group, or one more for yours. /lfg says a line there.
Both are opt-in, so your tab bar stays as it was until you want them. Press the new + beside the chat tabs to pick channels: one click joins or leaves, and joined channels show a checkmark.
You can also use /join trade, /join lfg, /leave trade and /leave lfg, or the switches in Settings > Other players > Chat. Saying /trade … or /lfg … before joining joins the channel for you.
/rp <text> says a line of roleplay on the tab you're on, in green italics: /rp draws her blade shows as *\*draws her blade\.
/help now lists /trade, /lfg, /join, /leave and /rp.

Sit on chairs. Use a chair, bench or throne inside a building to sit on it. Your character sits in the same pose as at the card tables, other players see you seated, and third person shows you on the chair. Move, jump, attack, press Escape or use it again to stand up.
The lamp keeper. Every so often a shopkeeper is... a lamp. Talk to it for its own lines, trade with it as usual, and earn the title I Love Lamp (online, signed in to a registered account).
Title and aura popups. A title or aura you earn now gets a loot popup (Enhanced Plus), including the Abyss Dungeon's Hourbreaker and The Turning Hour. It shows only the first time you earn each one.

Faster dungeon respawns. Chests and foes in Abyss Dungeons and Wrothgarian Zone dungeon halls now come back after 30 minutes instead of an hour. Normal dungeons are still 20 minutes and elite dungeons 40.
The Monument to Julian LeFay now stands outside Privateer's Hold, beside the path every new character walks out on, instead of in Gothway Garden.

The wagon wheels are back. Carts, open wagons and caravans roll on the painted wheels they had before the Daggerfall-texture pass: seven wooden spokes, a dark hub and an iron tyre with its rivets. Everything else on the wagons keeps its Daggerfall textures.

With Morrowind data attached, every face portrait now shows the 3D head your character wears: save tiles, profile and account cards, character creation, the large HUD, the tab dial, and the party panel.
NPC faces in the talk window, the family and succession pages, and the escort faces show the head their body wears too.
Portraits show the helmet or hood you are wearing, the vampire head when you are a vampire, and the werewolf head when transformed.
Catching vampirism now changes your body's face right away, and a cure changes it back - no reload needed.
The new Breton heads no longer sit backwards on the body.
The new Breton heads are for player characters only. NPCs wear Morrowind's own heads again.
Character portraits now show the face instead of the back of the head.
The Breton eyepatch face now sits on the right head, and wears its own hair instead of the red headband.
A new passive tree for everything you do online. Open it from the Firmament button on the Stats page (pause menu or character sheet).
Choose one of seven birthsigns, then spend Stars on combat stars and Craft points on the life ring - gathering, crafting, trading, hunting and sailing.
You earn 2 Stars for every Renown level, and 1 Craft point for every 8 profession ranks.
Changes are free to plan until you confirm them. Taking stars back is free below Renown 10, then costs 10 silver per star. A full reset costs 10,000 gold.
Your stars never affect hits or spells against other players, and they switch off in duels and while you mentor.
Works in Enhanced Plus and DFO Grimoire, and on phones: tap a star to read it, tap again to take it.
The Firmament's own text is English for now.
The main menu first asks one question: Online or Offline. Offline opens Continue, New Game, Load Game and the Test Room, with a way back.
Settings and Overhauls are now in the menu's bottom bar beside Screenshots and About.
The bottom bar no longer covers the menu's buttons on phones, small or short screens, and long languages.
In DFO Grimoire, the menu's two pages appear only where the screen is tall enough; otherwise one page is shown.
Double-clicking Offline no longer opens Load Game by accident.
Escape puts the keyboard back on the button you came from.
Tutorials and Screenshots are now translated.
Classes are grouped as Magic, Stealth and Combat, and each shows the two attributes it relies on.
The class card shows the class's attributes, skills and health per level before you read its description. Health now reads as the real range, for example "3-6 a level, more with Endurance".
On phones, "Begin your life" and "Play as..." stay on screen.
A greyed-out button that is waiting (for example "18 left to spend") is now readable.
The province names on the map no longer overlap or run off it.
Clicking through classes no longer plays the drums every time - only when you choose one.
Start over now sits beside Back.
Buttons say "Play as an Acrobat", not "Play as a Acrobat".
Calm HUD (Features, on by default): the health, fatigue and magicka bars fade out while all three are full and no enemy is targeted, and come back the moment you lose or spend a point.
The saddle panel is a small block in the bottom-right corner. F2 shows or hides it (rebindable in Controls). The Horse care setting chooses When needed, Always or Off.
On touch screens the saddle panel no longer covers the compass.
The temperature reading sits in the bottom-left corner.
DFO Grimoire no longer draws dotted lines.
The Stable's horse look is now swatches and arrows instead of large buttons.
Small text across Settings and character creation is now at least 12px and easier to read.
The pause window's tabs wrap instead of running off the window in long languages.
In DFO Grimoire on phones, the side menu (including "Main menu") is readable again.
Sit at any tavern's card table and press Play The King's Gambit on the Hold'em or Iliac Hand panel to start a battle of armies and kings against the tavern's regulars.
Choose whom to challenge. Each regular plays at a tier, from Amateur to Grandmaster, and their row tells you their army's size, their potions, how often they blunder and the least they will play for.
Put down a stake of 1, 2 or 5 times that least stake. Win and you take back twice your stake. A regular can only pay out so much in a night, and after that they play for fun.
Pick one of the Iliac Bay's four kings and build an army of up to 12 units from 300 points. Every unit wears its Iliac Hand card's picture.

Fight on a board laid across the table. Each turn you have two actions: move a piece, strike, or give it a potion. Fire, spikes and poison spread across the board as the rounds pass. Fell the other king to win, and guard your own.
Play with the mouse, a finger, the keyboard or a gamepad. On a touchscreen, a press snaps to your pieces and asks you to confirm a move or a strike.
Forfeiting or standing up while gold is down asks you twice, and you cannot save with gold on the table.
A built-in guide and glossary explain every rule. The game's words read in all thirteen fully translated languages.
You can turn the game off in Settings, on the World tab.
The board now stands on the table. Walls are stone blocks, pillars are columns, and water lies low with ripples drifting across it.
Every piece is its card standing in a stand. Your stands are pale, the regular's are dark with notched rims, and the kings stand on brass. A bar over each card shows its health.

Pieces walk the path they take, lunge at their foes, and shake and flash red when they are hit. A potion makes a card glow green. The damage or the healing rises over the piece as a number, and shots fly across the board.
A fallen piece topples and slides into its owner's pile beside the board, so you can count the losses at a glance.
Fire flickers, spikes stand up and poison bubbles. A warning pulses where a new hazard will appear.
When the battle starts, the cards are dealt onto the board one at a time, and your view leans over the table so the whole board fits beside the panel. Fold the panel to give the board more room.
With reduced motion turned on, a hit piece does not shake.
The King's Gambit now sounds as the mod does: dice as the game opens, coins as a stake goes down, a click as a unit joins or a piece is chosen.
Monsters cry as they move and strike, swords swing and bowstrings loose, spells crackle, potions bubble, and a fallen piece hits the cloth. Fire, spikes and poison each bite with their own sound.
A win ends in a fanfare (and the clink of coins when gold was down); a loss in a groan. Forfeiting is silent, as in the mod.

Online, sit at a tavern's card table and The King's Gambit offers the board's two seats: press Sit at the board, build your army, then press Ready. When both players are ready, the table lays the board and deals both armies.

The table runs the game: it lays the board, rolls every die and keeps a turn clock of 60 seconds. A turn that runs out ends as End turn does; three in a row stand that player up and give the game to the other.
Your king's row is always at your own edge of the board, and the board lies in the same place on the cloth for both players.
The other player's moves play out one at a time, half a second apart, so you can follow each.
Anyone else in the tavern can watch a game: the board stands on its cloth for everyone near the table.
Play a regular instead takes you back to the tavern's regulars at any time.

At a tavern's red table, a realm character can play another player for gold: stake 10, 50, 200, 1,000 or 5,000 gold, the same as your opponent. The realm holds both stakes, and the winner takes the whole pot.
Every online game between two registered accounts counts on The King's Gambit's season board. Press Season board to see the top ten and your own rank.
The season's first player, after ten counted games against five different opponents, wears the Grandmaster title.
No single press loses a staked game: a gamepad's Start button and a stray finger on a touchscreen now ask before you stand up, as Escape does.
Leaving the board just as a game is dealt cancels that game, and both stakes go home.
If your connection drops mid-game, the panel tells you how the game ended when you are back.
A move followed at once by End turn now goes through, and the realm's own reason is shown when it cannot hold your stake.
On a gamepad with the Enhanced Plus hotbar, the d-pad moves the board's cursor during a battle.
On a phone, the turn clock shows first, and anyone watching a game has Stand up, Play a regular instead and More.
A piece's information now names the foes it can strike and any hazard under it.
The online board's buttons read correctly in every translated language.

The Grizzly Bear, the Sabretooth Tiger, the Spider, the Slaughterfish, the Mummy, the Frost Daedra, the Fire Daedra, the Archer and the Ranger join the Iliac Hand set, each with its own painted picture.
Their creatures drop them, as every other creature drops its own card - and every creature in the game now has one.
Every Iliac Hand card's rules and flavor text now read in your chosen language, in all thirteen fully translated languages.
Points of interest built by the developers now stand in the world: ruins, shrines, camps and more, streamed in as you travel, solid to walk on and lit at night.
Places that ask to be marked show on the world map and the travel map.

Online, you are promoted the moment you qualify for your guild's next rank. Talk to a guild-service NPC at the hall to get it. There is no 28-day wait for a promotion any more. Demotion, probation and expulsion still wait 28 days, so one bad day doesn't cost you a rank. Offline play is unchanged.
Online, if you don't yet qualify, the guild popup lists what the next rank needs that you lack:
the rank's name ("Next rank: Swordsman")
your reputation against what's needed ("Reputation 14 of 20")
the guild-skill level you're short of, with your best guild skill named ("A guild skill at 31 - your best, Axe, is 25")
a second guild skill at the lower bar
the guild's own skills by name

Updates download only what changed. The desktop app now updates the game one file at a time instead of downloading about 130 MB and replacing the whole game folder. The full installer runs only when the app itself changes, or when a file-by-file update fails. This applies on Windows, macOS, Linux and the portable build.
Spellbook details. A spell you made now shows its real settings in the Spellbook, and only the parts its effects use.
Your ship's crew. Your crew no longer rushes the rail shouting at nobody while you stand at the helm. They muster only when a boarding can actually happen.
Shipyards by ponds. Towns away from the open sea, such as Ilessan Hills, no longer have a shipyard and a lighthouse beside a pond.
Enemies stuck in doorways. Tall enemies (mages, healers, spellswords, liches, Daedra lords) duck under dungeon doorways again instead of jamming in them.
Daedra summoning. A summoning whose quest cannot be offered where you are no longer takes your gold or marks the Daedra as summoned. Staff can repair characters already affected.
