PvP looting. A worn item you loot from a player in the open PvP zone now reaches you even if you share a guild or party with them. The item stays held until you collect it, and goes back to its owner if nobody does.
Quests sending you to a player's home. Quests no longer pick another player's home as a quest residence, in any town.
Party loot. Party members in a dungeon now see the same loot on the same body or container, and each player gets their own bonus on top. Taking an item no longer replaces the other players' list.
Overworld travel stuck at 1x. Overworld travel no longer drops to 1x speed and stays there. Land that fails to load is loaded again instead of leaving a hole.
Moving lights. Moving lights, such as a boss's glow, no longer redraw all their shadows every frame.
Guildmates are friends in the PvP zone. Members of the same guild can no longer attack each other there, as with a party.
Movable riding and helm panels. The riding panel and the ship's helm panel are now pieces in the HUD editor (Alt+U). You can move, resize or hide them.

Horse care and wagon upkeep tiers. Horse care and wagon upkeep each have Off, Boons (the default) and Hard, like Climates & Calories. On Boons nothing is taken: a hungry horse is no weaker, a worn wagon is no slower, and a wagon kept Sound rolls 10% faster. Hard is the system as it was. Off is the classic horse or wagon.
Many of a sign's stars added up past what the Firmament allows for that stat, so the last stars you bought did nothing. The values have come down so that every star in a sign now adds something.
Small stars and roads now give their attribute and skill bonus one for one as a percent (+2 Strength is +2% of your Strength; it was +4%).

Notables, keystones and life stars were scaled down to fit. Some examples: Night Mother's Embrace is +19% damage to unaware foes (was +30%), Merchant Prince is +11 Mercantile / +6 Etiquette (was +20 / +10), and Hermit's Covenant is +10% herb yield (was +20%).

A Firmament attribute bonus now counts on a stat already at 100. With the sky's full +15, a 100 Strength reads 115. A Fortify fills up to that raised cap but never passes it, and offline the cap is 100 again.
Looting a fallen enemy in a dungeon no longer turns its Morrowind body back into the old sprite while the loot window is open.
Morrowind bodies no longer clip through floors and walls: a body lying on the ground no longer sinks halfway into it, and a figure standing beside a wall is no longer sliced off by it.

Searching for a player in the chat now finds anyone online, not just the people listed on your screen. With hundreds of players online, the World list only shows part of the server, and the search used to look in that part alone. It now asks the server too, so players on other parts of the server show up a moment after you type.
The Dragonfire Oath is a Daedric Dai-Katana that can drop from the Warden of the Burning Gate, about one fight in a hundred. It gives +40% damage, +15 Strength, +30 Long Blade and +15 Endurance.
Dragonfire: a blow that lands on a Daedra burns it again for another third of the hit, and burns every other Daedra within 3 m for the same.
The Sunken Sovereign is an Ebony Saber that can drop from the Old Coil, about one kill in a hundred, for a ship that did damage. It gives +40% damage, +15 Agility, +30 Long Blade and 10% life leech.
Undertow: each blow on the same foe adds +10% damage, up to +50%, and the stacks fade after 6 seconds without a hit. A foe it kills heals you for 10%.
Both are shown in the Collections codex, each with its own hint.
Killing the sea serpent now has a rare chance to grant the title Coilbreaker (1 in 20 kills) and the aura The Maelstrom (1 in 50). You keep them for good.
The Maelstrom is a three-armed whirlpool of tide and foam around your feet, with a curling lip and spray.
An honour you have not held before is announced and shown in a popup.

Sending your wagon or horse away from the Stable now keeps them there. They no longer reappear outside the next building or dungeon you enter, and mounting your horse no longer drops a stabled wagon behind you. Summon them to bring them back. A wagon or horse you never sent away is shown as With you on the Stable page and is left outside doors as before. If you sent yours away before this update, send it away once more.

The Repairs Objects enchantment mends your worn gear first, then a worn Cast When Held or Item Deteriorates piece, and only then what you carry. Damaged loot in your pack no longer takes the repairs while the ring on your finger wears down. While such a piece is damaged it holds the repairs, so your pack waits.
Flying Kick can now be used while jumping, falling or stepping off a ledge. Every other leap and dash still needs solid ground. A kick near the ground no longer cancels the damage from a long fall.

If you die in the Wrothgarian Mountains while your wagon is parked outside the zone, or sent to the stable, nothing in it is lost. Its items and gold stay put. A wagon you drive, lead or park inside the zone still loses its cargo as before.
Slaughterfish from crates. Searching a crate or chest in a dungeon no longer wakes Slaughterfish, Dreugh or Lamia on dry land.

A duplicate player after a server restart. A player who reconnects now stands once. An old connection from before the restart, or a second tab, no longer leaves a frozen copy of them in town or in a dungeon.

Market stalls full of people. In towns with market stalls (such as Penbrugh), the food, goods and animals at the stalls show as themselves again with the Morrowind people on, instead of crowds of bowed, turning figures.
Bare feet in chain boots. Chain boots, gauntlets and pauldrons, including Legendary ones like The Wayrest Courier's Treads, now show on your Morrowind body (in iron) instead of bare skin.
Stuck quest foes. A foe that appears inside a pillar is moved out beside it.
Arrows from twigs. Using a twig makes 2 arrows again, as intended, so the workbench's 20 arrows from 4 twigs are worth their plank and ingot.
Missing quest residences. If a quest's residence is in another player's home, its door now shows the quest's name, for example "The Hawkley Residence (Aldric's home)".
Battle axes and war axes. With the Morrowind look, a Battle Axe (one-handed) now looks and swings like a one-handed axe, and a War Axe (two-handed) like a two-handed one.
Boulder glint. A boulder's glint now sits on its stones, not in the air above them.

Looted ingredients can be stored. Ingredients you looted, bought or were given now go into your Stores as "loose". You can craft with them at any station, but they can't be used for writs, your guild's Stores or market sales; only what you gathered can.
One player per account in a place. If you log in to the same account a second time in the same area, the older connection is closed.

How a person takes your tone now changes what they think of you. Townsfolk like plain speaking: a Blunt question raises their regard, and a Polite one lowers it. Before, being polite raised everyone's regard, even with the commoners who refuse polite questions.
Courtship works the same way. A tone they like helps the day's courtship, and one they dislike costs a little affection (never below nothing). They will tell you so.
The regard explanation on the talk panel now says which tone townsfolk prefer.

Gauntlets of the Rose (Open Hand): the second blow from a bare-handed hit now shows its own damage number, tagged "Open Hand", next to the first. The bonus was always being applied (each fist that lands hits again for half), but it never showed on screen, so it looked like nothing was happening.
Many Endings: its echo now shows its own number too, tagged "Many Endings".
The galleon, carrack and large boat wear their own painted liveries again: the oxblood strakes, the gilt and the stern gallery.
The wagons and the caravan have their own paint back, with the caravan's livery, shutters, curtains and sunburst.
The Stable, Wagon Yard, Joinery, shipyard and lighthouse signs have their emblems back: the horseshoe, the wheel, the saw, the anchor and the coil.
The town's banners and hangings show their regions' and gods' own charges again.
The LeFay monument has its painted stone and bronze plaque again.
Every one of these textures is now drawn in Daggerfall's own colour palette, with Daggerfall's grain, so they sit beside the classic walls and ships instead of standing out.

Invisibility in dungeons. Monsters that cannot see through Invisibility no longer swing at you just because you walked in front of them. The undead, vampires and Daedra still see through it, as in Daggerfall. Wilderness enemies also no longer notice an invisible traveller during fast travel.

Blocked temple entrances. Temples in Beautiful Villages towns, including the School of Julianos in Makehda and the temples of Kynareth, no longer sit behind a wall of stone. You can walk up their steps to the door again. The Akatosh Chantry's steps in Merdale are no longer buried under grass banks.
Getting wet when it isn't raining. You only get wet when rain or snow is actually falling on you, and a light shower soaks you slowly.

Boulders and market stalls. Boulders in Beautiful Villages and Beautiful Cities towns show at their real size (most had sunk out of sight), and market stalls stand where the town's author placed them.

Guild ranks online. Reputation you earn with a guild before joining still counts, but online a new member rises no faster than the guild records standing: about a rank and a half a day from the day you join. The guild hall now tells you when your next promotion can come at the earliest.

First-time crafting bonus. Crafting stations now show each pattern's XP and the 500 XP bonus for making it the first time. Pieces made only of cloth bought from the Weavers (Linen and Wool, including the Fishing Net) earn no first-time bonus. The stations and the craft messages now say so.

When assigning a key that is already in use, the confirmation now appears beside the binding being changed instead of at the top of the controls list. You no longer need to scroll away from the binding to choose whether to move the key or use it for both actions.

Instances. At a dungeon or building where one of your quests is running, at Privateer's Hold, or where a party member is already in an instance, the door now asks whether to enter the public world or your own instance. Only you and your party can enter your instance. It keeps its own looted chests and slain monsters (they return after half an hour, like everywhere else), and it closes for good when the quest that opened it ends.
Joining your party. A party member's instance shows at the door as "*Name*'s instance". Pick it to join them.
Privateer's Hold can be visited again. Its public hall is still for new characters only, but you can return to your own instance of the Hold at any time.

Quest dungeons are complete again. Quest targets, like the main quest's mummy, could end up in a part of a smaller online dungeon that can't be reached from its entrance. Quest dungeons are now always the full Daggerfall layout, in your instance or in the full public layout.
Quest teleports, Recall, loading a save and staff teleports return you to the instance you were in, or to the public room if that instance has closed. They never stop to ask.
The door only asks when there is a real choice. Every other door opens as it always did. Homes and the Wrothgarian open zone never have instances.
Press Esc at the door to leave without entering.
Weapons with a fire, frost or shock damage bonus now show it. Whether the bonus is the weapon's own or comes from a Ruby or Sapphire set in it, the weapon wears an animated outline of its element:
Fire gives off rising flames and drifting embers.
Frost forms a breathing rime with glinting ice spikes.
Shock crackles along the edge and throws off arcs.

On the Morrowind first-person and third-person models the outline wraps the 3D weapon, and the blade's surface is charged with its element as well. An enchanted Morrowind weapon with no element now glows with an arcane light, like classic enchanted weapons always have.
Once the servers are updated, other players' weapons glow on their Morrowind bodies as they do in their hands. Your Weapon glow switch decides only what you see.
A weapon you haven't identified keeps its element hidden until you identify it, as its card does.
Turn it off under Settings → Combat → Weapons in hand → Weapon glow. Off shows weapons exactly as before.
Towns with ships in port run smoother online. In our measurement the ships cost about a quarter of their old share of each frame, and they leave far less garbage behind, so there are fewer stutters.

Containers, the wagon, your storage and pack pages holding hundreds of items now open in a fraction of a second. A 700-item container used to freeze the game for many seconds while its item pictures loaded.
Clicking, taking and picking items in a long list is near-instant again, down from a second or more.
Item pictures fill in as they load without redrawing the whole window, so hover cards and drags are no longer interrupted.
Searching your wagon or storage keeps your place in the list.
On phones, the loot window's two columns stay the same width and no longer run off the side of the screen.

Your horse (and your cart's horse) now darkens with the world around it - at night, in a cave mouth or under a storm - instead of glowing as bright as noon under a dimmed weapon. It follows the same Features -> First-person lighting switch as your weapon and hands.

World and region chat, friends, parties and guild lines are steadier at busy hours. The relay had been refusing a large share of the messages passed between its chat servers, so lines, invites and counts could go missing for players on some chat shards. That traffic now flows a different way that can't be refused.
When a room's server restarts just as you connect, you now get in on the first try instead of waiting out a reconnect.

Logging in, saving, and the town, seat and notice-board panels should stay responsive at peak hours. The account database was hitting its limit on how many requests it could take each second; several of the busiest requests now ask it far fewer times, with the same answers.
A yard piece you just placed, moved or removed no longer snaps back on your own screen for up to a minute afterwards.

At rank 7 a guild hall now tells you the next rank is a chapter chair - a council chair or the Master's - won by Merit at each Sunday's Turning, and what it asks: reputation 80, 14 real days in the guild and an account 7 real days old.

A service only a chair opens (the Mages Guild's Teleport, Zenithar's summoning) now says so at any rank, instead of promising a review that never comes online. A knight is told a chair brings no house.
When your rank is held at 7, the new Guild Chapters tutorial page opens. You also see it the first time you come online as a member of a guild, temple or order.
Every change to a guild's standing online is said in chat: "Standing: Mages Guild +25 (now 40, 10 more to come)".
What the realm still owes you shows in the guild hall and on the Standing page, with the daily pace: 15 a real day, days turning at midnight UTC.
When a quest's reward passes the day's pace you're told how much more is owed; if you're already at 100, you're told the rest is lost.
Guild names appear in your language.
The guild hall and the Standing page now warn you before a review puts you on probation or lowers your rank, with when it happens and why.
On probation you're told the stakes: below -10 you're expelled at the review, below 0 it runs 28 more days, and at 0 or more it ends. Online, earning the next rank ends it sooner.

Online, "Guard the Guild" now needs Mages Guild standing 10 and "Protect an Honored Mage" standing 20 - the standing their own quest headers ask. New apprentices are no longer handed them. Their penalties are unchanged.
The guild window's rank text scrolls on its own, so Talk, Service and Reforge stay on screen.
Long refusals in the classic guild window no longer run off the screen.
Joining a guild in the same minute as a standing loss is no longer dropped by the server.
Translations updated in all 13 languages.

Bare-handed, both fists are now on screen. Punches alternate between the hands: the hand that leads opens, the other answers if you strike again quickly, and the idle fist tucks in toward the middle while the other punches.
Each punch shows the arm that throws it, on its own side. Daggerfall's own fist art has punches for both arms, and each hand now uses its own.
Equip a one-handed weapon in each hand (swords, daggers, maces, war axes) and both are drawn and swung. You no longer swap hands to use the second weapon.
H now chooses which hand leads ("Leading with the right hand." / "Leading with the left hand."). It no longer costs a switch delay with both hands up. With one weapon it still swaps hands, as before.
A shield, a two-handed weapon, a bow, or a torch or lantern held in a hand still means one weapon, as before.
With weapon glow on, each weapon in a pair shows its own element (a frost dagger beside a fire sword).
A pair is quicker, not twice as strong. The next blow straight after a strike comes from the other hand, a little sooner.
The off hand (the one not leading) does 80% damage and has -5 to hit at Agility 50. Higher Agility shrinks the penalty to nothing; lower Agility raises it to -10.
A heavy weapon in the off hand swings slower (a longer follow-through after its hit).

The off hand's blows count as 0.8 of a blow for everything a hit sets off: on-strike enchantments, per-hit item and set powers, and skill training. A pair doesn't proc or train faster than its damage.
When one weapon attacks, the other lowers slightly, straight down (it never slides sideways and shows where the sprite is cut off).

Measured, a matched pair of light weapons deals about 9% more damage per second than one of them, and a heavier pair about 4% (the off arm feels the weight). That holds at any frame rate. In return you spend up to a quarter more fatigue per second and give up your shield. A light off-hand weapon (a dagger next to a longsword) is quicker but weaker overall.
The same rules apply in duels, sieges and the open PvP zone.

Running with nothing in either hand shows your arms pumping in step with your stride (on the head bob's own rhythm), using Daggerfall's own fist-and-forearm frames. The arm always runs off the bottom of the screen; no floating hands.
The arms keep running through a short hop, stay smooth when you stop and start again, and ease away when you ready a spell.
Works with every mod switched off. A punch thrown mid-run shows at once.
both fists punch in turn, each with its own hand;

a pair of weapons shows the left weapon in the left hand, swinging with its own blows - now on the game's own skeletons too (they have no left weapon bone, so one is made by mirroring the right); the arm not attacking dips slightly at the shoulder;
the arms pump while you run empty-handed.
When the realm finds the same item in two places, it now locks that item only. Your character keeps trading, and nobody has to review it.
A locked item stays with you: it can't be traded, sold, dropped or left where others can take it. Your wagon and your own storage still take it.
You're told which item was locked, once on each device.
If you were handed an item by someone whose game closed before it saved the hand-off, your copy is locked, but it no longer counts against you.
Every character frozen for copied items has been unfrozen. The copied items themselves stay locked.
The third time the realm's rules hold a character's trading, it is frozen for a week and then reopens on its own. Each time after that, it's a month. Strikes clear a month after the last one.
The notice names the item and says when trading reopens.
Shop shelves no longer hand back an item you already took, which used to create a copy by accident.
Another player can no longer plant a copy of your item on you through a body or a container.
With two weapons in first person, the left arm and its weapon are now on screen. Before, only the right arm showed.
With two weapons in third person, the arms now swing against each other as you walk or run. Before, both swung the same way at once.
The running fists stay low and pump with your stride, rising about a third of the way up the screen. Before, they rose to half the screen and looked like uppercuts.
A running fist now shows its back and knuckles, like your fists at rest. Before, it showed its underside.
A home's furnishings load faster, especially when the server is busy.
Fixed online features (homes, the notice board, mail, gathering, the market and the arena board) taking up to a minute to answer, or failing, since this afternoon.

When the account service is overloaded, the game now backs off its background checks (mail, the notice board, the day's motherlodes) instead of asking again at once, so the service recovers instead of staying slow.

A party member's Resurrection now saves a Bloodline character. While the death screen is up (up to two minutes), their Resurrection brings you back with no death on your family tree, no Succession and no tombstone.
The death is now held by the server, so closing the tab, reloading or logging in from another device no longer escapes it.
If the death is already settled, the caster is told "<name> has fallen for good" and keeps their magicka.
Anything you steal is now marked stolen, including a robbed caravan's goods and the hold of a lawful ship you board or sink. A merchant still buys it but never puts it back on the shelf.
When you're found guilty (jail, a fine or banishment), the guards take every stolen item you carry and tell you how many. Win your case, or get out through the Thieves Guild, and you keep them.
Your own items put into someone else's cupboard and taken back are no longer marked stolen.
Paying a fine or doing a penance now restores your reputation with the people of the kingdom too, not only with the law.

Guards called into a building now walk round through the doorway to reach you, even between deep shelves or inside a closet, and they attack when they get there. A locked door or a ladder only keeps them out for two seconds.
Guards and dungeon enemies standing next to you now turn to face you and attack, instead of standing still.
A headstone your party has searched counts as searched for the whole party, and the game tells you who searched it. A stranger's search no longer locks it for you.
In tombs, coffins a stranger opened are yours to search, and you can search one standing right next to it.
Party members no longer vanish for a few seconds when you go through a tomb door.
The arena now waits for the server instead of briefly showing your offline rank and season. Your title and wins were never lost.
With a Repairs Objects enchantment worn, every worn piece of armour and clothing now repairs 2% of itself per tick, the same as weapons. A battered steel set is whole in about an hour.
With horse care Off, the Stable page now shows every horse you own and lets you ride any of them.
Another player's Disintegrate no longer deletes your revenant outright. It now counts as a killing blow, and only you decide your revenant's fate.
Market stalls now look the way the pack draws them: the keeper behind the counter, goods on the counter.
Stalls and boulders you placed in your own yard are back where you put them, at the size you placed them.
The shipyard's fleet page reads properly again.
A pending perk change no longer blocks you from choosing perks when you reach a new rank.
The guild hall now says what reputation still on its way means: it is already earned and arrives at most 15 a real day. Quests done the same day add to what is waiting, not to your standing.
A member on probation is no longer expelled over reputation the guild still owes them. The probation is renewed instead.
Pieces of Ruhn's Regalia (and the raiding parties' sets) that were enchanted before enchanting them was closed no longer freeze your trading. Holds placed because of them are lifted.
The loot panel and its tooltip no longer cover skinning, or any other gathering minigame, while it plays.
At a quest's dungeon whose shared version is laid smaller, the Public / Your instance prompt now says the quest's business is in your instance only.
Quest Repair in that shared dungeon now tells you where the quest's things are, instead of "Nothing was missing".
A dungeon's automap keeps your exploration of both the shared dungeon and your instance. Switching between them no longer wipes the map, its notes or its portals.
The tier above Dagon's Breach. Your party of up to 8 goes down through the torn halls of the Battlespire under a 30-minute count.
Open one with a Weir Key. Stand outdoors, online and signed in, and use the key from your inventory. Your party at that moment becomes the breach's company and is called.
No key yet? Choose *Rehearse* in the start window, or type /breach rehearse, to open the day's Rehearsal. It runs the first circle of five halls, needs no key, and pays nothing.
The breach rises for 5 minutes while your company gathers, then takes members for 5 more.
The start window. Using a Weir Key asks where to begin before any key is spent:
The Wager. Before you open, choose up to three decrees, one from each family, to take on from the first hall.

The arch. An arch of the gate's white marble and gold rises out of the ground in front of you, with a gold beacon 400 m tall. Other players nearby see it too. It burns open when the breach opens and sinks once the first hall wakes.

The key tells you why when it can't open here: indoors; in a duel or a siege; with enemies nearby; while travelling; in water or aboard a boat; inside a town; within 300 m of a Dagon's Breach or 150 m of another arch; while you already hold a breach; while the road is shut; or without 8 m of clear ground for the arch.

The call. Wherever your party is in the Bay, they hear a war horn and see a prompt with the time until the breach opens. Once it is open, press Enter (A on a gamepad) or the prompt's button to answer. A portal opens at your feet: step into it. The opener steps through the arch itself. A late step through the arch still admits you.

A key that fails to open comes back. If the Spire fails to open, your Weir Key comes back on its own the next time you are online within a week, even if you reload. A stake the Spire never settles is spent after two weeks, and a letter in your mailbox says why.
One breach at a time. A call to another breach while you stand in one no longer takes you out of yours.

Finding it: the breach is in the Timers row (its opening, then the hall and the count), you get a sight line (*You see an Elite Breach 140 metres to the North!*), and your company's arch is marked in gold on the map and the compass.
Closing a Dagon's Breach can drop a Weir Key:
Clearing an Abyss Dungeon's Hour drops one 1 in 3.
Everyone who has already closed a Dagon's Breach gets one key as a launch gift.
Opening a breach spends a key. You need to have closed a Dagon's Breach before you can open a keyed one.
The Broken Galleries (circles 1-5), the Soul Cairn (6-10), the Shade Perilous (11-15) and the Havoc Wellhead (16 and deeper). Each region has its own enemies, lords, platforms and element.

A Brink opens the Soul Cairn, the Shade Perilous and the Wellhead: a long crossing through the Spire's broken passages, ending in the new region's own set piece. The Brink into the Cairn always carries its Sinking Stair.
Each circle is five halls: a fight, a crossing, a trial, a second fight, then the lord's Court. Enemies get tougher every circle.

Entering a new region, you fall past the Spire's broken underside: torn floors, hanging spires, broken galleries and upside-down columns, lit by that region's glow. Other steps are a quick fade; reduced motion gives a plain cut. The hall number shows each time.
A hall is a way through the torn academy. Corridors turn, rooms have more than one way out, and the way climbs and falls between the arrival plate and the door, crossing over and under itself.

Rooms: stair halls with a grand stair up to a gallery, towers with spiral stairs, two-level gallery halls, cloisters round a court, broken halls whose floor fell into the undercroft, and crossings where two ways pass at two heights.

Climbing: short climbs on the main way, never more than two pitches in a row and never longer than 9 m, sized so a character at Climbing 0 with no grip left can make them. Each has a stair or ramp somewhere in the hall for anyone who would rather walk. Harder optional climbs lead off the way to the academy's caches and vantage points.
Floors can stand over other floors. Blows, danger shapes, the legion and the lords all judge the floor you are actually standing on, never the one above or below.
A fall that would skip you ahead along the way casts you back, as the void does.
Yards:
Ramparts:
Stairs climb to the Rampart's caster pillars, the Wyrm's perches and the Council Rotunda's balconies: every raised floor has its way up.
Crossings: the Span's platforms and, from circle 3, the Deepway's chambers. Deeper spans carry more passages. The platforms grow in kind as you go down:
walled Drops to a landing below, with a doorway onward and a lamp on the far wall;
in the Soul Cairn, Rails that carry you along the course (their tracks marked at both ends) and Gusts that push you sideways, with wind vanes and a rising wind a second before each gust;
Islands carry waystones that light up gold where you would be cast back. A teammate standing on a crumbling platform that already fell for you stands on a faint gold outline instead of floating.

Every crossing is proven crossable before you ever see it. The Spire checks every jump's timing at the slowest build the game makes, and lays the course again if a jump is ever unfair or if the usual crossing takes far longer than the fastest.

The toll. If you are still on the road when your company is pulled at the end of a crossing hall, you pay 5% of your health for each quarter of the road you didn't cross, at most 20%. Reaching a new island in your last 15 seconds waives it, and it never takes your last point of health. The toll rings when it is taken.
Late to the hall? After you have arrived late to two halls in a row, the next hall waits only 10 seconds for you instead of 30.
Trials:
Twists turn about one hall in four, trials included:
Sixteen kinds of enemy:
The legion hunts:
Enemies stand on the ground they're actually on: a Court raised above the hall, a chamber past a Deepway's shaft, Harriers following you down a course. Your blows reach them where they are.

Every enemy blow is drawn on the floor before it lands: a disc, a lane, a cone, a ring, or the whole floor with safe havens marked in gold. Every blow gives you time to step out of it, and the Spire never stacks blows so that nowhere is safe. A chained follow-up blow is drawn dim until the first one lands.
Your company gathers on each hall's arrival plate, and the hall wakes once everyone is there. When the door opens, step through it to be pulled to the next hall.
The Count: you have 30 minutes from the first hall. It runs during fights and pauses briefly between halls. If it runs out during a fight, the breach tears shut.
Falling into the void is not death. You are cast back to the last solid ground you stood on, for a tenth of your health. It never takes you below a quarter.

Two restoring potions a hall. Healing, Heal True and Purification count toward the limit; every other potion and every spell is free. The count refills at each hall's wake and at each Redoubt, and a reload keeps it. The desktop HUD shows it.
In the Spire you cannot save, rest, open the map, use Mark or Recall, levitate, or bring companions.
Ten places, each with its own danger:
in the Soul Cairn:
in the Shade Perilous:
in the Wellhead:

Cooling slag (the Wellhead's Forge Gut): two spouts take turns pouring magma, and you cross on the crust while it holds. Its edge glows white in the last second before it breaks, and the spill's warning is drawn on the slag itself.

Shafts: a Deepway goes down through a shaft of its region's kind, such as the Hollow Trunk's moonlit branches or the Slag Chute. Standing on a shaft's ledge facing the drop, the third-person camera tilts down and lifts over the edge so you can see where you'll land.
The fork. From circle 2 every Span splits at an island:
Set pieces, one per region:
The Molten Rim leaves gold causeways across its magma.
Chambers. Some Yards and Proving Walks stand in modelled chambers, with a second floor up a stair, a chokepoint arch, surging channels, or an engine.
Engines:
The Honour Horn (the Clan Pit). Answer the Kynval alone and the crowd throws every member a Reliquary. If anyone else steps into the ring, the crowd throws fire instead, for the rest of the hall.
Alcoves. Look for a faint gold seam in a wall. One blow breaks the false wall, and the alcove behind it holds lumen, a Vestige shard, or a page of the Annals.

The Annals of 3E 398. Thirty pages the Battlemages left behind: seventeen hidden in the alcoves, and thirteen that each lord gives up at its first fall. Read the pages you have found with /breach annals, anywhere: your account keeps them.
Grath's islands fall. In the first Court, the island Grath leaps from cracks and falls into the magma for 15 seconds. If you fall with it, you are thrown back onto an island that still stands.
In third person, walls, shelves, pillars and other rock between the camera and your character fade to a see-through dither instead of hiding you.
Each Court has its own lord, with phases, errands for the company to run, and a fury that builds. Every phase shows its card:
Courts of two lords (Garoth beside the Last Armsmaster, the Twin Lords) are won when both fall. Each lord keeps its own element, mirrors and decree, and the HUD shows a bar for each lord standing.
The lords' own marks:

The Proving Walks have their champions: the Kynreeve (Shield-Wall, facing where he guards), the Kynmarcher (The Citadel) and the Markynaz (The Grand Duke's Decree). The Markynaz's arrival card names the decree he lays, and his decree adds to the circle's decrees instead of replacing them.
Lords and champions walk around walls instead of through them: through an arch's opening, up a stair, across Grath's bridges. A Charge or Lunge stops at an arch's wall.
Lords resize with your company: when a companion falls, the lord loses that companion's share of health, and it comes back when they're recalled.
A Colossal lord looks as big as it is and can be struck at its true size.
Standing still, or with the game in a background tab, a lord's blow still lands on you.

A death in the breach is a fall, not the end. A FALLEN card says whether a Redoubt can call you back and how many Reliquaries you lost (reduced motion cuts straight through). The end theme plays. Then you become a witness who can ping the floor for the living.
The next Redoubt calls you back at full health, once a breach, at the cost of your newest Vestige. A companion can carry your Memento from where you fell to a niche to bring you back sooner.
A second fall is final. A witness can also leave for good with /breach forsake (press twice).

Witnesses see more: dormant Lurkers, hidden alcoves, and the next hall's twist. Pings show as blue pillars with a chime. A witness sees whom they watch, taps a row to watch another, and pings from the pad or touch.
If the whole company falls, the breach ends.

If your page reloads or your connection drops mid-breach, you're offered *Return to the Spire* while the breach still stands, even after the call has closed. You come back to the hall your company holds: at your last safe footing during a trial, or on the arrival plate between trials.
Returning from a new device or browser drops you straight into the right hall. If the Spire doesn't answer, you're told so and can try again.
Joining or reloading in the middle of a fight shows everything at once: burning ground, Grath's fallen islands, the lord's phase and where every enemy is.
Receipts wait for you. A breach that ended while you were offline keeps your receipts, and you collect them when you come back.
A server restart no longer loses a breach (see below).
Defeating a circle's lord takes its Redoubt:
Choose a Vestige. Each member is offered three. Press 1-3 or type /breach pick N.
Stoneskin's extra health is a true cushion: the Spire's percentage hits count against your health without it, and the Spire's one-life count includes it.
A companion who has gone home or been left behind no longer strengthens your blows.

Three of one family resonate into a capstone: Rooted makes you immune to pushes, Spellweave makes every fourth damage spell free, Rallying Cry gives back a spent Second Wind when a hall's door opens, Bladestorm's fifth melee blow strikes every foe around you, and Deadeye's long arrows pierce the add behind the target.

Accords take effect when their pair of holders stand within 10 m, among them Shield-Hymn (Bastion and Rally: the whole company gets Bastion's protection for 4 seconds when Rally heals at a door), Hammer and Anvil, Ambush, Kindled Steel, Living Wall and War-Chorus. The offer card names the Accord a pick would form with a companion.
Spare shards buy extra picks, and a Surplus buys a fourth card or a reroll.

Vote on the next circle's decrees. Each is a hardship with a reward: gusts on every span, crumbling halls, raging lords, a new one, The Fraying (the Athenaeum's Orrery frays sooner), and more. Press 1-3 or type /breach vote N. The decrees you choose are the next circle's, and the Redoubt's beacon names them and the next Court.
Ready up to end the rest early (Y, or /breach vote yes), or vote for a respite to make it longer. A respite can be asked for again after each one.
The way home opens at the Court's heart: press it twice, or type /breach home. Or stay, and the stair takes you down to the next circle.
Along the way:
A Redoubt raises a beacon at the Court's heart, and each recall stands as a blue pillar.
The damage chart: when a Court's lord falls, the gate's chart shows each member's damage, their share of the lord, blows, best hit, falls and healing.

At the end, the recap shows your depth, your time, the circles you crossed and your Vestiges, each member's share of the damage and what they healed, every fall, and your place on the boards (*The Descent, the Few: 14th*). It survives a reload and has a Close button.
Each Redoubt pays once per arena week (Monday to Monday). Taken again in the same week, it pays its gold only.
Spoils are thrown from the Court's heart when you stand in it, or go straight into your pack. They are decided when your claim is made:
A Valkynaz's Redoubt (every fifth) rolls its spoils twice.
Reliquaries: a circle's Reliquaries open once per account a week.
Silver: 20 Marks a Redoubt, inside the daily combat cap shared with gates, raids and serpents.
Guild deeds: three members of one guild taking the same Redoubt pay 25 silver to the guild's treasury.
Deadlands Embers go into your pack:
Weir Keys: a Valkynaz's Redoubt drops one 1 in 4, at most once a week. Elite foes in dungeons can drop one too:
A new Aetheric Sigil Set: nine Mithril pieces (the Warhelm, both Pauldrons, the Cuirass, Gauntlets, Greaves, Boots, the Spire-Shield and the Spire-Saber).
2 pieces, Battlemage's Bearing: +5 to +15 to every resistance and +10 to +30 magicka.

4 pieces, Battlemage's Discipline: a spell you cast arms your next weapon blow with its element for +20% to +50%. Weapon blows return 5% to 15% of your last spell's cost. With a weapon in each hand, an off-hand blow returns it only when it counts in full, like any other per-blow power.

6 pieces, Battlemage's Reprieve: a blow that takes you under 20% (never a killing blow) raises a shield of 15% to 40% of your health for 6 seconds. Party members within 8 m get half of it. It recovers in 240 down to 120 seconds.
Pieces drop from Redoubts: 1 in 12 at Redoubt 1, improving to 1 in 4 from Redoubt 16, and 1 in 3 at a Valkynaz's.

In an Elite Breach, the Reprieve and Shed Skin answer the Spire's blows, and death-saving powers (Unbroken, The Hour Turns, Shed Skin, the Reprieve, Divine Grace and the Ghost-King's Vigil) recover at the next Redoubt, not on a timer.
Feats: each lord has three:
New titles:
New auras: Beaconlight (Redoubt 10), The Burning Stair (Redoubt 20) and Firstlight.
The boards (/breach board, the *Boards* button on the Timers window's Elite rows, or the start window):
The herald posts to the gate's Discord channel when a company takes every tenth Redoubt, sets a new top of the Descent, earns First of the Spire or the Lone Beacon, or a sealed region opens.
The count chip is gold above 10:00, white to 2:00 and red below, pulsing in the last 30 seconds. When the count is held it shows a pause mark and why.
Arrivals: each hall announces itself with an arrival card naming the hall, its objective and its twist. Reduced motion stills the title cards.
First breach: short lines explain the Spire the first time you meet each part of it, once per account, so a new device doesn't repeat them.

Touch and gamepad: the panel, the votes and the Surplus work on touch and gamepad, and the pad reaches every panel choice. On touch screens you can flick up to jump and run at full speed on the spans.
Settings > Accessibility: *Danger colours* (Standard, High contrast, Deutan-Protan, Tritan), *Danger fill* (50-100%) and *Reduced motion*.
The Spire speaks English for now. Its own words (cards, lines, the panel) are in English whatever language you play in.
The relay judges where you really were when a blow landed: your movement history at that moment, on a clock corrected to yours. Lag no longer counts against you.
A feint is shown as a pulsing outline and fades out dashed when it's cut. A wind-up's sound plays only for a blow that will really land.

The next circle is built while you rest at the Redoubt, off the main thread, so stepping down is a swap rather than a fresh load: no stutter stepping into a new circle, in a breach opened before an update too.
A breach survives a server restart. It picks up where it was, and the time the server was down is given back to the Count, the hall and every timer.
Jumps are more forgiving in the Spire. A jump pressed just before you land fires as you land, and a jump pressed just after you step off an edge still leaps.
Leaping and dashing techniques don't work on the crossings (*The Spire's spans are walked, not flown.*). On fight floors they work as usual.

The Spire rebuilt to look like the Fractured Battlespire: every hall stands in the ruin of the Imperial Battlemages' academy - columns, arches, statues, cornices and lamps around and under every floor, in each region's own stone and forms.

Each region has its own air and light: ash and embers over the Deadlands' fire-sea in the Galleries, violet mist and drifting soul-motes in the Soul Cairn, near-black dusk and silver moon-dust under a great moon in the Shade Perilous, smoke and sparks over the magma in the Wellhead. Each has its own painted sky.
The lords are drawn as oversized sprites, towering over the company; their hit area grows with them.
Every platform edge has a thin, steady gold line, so you can read where the ground ends even in fog or the dark. It keeps its width in the Retro picture modes.
Danger shapes stay readable:

The Spire's own score: fourteen songs for the halls, the Courts, the Valkynaz, a lord's wake, the Redoubt's hymn, the last two minutes of the Count and the end. Each region and lord has its own motif.
The door: when the way down opens, a gold beam and a draining ring mark it, and it appears on the compass.

Danger shapes lie on every floor they cover, at that floor's height, instead of floating or hiding under ledges. A "move!" arrow points the way out over safe ground. Tethers, burning pools, marks over companions' heads and the Eclipse each have their own clear look.
Allies' spells are dimmed during trials so warnings stay readable, and a Vestige aura is a thin blue ring.
Each hall has its own echo: a cave, a stone room or open air, fading smoothly as you walk into a passage.
The Caverns' fire falls burn in Daggerfall's own fire, the camera no longer snaps back out of walls, a faded Spirebridge plank is no longer solid, and the Weir Key has its own icon.
Moving platforms are drawn in far fewer draw calls, and those out of view are skipped.

At an enchanting station, Reforge with Essence no longer stacks its buttons on top of each other. Each line of a piece now has its own Reforge button in a list under the piece's name and price, and the name is readable again instead of wrapping one word per line.

The profession stations' short notes ("Needs 2 Arcane Essence; your Stores hold 1.", "Needs 2 Steel Ingot.", the Stores-full note) now span the row under the piece, instead of being squeezed into a narrow column.
A stair rising above one of the Spire's chambers is now always there. Before, a handful of halls lost it, leaving the way on unreachable.
A Gust only pushes players on its own crossing, never someone on a bridge or floor high above it.

Chests, corpses and the wagon can be filtered by name, by item type, by rarity and by material. The rarity menu starts at Any Rarity and the material menu at Any Material. Each lists only what that pile holds, with a count beside each one. A piece whose card does not show its metal, such as an unidentified magic item or an artifact, is not listed under one.

Take all moves items from the list on screen into your pack, from the top, until the next item does not fit. Emptying someone else's cupboard this way is still stealing. Stash all does the same from the current pack page into your wagon, your own storage or the Materials Bag, and the button sits centred along the bottom edge of your item list. The pack page in use still starts on Weapons.
Looking at your own cupboard or chest, or at a stranger's cupboard that has already been stocked today, lists what it holds, the way a corpse or a pile does. Nothing is taken until you open it.

Armour and weapons of Rare quality and above say their metal (Iron, Ebony, and the rest) on the line under the name, even before they are identified. A Legendary keeps its own name, and so does one handed down as an heirloom.

The $50 Hierophant tier now grants its title and glyph in game: the rose "Hierophant" and the crown beside your name. If you have already linked your Patreon, it appears on your next sign-in. You don't need to relink.
WikiMaid - a new title, drawn amethyst into lilac into a bunny's blush.
Its glyph - a lilac bunny in a maid's lace headdress, beside her name (and on the account card, the chat roster and the travel view).

Lilac Warren - a new aura: six lilac bunnies with cotton tails and little maid's headdresses hop round your feet on a ring of lilac light, leaving paw-print tracks that fade behind them. Every so often one does a happy binky. Sparkles of lilac, pink and white rise around you.
Carrying a Weir Key no longer flags your character for review or freezes your trading. Any freeze and strike a Weir Key caused is lifted automatically.

The Possessed Child can turn out to be a scam: sometimes the "possessed" child is faking, the Daedroth the priest warned of never appears, and the child runs off with the relic. Before this fix the journal said nothing at that point, so the quest looked broken. Now a journal entry records what happened and sends you back to the tavern where the guardian was staying. Someone there knows where they went. The entry is translated into every fully supported language.
A player walking near you no longer stands frozen for minutes and then jumps to where they really are.
A player who dies is laid down once: no more second body and second cry, and they no longer stand up for a moment on their own body.
Coming into a place where someone has just died (in the Wild, for example) shows their body instead of showing them standing there alive.
A player who died in the Wild no longer stands up on their body for everyone when their connection blips.
Stepping into a building and back out beside a body no longer lays a second body on top of it, and a party member's body no longer appears twice.
A player who has already got up is no longer knocked down again by an old message about their death.
When you cross into the next area, the area you left now sees you change your armour or clothes.
Setting your computer's clock back no longer makes you vanish from everyone's screen, leaves the game stuck on "reconnecting", or gets you refused with "token expired" when you enter a new place.
Entering a siege no longer has a rare chance of the server refusing you for good.
When another tab or window takes over your session, the World tab no longer keeps showing the old "Online" count.
Crossing into the next area while the server is updating no longer disconnects you when the game looks for graves.

/block <name> hides everything a player says to you: chat, invites, notes, letters, and trade, duel, wedding, card or journal requests. /unblock <name> undoes it, and /blocked lists who you've blocked.
The block is tied to their account, so a new name or a new character doesn't get around it. It follows you to every device you sign in on.
Click a player's name on any chat line to Report or Block them. A report sends the moderators that line and the lines before it.
/report <name> [reason]: <note> sends everything that player said in your chat, with an optional note for the moderators. Reasons: harassment, hate, sexual, threat, spam, other.
The game server signs every line it relays. A report can only carry words that player really said, so it can't be faked.
/rules shows the Code of Conduct. Everyone agrees to it once, before their first chat line.
Breaking the rules leads to a mute, then longer mutes (30 minutes, a day, a week), then a ban.
Moderators now see every past mute and ban a player has had.
If three established players report someone within an hour, that player is muted for 30 minutes until a moderator looks.
Guest accounts and accounts under 14 days old can post one public channel line every 4 seconds. Party, guild and local chat aren't slowed, and a line sent too soon goes back in your chat box.
/cases lists open reports, /case <name> shows one (the lines, reasons, notes and the AI reviewer's view), and /dismiss <name> closes it. /modhelp lists them.

Under Physical Combat And Armor Overhaul (on by default), a weapon in your left hand no longer rolls a shield block. Dual wielding gives up the shield's block, as intended. An iron off-hand weapon had been blocking like a leather shield, taking 5-8% off the damage a nimble character took. Shields block as before.

Dual wielding in first person: the left-hand weapon is now the exact mirror of the right, in the left fist the way the right weapon sits in the right. Before, it could stand well off, depending on your Morrowind first-person skeleton. Third person is unchanged.
The Dwarven Thunderlock is held like a rifle.

A modified game client could stand huge hordes of enemies around nearby players, and mark every one of them as elite. Your game now refuses more enemies from any one player than an honest game can send, and believes only as many elites, revenants and Greater Giants as honest play produces.

A crafted piece could be listed on the market from a second device's stale tab while your live character still carried it. A crafted piece you list, auction or hand to a commission now leaves your character's own pack (or home) on the realm at the moment it goes up, and one you cancel, or that expires or goes unsold, comes back into your pack as the very piece that left.

Renown, raid rewards, bounty and orc camps, the Watch, silver finds and profession XP now count only for the realm character you are playing on this device. A character another device has taken up, or one whose trading is frozen, earns none until it is yours again. Honest play is unaffected.
Your family's record (Project Legacy) is checked against the family's own rules when it is saved to the realm.
A crafted piece you bought back from another player can be sold again even while the character who made it has its trading frozen.

Master any two weapon skills (Long Blade, Short Blade, Axe, Blunt Weapon, Archery, Hand-to-Hand) and you can choose one of fifteen martial paths, such as the Blademaster, Ranger, Juggernaut, Assassin or Brawler. The choice is permanent, like a mastery.
Each path has a passive of its own (for example the Vanguard's foes hit 10% lighter, and the Woodsman gets fatigue back on every kill) and a signature technique.

The signature technique uses your Weapon Technique key whenever you wield one of the path's two weapons and that weapon has no technique of its own. A path with Archery has a bow form and a melee form, and the two share one cooldown. It works with the loot ladder off, and with the ladder off a looted weapon's own technique sleeps, so the signature takes the key.
Techniques that give you a timed effect (Rallying Cleave, Cyclone, Phantom Strike, Earthsplitter, Savage Whirl) start it as you use them, so every foe the sweep reaches gets it.
You can hold an arcane path and a martial path at once if you master two schools and two weapons.
You choose on the skill screen: W on the classic sheet, or the Martial Specialisation card under Master Skills on the enhanced skin. The game also asks once, the first time a path opens.
A mastered weapon skill past 100 now pays in its own way. Until now it only raised your to-hit, which is capped at 97%.
Axe: up to 80% harder against wounded foes (under half health).
Short Blade: swings up to 40% faster.
Fists now benefit from your bonuses. Firmament fist stars, sets and loot powers never applied to bare-handed blows; now they do. Werewolf claws are unchanged.
Every short blade swings like a dagger. Tanto, Shortsword and Wakizashi were swinging at long-blade speed.

Firmament: every weapon family now has two notables that raise its skill, and Axe and Blunt get a third. Blade Dancer, Iron Knuckles, Headsman and Bonebreaker keep every stat they had and gain the skill on top. The Ritual's *Battlemage's Focus* is now *Templar's Mace*, a mace notable. No star moved, so shared build codes still load.
Opening the Stats page no longer changes your next blows. It used to spend a set's Riposte or Battlemage's Discipline and nudge the rounding of your damage bonuses.
Choosing a specialisation (arcane or martial) now says so in one line that fits the classic screen.

F4 (rebindable, "Cargo" under Come Sail Away) opens the hold of the ship you're on: at the helm, on deck or in the cabin. Away from it, F4 opens the last ship you helmed, or the first ship in your fleet with a hold, wherever it's moored or laid up.
The helm panel has a Hold button, and so does each ship on the Fleet page.

If pirates raid you while you're ashore with your cabin ship and you beat them, the raid now ends. The crews that kept spawning, passive, after the fight are gone, and leftover raiders are removed from the street and from the room you're in.
Ram a ship hard enough and the two ships lock together for 20 seconds. The enemy ship lowers its sails and slows to a crawl, but its guns keep firing.
Each battery can be loaded with round, grape, chain or heated shot. The broadsides share one load; the bow chasers and the stern guns each have their own.

Change the load with the mouse wheel while aiming, with the helm's Shot button, or with the new Shot key (unbound by default, under Combat). Switching unloads a ready battery and reloads it with the new shot.
Gun smoke drifts with the wind. A broadside leaves a bank of smoke that hangs over the fight and drifts downwind. Smoke from a burning or damaged ship trails away from it.
Near misses. A ball passing close to your ship whistles, louder the closer it passes. One landing right beside you throws water over the rail and rocks the deck.
Sinking ships. A ship that sinks while on fire may blow its powder magazine, and every player sees the same blast. Air bubbles up where a ship goes under.
Enemy crew on the card. The target card now shows the enemy's crew, and your broadside's tally says how many crew went down, so you can see grapeshot working.

Within 700 m of a hostile ship, a journey now runs at normal speed. Before, an avoided encounter could carry you past a pirate at up to 60x speed, with the pirate firing at that speed while you couldn't fire back from the Overworld.
Online, sea combat near another player always runs in real time. One player's fast travel or helm time acceleration can no longer speed up enemy ships fighting someone else.

On the Fleet page, Colours opens a flag designer. Pick a shape (flag, swallowtail, pennant or burgee), a field colour with an optional division and second colour, a border, and a device with its own colour.
The flag is real waving cloth at the masthead, in place of the old pennant, sized to the hull. Every player sees it.
Navies use their kingdom's paint and royal ensign: Daggerfall's blue with the dagger, Wayrest's crimson with the rose, Sentinel's gold with the sun.

A ship that surrenders, sinks or is captured lowers its flag. Every player sees the same ship in the same colours. Cloth flags show on ships within 450 m, up to 24 at once. Further away, ships fly the old pennant, and a ship fading in or out of view fades its flag too.
On the Fleet page, Paint lets you choose a colour for each part of your ship:
Painting is free, works wherever the ship is, and every player sees it. Remove paint puts the ship back to its original look.

Ships with a cabin (Small Ship, Large Galley and Carrack) can also choose a wood stain for the cabin in the Paint panel. Walls, floor, beams and built-in furniture all take that stain. It applies the next time you enter the cabin, and the windows light up as before.
On the Fleet page, Deck opens a top-down plan of the deck. On a wide screen a long hull is shown bow to the right, so it's drawn larger.
Fittings stand on the deck in the world and rock with the ship. You can walk around them and climb on them. Every player sees them.

On the Fleet page, Show name puts your ship's name on both sides of the bow: a dark wooden board with the name in gold, in Daggerfall's own lettering, fitted to the curve of the hull just below the rail. Hide name removes it.

You now have a captain level (up to 30). Captain XP comes from sinking and capturing ships, beating off boarders, claiming prizes, finishing contracts, distance sailed, treasure charts, charting isles and selling goods at the exchange.
The Master (left) improves seamanship: speed under sail and oars, turning, cargo, hull, repairs, and better prices at the exchange.
Keystones give a big bonus with a cost (for example, Master of the Wind: +12% speed under sail, -12% under oars). Stars apply to every ship you own. Removing or changing stars is free.

After the shipwright's three refit tiers, each upgrade line now has nine metal tiers: Steel, Silver, Elven, Dwarven, Mithril, Adamantium, Ebony, Orcish and Daedric. Each needs a captain level, from 3 for Steel up to 28 for Daedric.

Each tier needs ingots of its metal, or weapons and plate armour of that metal for the shipwright to melt down. Only plain items are melted: never gear you're wearing, locked or bound gear, quest items, artifacts, player-made, enchanted, conjured, Magic-or-better, Legendary or socketed items. Ingots are used first.
With no enemies near, no ship chasing you, and no boarding or aiming going on, your ship's sails and oars give 15% more speed.
Every port isle in the Eltheric Ocean now sells at least one ordinary trade good alongside its ether goods. Veilhaven sells spice. The sea chart's isle card shows it.

Ship text no longer calls a ship "her" or "she". Messages, buttons, cards and hints across the sea, the Fleet page, the shipyard, the crew hall, the Captain's Stars, the sea chart, the tutorials and the crew's chatter now say "the ship", "this ship" or "it", in plain wording.

Metal refits never melt valuable gear. The shipwright only melts plain items, never ones you're wearing, locked or bound, player-made, enchanted (including your own enchantments), conjured with Create Item, Magic or better, Legendary, or socketed. Ingots still go first, with iron ingots before steel ones for an Iron requirement. A refit you can pay for with steel ingots and steel weapons together is no longer refused.

The Captain's Stars apply to every ship. Accepting stars now updates laid-up and packed ships too, so a ship summoned later no longer uses stars you've since removed. Keystone costs (like Boarders Away's hull penalty or Merchant Prince's gun damage penalty) now apply in combat. Taking a star mid-fight no longer reloads your guns. The Quick Dial key now asks before closing the stars window with unaccepted changes.
The exchange no longer lets you buy a cheap good back at the price you sold it for when your trade stars are maxed.

Other players see the same fight. A ship sinking on another player's screen now plays its sinking sound, and its powder magazine explodes on every screen alike. Chain shot and grapeshot now kill crew on ships another player controls. A rammed ship being boarded keeps its flag up on other players' screens. Ramming a ship another player controls locks it for boarding on every screen.

Combat fixes. The shot wheel steps once per scroll on a trackpad. The tally's crew count matches what the enemy actually loses. A hit on one of your moored ships no longer flashes your helm plate or shakes your camera. Sailing up to a ship that's already sinking no longer replays its sinking or explosion. A ram that sinks a ship no longer tells you to board it. Your hull bar is correct when you take the helm of a different ship.
Name boards no longer show on hidden players' boats or float in the room when you're indoors, and other players see a board shown or hidden right away.
Deck crates no longer disappear from the deck after you've visited several houses.
Another player's cabin shows its original look, not your own ship's stain.

The hold. Taking cargo out of a packed ship's hold no longer counts its weight twice. Putting a packed ship's parts in its own hold no longer loses the ship. A rowboat's plunder can now be opened. F4 no longer opens a ship you can't otherwise reach. The ship's hold can now be bound to a controller button.
The Fleet page no longer says a hold or deck plan opened when it didn't.
The aiming arcs stay visible in a crowded fight full of grapeshot and chain shot.

Smoother frames. No stutter the first time a named or painted ship comes into view. Painted sea ships no longer slow rendering. Deck fittings, near-miss checks, the out-of-combat speed check and damaged-ship smoke are all faster.

Sworn revenants now have ten gear slots: a weapon, a shield, a helm, two pauldrons, a cuirass, gauntlets, greaves, boots and a charm. Open the Companions page (pause menu, Holdings), press Gear on a companion's card, and give it pieces from your pack. Take back returns a piece to your pack.
A revenant's rank limits what it can bear:
A piece you give replaces the one it would have rolled for itself, and its rarity bonuses apply to it.
One revenant in three is born with an art: Mending, Ward, War Cry, Siphon, Barrage or Nova.
Against you, from Rank II (with Enhanced AI):
For you, once sworn, at any rank:
Press Mission on a sworn revenant to send it to any of Tamriel's nine provinces.
Each province has its own danger and its own goods: Skyrim's orichalcum and pelts, Morrowind's ebony and Dwemer metal, Black Marsh's venom.
Up to two revenants can be abroad at once. Recall brings one back at once, empty-handed, and it must rest from the road. The page asks before recalling.

The Athenaeum can be solved again. In most breaches the Orrery's stones could not be turned. The crosshair never named a stone, the count stayed at "Stones true: 0 of 6", and the hall's door never opened. Each stone now answers your crosshair just above its gold ring: look there to turn it forward or back an hour.

Becoming a vampire no longer shuts you out of the Dark Brotherhood or the Thieves Guild. You can only join those two by invitation, and the invitation is never sent twice, so turning used to lock members out until they were cured. Your membership and rank now carry over when you turn, and stay with you if you're cured.
If you're already a vampire and lost the Brotherhood or the Thieves Guild, you get it back, rank and all, the first time the game reads your guilds after this update.

Expelled from a guild, or turned away for your standing? The guild now tells you how to get back in. At its hall, you see your standing, the standing it takes members at, how many quests bring you back there, and how fast it recovers on its own. On the classic look, the guild's refusal when you ask to join says the same.
You can always ask a guild's quest-giver for work as a stranger, even after an expulsion. Each quest done raises your standing with that guild by 5.
A standing below 0 also recovers a point every 7 days of your character's own time. Resting and travelling count, and online so does time logged off.
If the guild also wants skills you don't have yet, it says which. A hall shut for the Season says the guild's halls in other regions still have work.
The Standing page shows the quest count under each guild, temple or knightly order that would turn you away.
Every sworn revenant now has its own star tree, built like the Firmament and the Captain's Stars. Open the Companions page (pause menu, Holdings) and press Stars on a companion's card.
Levels:
The Blade: health and damage. Its keystones are Deathless (+25% health, -10% damage) and Bloodrage (+20% damage, -10% health).
The Road: missions and loyalty.
It uses the same window as the Captain's Stars: click a star to take it and the stars on the way to it, and right-click to remove it. Changes are pending until you press Accept.
Health and damage change at once, and taking a star back takes its health back too.
However many Menders are at your side, together they heal you at most once a minute (every 45 seconds with a fully hasted Grave).
In an Athenaeum, the six riddles that give each Orrery stone its true hour now appear on the HUD, under "Turn the Orrery true."
Each stone shows its name and the hour its hand stands at (*Wayrest - 4*) above it. The labels update after every turn.
Turning a stone from too far away now tells you to "Stand closer to the stone." Before, the turn was silently ignored.

Type /bug in chat to tell the developers about an exploit, a bug or a security problem. On the enhanced skin you can also open the mailbox beside the hourglass in the pause menu and press Report a bug or exploit. Only the developers who read reports can see it. Other players and moderators can't.
Choose what it is, give it a short title, and say what happens and how to make it happen. The form shows what's sent with it (your username and the game's build) before you send.
Your reports are listed under the form, each showing whether a developer has read it and whether it was fixed.
Please keep exploits out of chat, Discord and the Notice Board until they're fixed. (To report another *player*, /report <name> still goes to the moderators.)

From character level 10 and Renown 15, the foes in dungeons and the wilds now keep pace with you. Each level past 10 a foe hits 7% harder and stands 4% tougher. Each Renown past 15 adds 1% to its hits and 0.5% to its health. Both compound, up to level 30 and Renown 50:
Plain foes, champions, elites, revenants and the open zone's foes all answer you, on top of what they already were. The early game is unchanged: nothing moves at or under level 10 and Renown 15.
Towns and buildings, the city watch and your allies.
A foe hits each player at that player's own level. Its health is set by whoever's game built it.

Characters whose trading was still frozen for a week ("The realm's law has held this character three times...") because of the Weir Key are unfrozen. A forged piece a character still carries still holds its trade until it is gone.

Other players no longer float in mid-air for players on an outdated copy of the game. An outdated copy (an old desktop app or a page left open since an update) is now asked to update before it joins the world online: reload the page, or download the latest desktop release.
Not every elite or champion can become a revenant any more. About one in four is marked Unquiet, and its title says so ("Unquiet Elite Orc"). Only a marked foe can rise.
At most three revenants hunt you at once, and no new one rises while three do. None of yours is pushed out to make room.
A revenant comes back after two to four days (it was one to three).
A marked foe breaks and runs at a third of its health, one time in two, as fast as a bolting beast. Most revenants are now born by getting away, not by killing you - however fast you run.
A revenant ranks up every time it gets away from you, or you from it.
When a revenant gets away in the open, it goes to ground in the nearest dungeon and leaves a trail there. The dungeon appears on your map at once.
Leave it alone and its wounds heal: the oldest one every five days. The Revenants page says when the next one will.

A revenant that seeks mastery trains while it waits. It learns to counter whatever weapon or habit you have hurt it with most, such as your blade, your arrows or your footwork, and a card tells you when it has.
The day a revenant comes back to hunt you, you are warned in its own way:
Each rank adds more: +40% health, +15% damage and +3 levels for a class foe. Your sworn revenants keep the old values.
Smoke (people): it throws down smoke and is lost to sight as it runs. A blow still finds it.
When it gets away, the blow that broke it leaves a wound, and the card says which ("It bears the wound you left: Lamed").
Vengeance (the brutal, the zealous, the unhinged): it comes for you sooner, and more often.
A rank-V revenant that gets away once more becomes the Dread. It goes to ground in its lair for good, and every town knows where. Only one Dread waits for you at a time.
Online, another player's revenant that kills you no longer becomes a fourth revenant of yours and pushes one of yours out.
A foe that was running to become a revenant no longer vanishes without a body when you already have three: it turns and fights.
A revenant's blink or sink no longer completes while a window is open over the game.
Another player's monsters can no longer hit you twice as hard by claiming a revenant's signature strike. Only real revenants strike that way.
In dungeons, another player's monsters can only cast spells their own kind knows, and a paralysed one casts nothing.
One player can no longer make every monster near you a champion: at most 17 of theirs count as champions on your screen, more than honest play ever reaches.
A new Growth tab in the pause menu, next to Stats. Everything about how your character grows is in one place:

Level: your attributes, and when you have a level up waiting, where you place your points and press Ascend. On a smaller window it opens full screen. If you leave before pressing Ascend, your points stay unspent and the bonus never re-rolls.
Specialisations: a guide to all thirty paths, fifteen arcane and fifteen martial, including the ones you can't choose yet. Each path shows:
Firmament: the online passive tree, now drawn inside the menu.
Captain's Stars: your ship captain's tree, now drawn inside the menu too.
The Firmament and the Captain's Stars can go full screen with one press. On a phone, each opens over the whole screen.
The page list marks what's waiting: a level up, a specialisation to choose, captain's stars to set. The Stats page's Growth button shows the total.
The Stats page's Ascend and Firmament buttons, the specialisation cards on the Master Skills page and the Captain page's Open the stars now all lead to the Growth tab.
Classic interface: the S (arcane paths) and W (martial paths) rows on the character sheet now show whenever your class can earn a path, and open the same guide.

Clearer descriptions: every specialisation's passive and signature, the level-up screen and the Firmament are reworded in plain terms - for example "deal 20% more damage" instead of "strike 20% harder", "Spend your points" instead of "Choose what rises", "Not enough points." instead of "You lack the points for that." The level-up screen and the Firmament are now translated into every language.

With unsaved star changes, switching page or tab, pressing the character sheet key, the pack key, the QuickDial key, tapping outside the menu or opening a timer's board now asks first, the same way Escape does - and asks again if you change more stars after the first warning. This includes a revenant's stars.
Classic interface: with a level up being spent on the character sheet, the S and W rows no longer open the Growth tab, which could lose the level's bonus points.
The guide no longer shows a path as reachable when your mastery slots can't hold both of its skills (for example two minor schools of magic).
The level-up fanfare plays once per level, not every time you open the Level page.
Enter on a menu tab no longer presses Ascend; typing in the account window no longer moves the sky behind it.
The Brawler's, Bloodmage's and Berserker's descriptions now say exactly what they do.

Your own Disintegrate no longer deletes your revenant. It still breaks through a revenant's last stand and its will, but now it brings the revenant to its knees like any other killing blow. You choose to Kill it (its trophy weapon drops) or Spare it (it joins you as a companion). A revenant already killed this way stays dead.

With two weapons drawn in the Morrowind first-person view, your arms now stand a little wider. Long blades no longer cross over each other in the middle of the screen. How far the arms spread depends on the weapons: a pair of longswords spreads further than a pair of daggers. The arms ease out when you draw and ease back when you sheathe. Third person is unchanged.

In the Morrowind first-person view, the Dwarven Thunderlock no longer rides up over your crosshair when you raise it to shoot. The aimed gun now sits below the middle of the screen, with your left hand still visible on its forend. The lowered idle stance and third person are unchanged.

When your wagon stops, companions riding in the back now climb down over the side, where a player rider would, instead of dropping through the bed and getting stuck inside the wagon. A parked wagon also no longer closes its body around a companion standing where it was laid.
The FPS counter's draw count now includes what a building draws through its windows (view) and the shadow maps (shadow). It also shows whether VSync is off or a Frame Rate Cap is set.

Animated loot piles no longer keep being animated behind the scenes after you leave a room, load a save or a pile is emptied. A pile laid again where it now lies keeps animating instead of standing still.
Putting a helm on or taking it off no longer leaves the old head picture in GPU memory, and a slow load can no longer put back the helm you just took off.
A helm put on while the large HUD is first loading now shows on its head.
Players can fight each other in the PvP zone's dungeons again, as intended. Before, every attack on another player underground was refused. Their blood now shows in the dungeon.

You can now give up your arcane or your martial specialisation for 200,000 gold each. Open the Growth tab in the pause menu, go to Specialisations, open your chosen path, and press Reset. A confirmation shows the price, what you lose, and which paths you can pick afterwards.
Your mastered skills stay mastered. After a reset you can choose any path your masteries unlock, including the same one.
If you bought the path's signature spell, it stays in your spellbook as an ordinary spell.
Online, the price is paid from your coins, then letters of credit, then your bank account. Offline it is paid in coins or letters of credit.
If no other path of that kind could ever open for you, the Reset button explains why instead of charging you.
The specialisation choice boxes now say what a later reset costs instead of "cannot be undone".
A newly chosen specialisation's stat bonuses apply at once instead of at the next magic round.
The Yes/No confirmation in the pause menu now keeps keyboard focus inside the box and answers only once.
When you travel fast in the Overworld, the world no longer spends time building ground you've already passed. Holes in the view and drops to 1x speed on roads with turns are much rarer.

A party member's kill no longer reads "Empty" when it is full. Press it and you open the body like any other: you see what is in it and take what you choose, piece by piece, with Take all, or with Quick Loot.

Taking from a body someone else killed can no longer wipe out their loot. A slow connection used to destroy the pieces in transit; a take now lands exactly once, however late the answer comes, and two players taking the same piece at the same moment get one copy between them - the second hears "Someone took that first."
Anything you put into another player's kill comes back to you when you close the window, even if they left or lost connection while it was open.

A building's cupboards and chests are one shared list for everyone inside. Closing a window no longer brings back an item someone else took, and no longer erases one someone else put in. Two players opening a cupboard at the same moment now see the same contents, and nothing either of them took or put in is lost when the game settles on one.
Taking part of a stack from someone else's cupboard can no longer leave you with a copy when another player took it first.
An item you put into a cupboard that the building's host never accepted (an older game version) comes back to you when you leave.
Take all and Stash all on a cupboard land every piece, however many there are.
A find from a coffin or other search spot is shared by your party the same way a dungeon pile is: one list, one copy of each piece, no matter who closes their window first.
Two separate groups searching the same coffin each loot their own find.
Searching a spot again after its five hours locks it for your whole party again.
Take all on a long dungeon list now always lands every piece. A pile from a newer game version shows its name instead of "Empty".
Putting a stack into a dungeon pile and taking part of it back no longer loses the rest.
Players on an older version of the game still see the old behaviour in the same room; reloading the page brings them onto the new rules.

A boss no longer throws a blow you have no fair way out of. It weighs each attack first and picks another, or moves in, if the attack would leave someone nowhere to stand. This includes the safe havens of a pending CHECK, burning pools from earlier blows, and a duel's ring of fire.
If a boss can't fairly hit someone, for example a player on a balcony, it now turns on the rest of the party for a few seconds instead of walking at them.
Feints no longer glint. A feint that is cut off is cancelled at the right moment on every screen.
A burst of damage that crosses two phase lines now plays both phase turns in order, each with its card.
